For a very small profit, every day we tear their own children out of mothers' arms, and make them take ours in their place; we make them hand over their own to some pitiful nurse, to whom we would not dream of entrusting our own, or to some she-goat, forbidding them not only to give the children suck — whatever danger they may incur by it — but also to take any kind of care of them, so that they may be wholly occupied with the care of and attention to ours. And we see in most of these nurses an adopted affection, more violent than the natural one, springing up by habit towards the foster children, and a greater concern for the preservation of those they have taken charge of than of their own. And what I was saying about goats was on this account: that all around where I live it is common, when country women run short of milk for their own children, to call goats in to help; and I have at this moment two men-servants who never sucked women's milk for more than eight days after they were born. These goats are quickly taught to come and nurse the little children, know their voices when they cry, and come running to them. If anyone else but the foster-child is presented to them, they refuse to let it suck, and the child likewise will refuse to suck another goat. I saw one the other day from which they had taken away the goat that used to nurse it, because the father had only borrowed it from a neighbour; the child would not touch any other they could bring, and died, no doubt of hunger. Beasts can change and corrupt their natural affection as easily as we do: I think there are many mistakes in what Herodotus relates about a certain region of Libya, where, he says, the women are held in common but the child, as soon as it can walk, picks his father out from the crowd, drawn to him first by natural inclination.

Now, considering this simple reason for loving our children — that we have begotten them, and so call them our second selves — it strikes me that there is another kind of offspring that comes from us no less deserving of recognition. For what we engender by the soul, the children of our understanding, of our courage, and of our abilities, springs from nobler parts than those of the body, and is much more our own; in this generation we are both father and mother. These cost us a great deal more and bring us more honour, if there is anything of good in them. As for our other children, their value is far more theirs than ours; the share we have in them is very little. But of these the whole beauty, all the grace and value, is ours, and they also represent us more vividly than the others. Plato adds that these are immortal children, who immortalise and deify their fathers, like Lycurgus, Solon, and Minos. Now, since history is full of examples of the common affection of fathers for their children, it does not seem inappropriate to bring in a few examples of this other kind. Heliodorus, that good bishop of Trikka, chose rather to lose the dignity, the income, and the devotion of so venerable a prelacy than to lose his daughter — a daughter who survives to this day, very graceful and shapely, but perhaps a little too carefully and wantonly dressed up, and too amorous for a clergyman's daughter. There was in Rome a certain Labienus, a man of great worth and authority and, among other qualities, excellent in every branch of literature, who was, I take it, the son of that great Labienus, the chief of Caesar's captains in the Gallic wars, who, afterwards taking Pompey's side, so valiantly held out his cause until he was beaten by Caesar in Spain. This Labienus I am now speaking of had several enemies, envious of his good qualities; and, very likely, the courtiers and favourites of the emperors of his time, who were highly offended at his independence and at the paternal spirit, hostile to tyranny, which he still kept up — with which we may suppose he had tinged his books and writings. His adversaries prosecuted several pieces he had published before the magistrates in Rome, and managed to have them condemned to the fire. It was on him that this new form of punishment was begun, which was later carried on against others at Rome: to punish writings and studies themselves with death. There would not be cruelty and material enough for cruelty, if we did not mix into it things that nature has exempted from all feeling and suffering, such as reputation and the products of the mind — if we did not extend bodily punishment to the teachings and monuments of the Muses. Now, Labienus could not endure this loss, nor outlive his so dear offspring, and so had himself conveyed and shut up alive in the tomb of his ancestors, where he managed to kill and bury himself at the same stroke. It is hard to show a more violent fatherly affection than this. Cassius Severus, a man of great eloquence and his very intimate friend, on seeing the books burned, cried out that by the same sentence they ought to condemn him to the fire as well, since he carried in his memory everything they contained. The same thing happened to Cremutius Cordus, who, being accused of having praised Brutus and Cassius in his books — that filthy, slavish, and corrupt Senate, worthy of a worse master than Tiberius, condemned his writings to the flames. He was willing to keep them company, and killed himself by starvation. The good Lucan, condemned by that scoundrel Nero, at the last gasp of his life, when most of his blood had already run out through the veins of his arms, which he had had his physician open to make him die, and when the cold had taken hold of his extremities and was creeping up towards his vitals, the last thing he had in his memory was some verses of his Pharsalia, which he recited, dying with them on his lips. What was this, but a tender and fatherly farewell to his children, in imitation of the goodbyes and embraces with which we part from ours when we come to die — and an effect of that natural inclination which suggests to our memory, in this last extremity, those things which were dearest to us during the time of our life?

Can we believe that Epicurus — who, as he says himself, dying of the unbearable pain of the stone, had all his consolation in the beauty of the doctrine he was leaving behind him — could have received the same satisfaction from many children, however well-conditioned and brought up, if he had had them, as he did from the production of so many rich writings? Or that, had it been his choice to leave behind him a deformed and dull child or a foolish and ridiculous book, he, or any other man of his understanding, would not rather have chosen to run the first misfortune than the other? It might, perhaps, have been an impiety in Saint Augustine, if, on the one hand, it had been proposed to him to bury his writings, from which religion has received such great fruit, or, on the other, to bury his children (had he had them), if he had not rather chosen to bury his children. And I do not know whether I would not much rather have begotten one perfectly beautiful book through association with the Muses than by lying with my wife. What I give to this, such as it is, I give absolutely and irrevocably, as men do to their bodily children. That little I have done for it is no longer at my own disposal; it may know things that have gone from me, and may hold from me what I have not kept; and which, as from a stranger, I should have to borrow back from it, if I needed it. If I am wiser than my book, it is richer than I. There are few men addicted to poetry who would not be much prouder to be the father of the Aeneid than of the handsomest youth in Rome, and who would not bear the loss of the one much better than the loss of the other. For according to Aristotle, the poet, of all artists, is the fondest of his work. It is hard to believe that Epaminondas, who boasted that, in lieu of any posterity, he was leaving behind two daughters who would one day do their father honour (meaning the two victories he won over the Spartans), would have willingly consented to exchange these for the most beautiful creatures in all Greece; or that Alexander or Caesar ever wished to be deprived of the greatness of their glorious deeds in war, for the convenience of children and heirs, however perfect and accomplished. Indeed, I greatly doubt whether Phidias, or any other excellent sculptor, would be as anxious about the preservation and continuance of his natural children as he would be about a rare statue, which he had brought to perfection by long labour and study according to his art. And as for those furious and disordered passions which have sometimes inflamed fathers towards their own daughters, or mothers towards their own sons, the like is also found in this other kind of parenthood: witness what is told of Pygmalion, who, having made the statue of a woman of singular beauty, fell so passionately in love with this work of his that the gods, in favour of his passion, breathed life into it.
"Tentatum mollescit ebur, positoque rigore, Subsidit digitis."
["The ivory grows soft under his touch and, its hardness gone, yields to his fingers." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, x. 283.]

chapters.title: Of the arms of the Parthians
paragraphs: It is a bad and unmanly custom that the gentlemen of our time have got into, of not putting on their armour until they are at the very point of extreme necessity, and laying it aside again as soon as there is the slightest sign that the danger is over. Plenty of disorders come of this: with everyone scrambling for his arms at the very moment when he should be charging, you have men still buckling their cuirass when their fellows are already being routed. Our ancestors used to give their helmet, lance, and gauntlets to be carried for them, but never took off the rest as long as there was any work to be done. Our troops nowadays are cluttered and made unsightly with the mess of baggage and servants, who can never be away from their masters because they are carrying their armour. Livy says of our nation:
"Intolerantissima laboris corpora vix arma humeris gerebant."
["Bodies most impatient of labour could scarcely bear the weight of their arms on their shoulders." — Livy, x. 28.]
Many nations still go to war, and anciently did, without any defensive arms, or with such as offered very little protection:
"Tegmina queis capitum, raptus de subere cortex."
["Whose head-coverings are bark stripped from the cork-tree." — Aeneid, vii. 742.]

Alexander, the boldest captain who ever lived, very seldom wore armour; and those of our own day who slight it do no great harm to the main concern. For if we sometimes see men killed for lack of armour, there are about as many whom the burden of arms helps to destroy — overloaded, cramped, and bruised by the weight, by a sudden shock, or otherwise. To tell the plain truth, if you look at the weight and thickness of the armour we now use, it seems as if we are aiming only at defending ourselves, and are more weighed down than protected by it. We have all we can do to bear up under its weight, so handcuffed and walled in that we might as well be at odds with our own arms, as if we had no more obligation to defend them than they have to defend us. Tacitus gives an amusing description of the men-at-arms among our ancient Gauls, who were so armed that they could only stand still, with no power to harm or to be harmed, or to get up again once knocked down. Lucullus, seeing certain soldiers of the Medes, who formed the vanguard of Tigranes' army, heavily armed and very awkward, as if in iron prisons, took heart from this and easily defeated them; and it was through these men that he began his charge and his victory. And now that our musketeers are in fashion, I expect some invention will be found to wall us up in for our safety, and bring us into battle in castles, like those the ancients used to load on their elephants.

This attitude is quite different from that of the younger Scipio, who sharply rebuked his soldiers for having planted caltrops under the water, in a ditch by which the men of the town he had under siege might have sallied out against them, saying that those who attacked should think of attacking, not of being afraid; suspecting, with good reason, that this obstacle put in the enemies' way would make his own men less vigilant on guard. He also said to a young man who showed him a fine buckler of which he was very proud, "It is a very fine buckler indeed, but a Roman soldier ought to put more trust in his right hand than in his left."
Now, it is nothing but the lack of being used to it that makes the weight of our armour so unbearable:

"L'usbergo in dosso haveano, et l'elmo in testa, Due di questi guerrier, de' quali io canto; Ne notte o di, d'appoi ch'entraro in questa Stanza, gl'haveano mai messi da canto; Che facile a portar come la vesta Era lor, perche in uso l'havean tanto."

["Two of the warriors of whom I sing had their cuirass on their backs and their helmet on their heads; and never, night or day, since they entered that lodging, had they once laid them aside; those arms, by long practice, had become as light to bear as a garment." — Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, xii. 30.]

The Emperor Caracalla used to march on foot, fully armed, at the head of his army. The Roman infantry always carried not only a helmet, a sword, and a shield (for as to arms, Cicero says, they were so used to having them always on that they were no more trouble to them than their own limbs):
"Arma enim membra militis esse dicunt."

— but also, fifteen days' provisions and a certain number of stakes for fortifying their camp, amounting to sixty pounds in weight. And Marius' soldiers, loaded at the same rate, were trained to march in battle order five leagues in five hours, and sometimes, when the situation called for it, six.

Their military discipline was much harsher than ours, and accordingly produced much greater effects. The younger Scipio, reforming his army in Spain, ordered his soldiers to eat standing, and nothing that was cooked. The joke made at the expense of a Spartan soldier is wonderfully to the point here: he was on a campaign and was reproached for having been seen under the roof of a house. They were so accustomed to hardship that, whatever the weather, it was a shame to be seen under any cover other than the sky. We would not march our people very far at that rate.

As for the rest, Marcellinus, a man brought up in the Roman wars, gives a careful account of the way the Parthians armed themselves, all the more interesting because so different from the Roman way. "They had," he says, "armour so woven that all the scales lay over one another like so many little feathers, in no way hindering the body's motion, and yet of such resistance that our darts hitting on it bounced off" (these were the coats of mail our forefathers were so constantly wont to use). And in another place: "they had," he says, "strong and capable horses, covered with thick tanned hides of leather, and were themselves armed from head to foot with great plates of iron, so skilfully arranged that, in every part of the limbs which required bending, they bent with the motion. You would have said they were men of iron; with armour for the head so neatly fitted, and so naturally representing the form of a face, that they were nowhere vulnerable except at two little round holes, which let in some little light corresponding to their eyes, and certain small chinks about their nostrils, through which they breathed with great difficulty."

"Flexilis inductis animatur lamina membris, Horribilis visu; credas simulacra moveri Ferrea, cognatoque viros spirare metallo. Par vestitus equis: ferrata fronte minantur, Ferratosque movent, securi vulneris, armos."

["Plates of steel are laid over the body, so flexible that, dreadful to behold, you would think these not living men but moving images. The horses are armed alike, and, secure from wounds, move their iron shoulders." — Claudian, In Rufinum, ii. 358.]

This is a description fairly close to that of the men-at-arms in France, with their barded horses. Plutarch says that Demetrius had two complete suits of armour made for himself and for Alcimus, a captain of the highest reputation and authority around him, each of one hundred and twenty pounds in weight, whereas the ordinary suits weighed only half as much.

chapters.title: Of books
paragraphs: I have no doubt that I often happen to speak of things that are handled much better, and more truthfully, by those who are masters of the trade. What you have here is purely an essay of my natural parts, not of those acquired by study; and whoever catches me tripping in ignorance will get no advantage over me, for I would be very unwilling to be answerable to anyone else for my writings, since I am not answerable to myself, nor satisfied with them. Whoever goes hunting after knowledge, let him fish for it where it is to be found; there is nothing I so little profess. These are fancies of my own, by which I do not pretend to discover things but to lay myself open; they may, one day, be known to me, or may have been once, depending on whether fortune brought me to the place where they were explained — but I have utterly forgotten it. If I am a man of some reading, I am a man of no retention. So I can promise no certainty beyond making known to what point the knowledge I now have has risen. Therefore let no one lay weight on the matter I write, but on my method of writing it. Let them observe, in what I borrow, whether I have known how to choose what suits to lift or help the invention, which is always my own. For I make others say for me, not before but after me, what — for want of either language or sense — I cannot myself express so well. I do not count my borrowings; I weigh them. If I had wanted to raise their value by number I would have made them twice as many. They are nearly all from such famous and ancient authors that they seem, I think, to identify themselves without my having to do the work. In reasons, comparisons, and arguments, if I transplant any into my own soil and mingle them with my own, I deliberately hide the author, to keep in check the recklessness of those snap critics who fall on every kind of writing, particularly the recent ones, by men still living, and in the common tongue, which puts everyone in a position to criticise and seems to convict the conception and design of being vulgar too. I want them to give Plutarch a flick on the nose, and to rail at Seneca when they think they are railing at me. I have to shelter my own weakness under these great reputations. I will love anyone who can strip my plumage from me — that is, by clearness of understanding and judgment, and purely by distinguishing the force and beauty of the words. For I, who for lack of memory am at every turn unable to pick them out by their national livery, am nevertheless wise enough to know, by the measure of my own abilities, that my soil is incapable of producing any of those rich flowers I find growing there, and that all the fruits of my own growth are not worth one of them. For this much, indeed, I hold myself responsible: if I get in my own way; if there is any vanity or defect in my writings that I do not myself perceive nor can recognise when pointed out by another. Many faults escape our eye, but the weakness of judgment consists in being unable to see them once another lays them open. Knowledge and truth can be in us without judgment, and judgment without them; but the confession of ignorance is one of the finest and surest signs of judgment that I know. I have no other officer to put my writings in rank and file, only chance. As things come into my head, I heap them one on top of another; sometimes they advance in whole bodies, sometimes in single file. I would have everyone see my natural and ordinary pace, irregular as it is; I let myself jog on at my own rate. Nor are these subjects in which one is forbidden to be ignorant, or to speak of casually and at random. I could wish for a more complete knowledge of things, but I will not pay for it at the price it costs. My plan is to pass over the remainder of my life easily, not laboriously; there is nothing I will rack my brains about, not even knowledge, however valuable.
In reading books, I seek only to please myself by an honest diversion; or, if I study, it is for no other science than what treats of knowing myself and instructs me how to die and how to live well.
"Has meus ad metas sudet oportet equus."
["My horse must sweat to keep my pace." — Propertius, iv.]

I do not bite my nails over the difficulties I meet with in my reading; after a charge or two, I give them up. If I kept at them, I would lose both myself and time, for I have an impatient understanding that has to be satisfied at first attempt: what I do not grasp at once is only made more obscure by persistence. I do nothing without good cheer; continuation and a too obstinate effort darken, stupefy, and tire my judgment. My sight is confounded and dispersed by staring; I have to withdraw it and refer my discovery to fresh attempts — just as, to judge of the lustre of scarlet rightly, we are taught to pass the eye lightly over it and then to run it across again in several sudden and repeated glances. If one book does not please me, I take another; and I never touch any of them except when I am tired of doing nothing. I do not much care for new ones, because the old ones seem fuller and stronger; nor do I converse much with Greek authors, because my judgment cannot do its work on imperfect comprehension of the material.

Among books that are simply pleasant, of the moderns, Boccaccio's Decameron, Rabelais, and the Basia of Johannes Secundus (if those can be classed under that heading) are worth reading for amusement. As for the Amadis and that kind of stuff, they did not have enough credit to arrest even my childhood. And I will say further, whether boldly or rashly, that this old, heavy soul of mine is no longer tickled by Ariosto, no, not even by the worthy Ovid; his facility and inventions, which once ravished me, are now no longer to my taste, and I can hardly have the patience to read him. I speak my opinion freely about everything, even about things that perhaps exceed my capacity and that I do not consider in any way under my jurisdiction. Accordingly, the judgment I deliver is meant to show the measure of my own sight, not of the things I am so bold as to criticise. When I find myself put off by Plato's Axiochus, as by a work — with all due respect to such an author — without force, my judgment does not believe itself: it is not so arrogant as to set itself against the authority of so many other famous judgments of antiquity, which it considers its tutors and masters, and with whom it is rather content to err. In such a case, it condemns itself either to stop at the outer bark, being unable to penetrate to the heart, or to consider the work by some false light. It is content with only sparing itself trouble and confusion; as to its own weakness, it frankly acknowledges and confesses it. It thinks it gives a just interpretation to the appearances presented to it by its own conceptions, but they are weak and imperfect. Most of Aesop's fables have several senses and meanings, of which the mythologists chose some one that fits the fable; but for the most part, this is only the first face that presents itself, and a superficial one; there still remain others, more vivid, essential, and profound, into which they have not been able to penetrate. And so it is with me.

But to keep to the business of this essay: I have always thought that, in poetry, Virgil, Lucretius, Catullus, and Horace by many degrees outshine the rest; and especially Virgil in his Georgics, which I take to be the most accomplished piece in poetry — by comparison with which one can easily see that there are some places in his Aeneid to which the author would have given a little more of the file, had he had leisure; and the fifth book of his Aeneid seems to me the most perfect. I also love Lucan, and willingly read him, not so much for his style as for his own worth, and for the truth and solidity of his opinions and judgments. As for good Terence — the refined elegance and grace of the Latin tongue — I find him admirable in his vivid depiction of our manners and the movements of the soul; our own actions throw me back upon him at every turn, and I cannot read him so often that I do not still find some new grace and beauty. Those who lived near Virgil's time complained that some compared Lucretius with him. I am of the opinion that the comparison is, in truth, very unequal — though I have a hard time convincing myself of it when I come across some excellent passage in Lucretius. But if they were so angry at that comparison, what would they say to the brutish, barbarous stupidity of those who, nowadays, compare him with Ariosto? Would not Ariosto himself say:
"O seclum insipiens et inficetum!"
["O stupid and tasteless age." — Catullus, xliii. 8.]

I think the ancients had more reason to be angry at those who compared Plautus with Terence, though that comparison was much closer than the one between Lucretius and Virgil. It counts for the estimation and preference of Terence that the father of Roman eloquence has him so often, and alone of his class, on his lips — and the opinion the best judge of Roman poets passed on his companion. I have often noticed that those of our day who take it upon themselves to write comedies (in imitation of the Italians, who are happy enough in that line) take three or four plots from Plautus or Terence to make one of their own, and crowd five or six of Boccaccio's novellas into a single comedy. What makes them load themselves with so much material is the lack of confidence they have in their own ability to support themselves on their own strength. They have to find something to lean on; and not having stuff of their own to entertain us with, they bring in the story to make up for the want of language. With my author, it is quite the other way: the elegance and perfection of his speech makes us lose our appetite for his plot; his refined grace and elegance of style occupy us everywhere; he is so pleasant throughout —
"Liquidus, puroque simillimus amni,"
["Clear and most like a pure river." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2, 120.]

and so possesses the soul with his graces that we forget those of his story. This same consideration carries me further: I notice that the best of the ancient poets avoided affectation and the hunt after, not only fantastic Spanish and Petrarchan flights, but even those softer and gentler touches that are the ornament of all subsequent poetry. And yet there is no sound judgment that will condemn this in the ancients, and that does not incomparably more admire the even polish and that perpetual sweetness and flourishing beauty of Catullus's epigrams, than all the stings with which Martial arms the tails of his. The reason is the one I gave before, and as Martial himself says of himself:
"Minus illi ingenio laborandum fuit, in cujus locum materia successerat:"
["His wit had less work to do, because the subject itself supplied what was needed." — Martial, praef. ad lib. viii.]

The first sort, without being moved, without getting angry, make themselves sufficiently felt; they have laughter enough throughout, without having to tickle themselves; the others need outside assistance. The less wit they have, the more body they need; they get on horseback because they cannot stand on their own legs. Just as in our balls, those mean fellows who teach dancing, unable to represent the bearing and dignity of our nobility, are reduced to throwing themselves forward with dangerous leaps and other strange motions and tumblers' tricks; and the ladies are less troubled in dances where there are various coupees, changes, and quick body-movements, than in some other, more sedate kind, where they only have to move at a natural pace and represent their ordinary grace and presence. So I have seen good comic actors who, in their everyday clothes and with the same face they always wear, give us all the pleasure of their art, while their apprentices, not yet arrived at such a pitch, are obliged to plaster their faces, put on absurd disguises, and make a hundred grotesque grimaces to give us something to laugh at. This idea of mine is nowhere more demonstrable than in comparing the Aeneid with Orlando Furioso: the first, by dint of wing, flies in a brave and lofty place and always keeps to his point; the latter, fluttering and hopping from tale to tale, as from branch to branch, daring to trust his wings only in very short flights, perching at every turn lest his breath and strength fail him.
"Excursusque breves tentat."
["And he attempts short excursions." — Virgil, Georgics, iv. 194.]
These, then, as to this sort of subject, are the authors who please me best.

As to the rest of my reading, which mixes a little more profit with the pleasure, and through which I learn how to order my opinions and conduct, the books that serve me to this purpose are Plutarch (since he was translated into French) and Seneca. Both have this notable convenience suited to my temperament, that the knowledge I seek there is set out in loose pieces, not requiring long stretches of reading, of which I am incapable. Such are the minor works of the first and the Epistles of the second, which are the best and most profitable of all their writings. It is no great undertaking to pick one of them up, and I leave off at pleasure, for there is no sequence or dependence between the pieces. These authors for the most part agree in useful and true opinions; and there is this parallel between them — that fortune brought them into the world around the same century, that they were both tutors to two Roman emperors, both fetched from foreign countries, both rich, both great men. Their instruction is the cream of philosophy, delivered in a plain and pertinent way. Plutarch is more uniform and steady; Seneca more various and shifting: the latter toiled and bent his whole strength to fortify virtue against weakness, fear, and vicious appetites; the former seems more to slight their power, and disdains to alter his pace or stand on his guard. Plutarch's opinions are Platonic, gentle, accommodated to civil society; the other's are Stoic and Epicurean, further from common use, but in my opinion more personally serviceable and more firm. Seneca seems to lean a little toward the tyranny of the emperors of his time — but only seems; for I take it as certain that he speaks against his own judgment when he condemns the act of the generous murderers of Caesar. Plutarch is frank throughout; Seneca abounds in lively touches and sallies; Plutarch in things that warm and move you more; this one contents and pays you better — he guides us, the other pushes us on.

As to Cicero, his works most useful to my purpose are those that treat of manners and the rules of our life. But to confess the truth boldly (since one has crossed the barriers of impudence, there is no holding back), his way of writing strikes me as careless and uninviting; his prefaces, definitions, divisions, and etymologies take up most of his work, and whatever there is of life and marrow is smothered and lost in the long preparation. When I have spent an hour reading him — which is a great deal for me — and try to recollect what juice and substance I have extracted, for the most part I find nothing but wind. He has not yet come to the arguments that serve his purpose, nor to the reasons that properly help to form the knot I am after. For me, who only want to become wiser, not more learned or eloquent, these logical and Aristotelian arrangements of parts are of no use. I would have a man start with the main proposition. I know well enough what death and pleasure are; let no one go to the trouble of dissecting them for me. I look for good, solid reasons, at the first stroke, to teach me how to stand their shock — for which neither grammatical subtleties nor the quaint texture of words and arguments are of any use at all. I am for discourses that drive the first charge into the heart of the redoubt; his languish about the subject. They are well enough for the schools, the bar, and the pulpit, where we have leisure to nod and may wake up a quarter of an hour later in time to find the thread of the discourse again. One must speak this way to judges, whom one means to win over by right or wrong, to children and the common people, to whom one must say everything and see what comes of it. I would not have an author make it his business to render me attentive, or cry "Oyez!" fifty times, as the heralds do. The Romans in their religious exercises began with Hoc age, as we in ours do with Sursum corda; these are so many words wasted on me — I come fully prepared from my chamber. I need no allurement, no invitation, no sauce; I eat the meat raw, so that, instead of whetting my appetite, these preparations tire and dull it. Will the licence of the times excuse my sacrilegious boldness if I find even Plato's dialogues themselves dull and heavy, smothering the matter too much, and lament so much time lost by a man who had so many better things to say, in so many long and needless preliminary exchanges? My ignorance excuses me better here, in that I do not know Greek well enough to discern the beauty of his language. I generally choose books that use sciences, not those that only lead to them. The two first, and Pliny, and their like, have none of this Hoc age; they want to deal with men already instructed; or if they do offer it, it is a substantial Hoc age, with a body of its own. I also delight in reading the Letters to Atticus, not only because they contain a great deal of the history and affairs of his time, but much more because in them I uncover much of his own private temper; for I have a singular curiosity, as I have said elsewhere, to pry into the souls and the natural, true opinions of the authors with whom I converse. One may judge their parts, but not their manners or themselves, by the writings they display on the theatre of the world. I have a thousand times lamented the loss of the treatise Brutus wrote on Virtue, for it is well to learn the theory from those who best know the practice.

But since the matter preached and the preacher are different things, I would as gladly see Brutus in Plutarch as in a book of his own. I would rather be certainly informed of the conversation he had in his tent with some particular friends of his the night before a battle, than of the harangue he made to his army the next day; and of what he did in his study and chamber, than of what he did in the public square and in the senate. As to Cicero, I am of the common opinion that, learning aside, he had no great natural excellence. He was a good citizen, of an affable nature, as all fat, heavy men such as he was usually are; but given to ease, and had in truth a mighty share of vanity and ambition. Nor do I know how to excuse him for thinking his poetry fit to be published; it is no great fault to make bad verses, but it is a fault not to be able to judge how unworthy his verses were of the glory of his name. As for his eloquence, that is wholly beyond comparison, and I believe it will never be equalled. The younger Cicero, who resembled his father in nothing but the name, was once commanding in Asia, and had several strangers at his table, with Cestius seated at the lower end, as people often intrude at the open tables of the great. Cicero asked one of his people who that man was, who promptly told him the name; but he, as one whose thoughts were taken up with something else and who had forgotten the answer given him, asked the same question three or four times over. The fellow, to deliver himself from so many answers and to make him remember the man by some particular detail, said, "It is that Cestius, of whom you were told that he makes no great account of your father's eloquence in comparison with his own." At which Cicero, suddenly stung, ordered poor Cestius to be seized at once, and had him very well whipped in his own presence — a very discourteous host! Yet even among those who, all things considered, have reputed his eloquence incomparable, there have been some who have not hesitated to note some faults in it: as that great Brutus, his friend, for example, who said it was a broken and feeble eloquence, fractam et elumbem. The orators nearest to the age in which he lived also reproached him for the care he took with a certain long cadence in his periods, and particularly noticed his repeated use of the words esse videatur. For my part, I prefer a shorter style, that comes off more roundly. He does sometimes shuffle his parts more briskly together, but very seldom. I have myself noted this one passage:
"Ego vero me minus diu senem mallem, quam esse senem, antequam essem."
["I would rather be old for a short time than be old before I was old." — Cicero, De Senect., c. 10.]
The historians are my right ball, for they are pleasant and easy, and in them man in general — the knowledge of whom I hunt after — appears more vividly and whole than anywhere else:
[The easiest of my amusements — the right ball at tennis being the one that, coming to the player from the right hand, is much easier to play. — Coste.]

the variety and truth of his inner qualities, both in bulk and piecemeal; the diversity of means by which he is held together and knit; and the accidents that threaten him. Now those who write lives, because they insist more on counsels than on events, more on what comes out from within than on what happens without, are the most suitable for my reading; and so, above all others, Plutarch is the man for me. I am very sorry we do not have a dozen Laertiuses, or that he was not more extended; for I am equally curious to know the lives and fortunes of these great instructors of the world as to know the varieties of their doctrines and opinions. In this kind of study of histories, one must tumble over, without distinction, all sorts of authors — old and new, French or foreign — to learn the matters they variously treat. But Caesar, in my opinion, particularly deserves to be studied, not only for the knowledge of the history but for himself, so great is his excellence and perfection over all the rest, though Sallust is one of the number. In earnest, I read this author with more reverence and respect than is usually allowed to human writings: now considering him in his person, by his actions and his miraculous greatness; now in the purity and inimitable polish of his language, in which he excels not only all other historians, as Cicero confesses, but, perhaps, Cicero himself. He speaks of his enemies with so much sincerity in his judgment that — apart from the false colours with which he tries to gloss over his evil cause, and the filth of his pestilent ambition — I think there is no fault to be objected to him, save this: that he speaks too sparingly of himself, seeing that so many great things could not have been accomplished under his conduct without his own personal acts having had a greater share than he attributes to them.

I love historians, whether of the simple sort or of the higher order. The simple, who have nothing of their own to mix in and only make it their business to collect everything that comes to their knowledge and to record all things faithfully, without choice or discrimination, leave us the whole judgment of discerning the truth. Such, for example, is honest Froissart, who has proceeded in his work with such frank plainness that, having committed an error, he is not ashamed to confess and correct it where the finger has been laid; he even reports for us the variety of rumours that were going around and the different accounts given to him. This is the naked and unformed matter of history, of which everyone may make his profit according to his understanding. The more excellent sort of historians have judgment to pick out what is most worthy of being known and, of two reports, to examine which is most likely true; from the condition of princes and their tempers they deduce their counsels, and assign them words appropriate to the occasion. Such have title to claim the authority of regulating our belief by what they themselves believe; but certainly this privilege belongs to very few. As for the middle sort, of which most are, they spoil everything; they want to chew our meat for us; they take it upon themselves to judge of, and consequently to incline, the history to their own fancy. For if the judgment leans one way, one cannot avoid wresting and twisting the narrative to that bias. They undertake to select things worthy of being known, and yet often hide from us such a word, such a private action, as would much better instruct us; they omit, as incredible, things they do not understand, and some, perhaps, because they cannot put them into good French or Latin. Let them display their eloquence and intelligence, and judge according to their own fancy; but let them also leave us something to judge of after them, and neither alter nor disguise, by their abridgments and choices, anything of the substance of the matter, but deliver it to us pure and entire in all its dimensions.

For the most part, and especially in these recent ages, people are picked out for this work from among the common sort on the sole consideration of well-speaking, as if we were to learn grammar from them; and the men so chosen have fair reason — being hired for nothing else, and pretending to nothing but babble — not to be very concerned with anything but that, so that, with a fine jingle of words, they prepare for us a pretty piece of reports they pick up in the streets. The only good histories are those written by men who held command in the affairs they write about, or who took part in conducting them, or at least had the conduct of others of the same kind. Such are almost all the Greek and Roman histories: for, several eyewitnesses having written on the same subject, in a time when grandeur and learning commonly met in the same person, if any error has crept in it must of necessity be a very slight one, and on a very doubtful incident. What can one expect from a physician writing of war, or from a mere scholar treating of the designs of princes? If we wanted to note how scrupulous the Romans were in this matter, only one example would be needed: Asinius Pollio found in the histories of Caesar himself something misreported — a mistake caused either by Caesar's inability to have his eye in every part of his army at once, having credited certain individuals who had given him an inaccurate account, or by his not having had a sufficiently exact account from his lieutenants of what they had done in his absence. From this we may see how delicate the search for truth is, when one cannot trust the report of a battle from the knowledge of the man who commanded there, nor from the soldiers who were engaged in it, unless, after the method of a judicial enquiry, the witnesses are confronted and objections weighed on each least detail of every incident. In good earnest, the knowledge we have of our own affairs is much more obscure; but this has been sufficiently dealt with by Bodin, and according to my own view. To support a little the weakness of my memory (which is so extreme that more than once I have happened to pick up books again as new and unseen, that I had carefully read a few years before and scribbled over with my notes), I have lately adopted the custom of noting at the end of every book (that is, of those I never intend to read again) the time when I finished it and the judgment I had formed of it, so that this might at least represent to me the character and general idea I had conceived of the author in reading it; and I will copy out some of those notes here.

I wrote this, some ten years ago, in my Guicciardini (whatever language my books speak to me in, I always speak to them in my own): "He is a diligent historian, from whom, in my opinion, one may learn the truth of the affairs of his time as exactly as from any other; in most of which he was himself a personal actor, and in honourable command. There is no sign that he disguised anything out of hatred, favour, or vanity; of which the free verdicts he passes on the great ones, especially those by whom he was promoted and employed in offices of great trust and honour, like Pope Clement VII, give ample testimony. As for the part he thinks himself best at — namely, his digressions and discourses — he has some very good ones, enriched with fine touches; but he is too fond of them. For, leaving nothing unsaid, with a subject so full, ample, almost infinite, he degenerates into pedantry and smacks a little of scholastic prattle. I have also noticed this in him: that of so many souls and so many effects, so many motives and so many counsels as he judges, he never attributes any one to virtue, religion, or conscience — as if all these were utterly extinct in the world. Of all the actions, however brave they appear in outward show, he always traces the cause and motive to some vicious occasion or some prospect of profit. It is impossible to think that, among such an infinite number of actions as he mentions, there should not be some produced by way of honest reason. No corruption could so universally have infected men that some would not escape the contagion; which makes me suspect that his own taste was vicious, from which it may have happened that he judged other men by himself."

In my Philippe de Commines is written: "You will find the language here sweet and pleasant, with a natural simplicity; the narration pure, with the good faith of the author conspicuous throughout — free from vanity when he speaks of himself, and from partiality or envy when he speaks of others; his discourses and exhortations accompanied rather by zeal and truth than by any exquisite ability; and, throughout, authority and gravity that bespeak a man of good extraction, brought up in great affairs."

On the Memoirs of Monsieur du Bellay I have this: "It is always pleasant to read things written by those who have experienced how they should be conducted; but it cannot be denied that there is a manifest falling-off in these two lords from the freedom and liberty of writing that shine in the earlier historians — such as the Sieur de Joinville, the familiar companion of St Louis; Eginhard, chancellor to Charlemagne; and, more recently, Philippe de Commines. What we have here is rather an apology for King Francis, against the Emperor Charles V, than history. I will not believe that they falsified anything as to matter of fact; but they make a common practice of twisting the judgment of events, often against reason, to our advantage, and of leaving out whatever is ticklish to handle in their master's life — witness the affairs of Messieurs de Montmorency and de Biron, which are omitted here; even the very name of Madame d'Étampes is not to be found. Secret actions a historian may keep quiet; but to pass over in silence what all the world knows, and things that have drawn after them public and momentous consequences, is an inexcusable defect. In short, whoever wants a thorough knowledge of King Francis and the events of his reign, let him seek it elsewhere, if my advice prevails. The only profit one can reap from these Memoirs is in the particular accounts of the battles and other exploits of war in which these gentlemen were personally engaged; in some words and private actions of the princes of their time; and in the treaties and negotiations carried out by the Seigneur de Langey, where there are things everywhere worth knowing, and discourses above the common strain."

chapters.title: Of cruelty
paragraphs: I take virtue to be something other, and something nobler, than good nature and the mere leaning toward goodness we are born into the world with. Well-disposed and well-descended souls do indeed follow the same paths, and present in their actions the same face that virtue itself does; but the word virtue carries with it, I don't quite know what, more great and active than just letting oneself be gently and quietly drawn, by a happy disposition, into the rule of reason. The man who, by a natural sweetness and easiness of nature, would shrug off injuries received, would no doubt do a very fine and praiseworthy thing; but the man who, provoked and stung to the quick by some offence, fortifies himself with the arms of reason against the furious appetite for revenge, and, after a great struggle, masters his own passion, certainly does a great deal more. The first does well; the second virtuously. One action might be called goodness, the other virtue; for, to my mind, the very name of virtue presupposes difficulty and contention, and cannot be exercised without an opponent. It is for this reason, perhaps, that we call God good, mighty, generous, and just, but we do not call Him virtuous, since all His operations are natural and without effort. It has been the opinion of many philosophers, not only Stoics but Epicureans — and this addition —

[Montaigne stops here to make his excuse for naming the Epicureans alongside the Stoics, in conformity with the common opinion that the Epicureans were not so rigid in their morals as the Stoics — which is not true in the main, as he demonstrates at a stroke. This involved Montaigne in a tedious parenthesis, during which the reader had best stay attentive, so as not to lose the thread of the argument entirely. In some later editions of this author it has been tried to remedy this inconvenience, but without noticing that Montaigne's argument is made weaker and more obscure by such vain repetitions: it is a licence that ought not to be taken, because whoever publishes another man's work ought to give it as the other composed it. In Mr Cotton's translation, however, he was so puzzled by this enormous parenthesis that he left it out altogether. — Coste.]

I am borrowing here from the common opinion, which is false — for all the witty remark of Arcesilaus in answer to someone who, reproached that many students went from his school to that of Epicurus but never any from Epicurus to him, replied, "I quite believe it; plenty of capons are made out of cocks, but never any cocks out of capons." For, in truth, the Epicurean sect is in no way inferior to the Stoic in steadiness and in the rigour of its opinions and precepts. And a certain Stoic, showing more honesty than those disputants who, in order to pick a quarrel with Epicurus and throw the game into their own hands, made him say things he never thought — putting a wrong construction on his words, dressing his sentences, by strict grammar, in another meaning and a different opinion from what they knew he held in his mind and in his morals — that Stoic, I say, declared that he abandoned the Epicurean sect among other reasons because he found their road too lofty and inaccessible;
["And those are called lovers of pleasure, who are in effect lovers of honour and justice, and who cultivate and observe all the virtues." — Cicero, Ep. Fam., xv. 1, 19.]

These philosophers say that it is not enough to have the soul seated in a good place, of a good temper, and well disposed toward virtue; it is not enough to have our resolutions and our reasoning fixed above all the power of fortune; we must also seek out occasions to put them to the proof. They would seek pain, hardship, and contempt to contend with, to keep the soul in breath:
"Multum sibi adjicit virtus lacessita."
["Virtue when assailed adds much to its own strength." — Seneca, Ep., 13.]

This is one of the reasons why Epaminondas, who belonged to yet a third sect, refused the riches fortune offered him by very lawful means — because, he said, he had to contend with poverty; in which extreme he kept himself to the last. Socrates put himself, I think, to a still harder test, keeping for his exercise a confounded scolding wife — a sparring partner with sharp blades. Metellus, alone of all the Roman senators, having attempted, by the power of virtue, to withstand the violence of Saturninus, tribune of the people at Rome, who was bent on passing an unjust law in favour of the commons — and, by so doing, having incurred the capital penalties Saturninus had set against the dissenters — addressed those who, in this extremity, were leading him to execution with words to this effect: that it was too easy and too base to do ill; and that to do well where there was no danger was a common thing; but that to do well where there was danger was the proper office of a man of virtue. Metellus's words show very clearly what I want to make out: that virtue refuses ease for a companion; that the easy, smooth, downhill way along which the regular steps of a sweet disposition are conducted is not the way of true virtue; she demands a rough and stormy passage. She wants either outward difficulties to wrestle with — like Metellus's, by means of which fortune delights to interrupt the speed of her career — or inward difficulties, brought on by the disordered appetites and imperfections of our condition to disturb her.

I have come this far at my ease; but here it comes into my head that, by this rule, the soul of Socrates — the most perfect that ever came to my knowledge — would deserve very little recommendation; for I cannot conceive in that person any movement at all of vicious inclination. I cannot imagine there could have been any difficulty or constraint in the course of his virtue. I know his reason to be so powerful and sovereign over him that she would never have allowed a vicious appetite so much as to stir in him. To a virtue so elevated as his, I have nothing to oppose. I think I see him march with a victorious and triumphant step, in pomp and at his ease, without opposition or trouble. If virtue can only shine bright by the conflict of contrary appetites, are we to say she cannot subsist without the assistance of vice, and that it is to vice she owes her reputation and honour? What then would become of that brave and generous Epicurean pleasure that prides itself on cherishing virtue tenderly in its lap, and letting it play and frolic there, giving it for toys shame, fevers, poverty, death, and torments? If I suppose that a perfect virtue shows itself in contending, in patiently enduring pain, and bearing the utmost extremity of the gout without being moved from her seat; if I give her troubles and difficulty for her necessary objects — what will become of a virtue elevated to such a degree as not only to despise pain but to rejoice in it, and be tickled by the throes of a sharp colic, such as the Epicureans set up, and of which many of them, in their actions, have given the clearest proof? As have several others, who I find to have surpassed in deed even the very rules of their discipline. Witness the younger Cato: when I see him die, tearing out his own bowels, I am not satisfied to believe simply that his soul was at that moment wholly free from trouble and horror; I cannot think he merely kept himself in the steadiness the Stoic rules prescribed for him — temperate, without emotion, undisturbed. There was, I think, something in this man's virtue too lively and fresh to stop there. I believe that, without doubt, he felt a pleasure and a delight in so noble an action, and was more pleased in it than in any other of his life:
"Sic abiit a vita, ut causam moriendi nactum se esse gauderet."
["He so departed from life, rejoicing that a reason for dying had been given him." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 30.]

I believe it so thoroughly that I question whether he would have been content to be deprived of the occasion of so brave an exploit; and if the goodness that made him embrace the public cause more than his own did not hold me back, I should easily fall into the opinion that he held himself obliged to fortune for having put his virtue to so brave a trial, and for having favoured that thief in trampling underfoot the ancient liberty of his country. I think I read in this action I know not what exaltation in his soul, and an extraordinary, manly stirring of pleasure, when he looked on the generosity and height of his enterprise:
"Deliberata morte ferocior,"
["The more fierce for having resolved on death." — Horace, Od., i. 37, 29.]

not goaded by any hope of glory, as the vulgar and effeminate judgments of some have concluded (for that consideration was too mean and low to take hold of so generous, so haughty, and so determined a heart as his), but for the very beauty of the thing in itself, which he, who had the handling of the springs, saw more clearly and in its full perfection than we are able to. Philosophy has obliged me by deciding that so brave an action would have been out of place in any other life than Cato's, and that it belonged only to his to end so. Nevertheless, and according to reason, he commanded his son and the senators who accompanied him to take another course in their affairs:

"Catoni, quum incredibilem natura tribuisset gravitatem, eamque ipse perpetua constantia roboravisset, semperque in proposito consilio permansisset, moriendum potius, quam tyranni vultus aspiciendus, erat."

["Cato, whom nature had endowed with an incredible gravity, which he had fortified by perpetual constancy, ever remaining of his predetermined resolve, had rather to die than to look on the face of a tyrant." — Cicero, De Off., i. 31.]

Every death ought to hold proportion with the life that went before it; we do not become other people for dying. I always interpret the death by the preceding life; and if anyone tells me of a death strong and steady in appearance attached to a feeble life, I conclude it was produced by some feeble cause and was of a piece with the life before. Then is not the easiness of his death, and the facility of dying that he had acquired by the vigour of his soul, something to be reckoned to him? Are we to say it should take anything from the lustre of his virtue? And who, with the least tincture of true philosophy in his brain, can be content to imagine Socrates only as free from fear and passion in the affair of his prison, his fetters, and his condemnation — and not discover in him not just firmness and constancy (which was his ordinary state), but, on top of that, I do not know what new satisfaction, a frolic cheerfulness in his last words and actions? In the start he gave at the pleasure of scratching his leg when his irons were taken off, does he not show an equal serenity and joy in his soul at being freed from past inconveniences, and at the same time entering into the knowledge of things to come? Cato will pardon me, please; his death is indeed more tragic and more lingering, but this one, somehow, is the finer. To one who lamented this death, Aristippus said: "May the gods grant me such a one." In the souls of these two great men, and of their imitators (for I much doubt whether they ever had their equals), one sees so perfect a habit of virtue that it had turned into a temperament. It is no longer a laborious virtue, nor the precepts of reason, to maintain which the soul has to be racked; it is the very essence of their soul, its natural and ordinary disposition. They have made it so by a long practice of philosophical precepts, having lit upon a rich and fine nature; the vicious passions that spring up in us can find no entrance into them; the force and vigour of their soul stifle and extinguish disordered desires the moment they begin to stir.

Now, that it is nobler — by a high and divine resolution — to prevent the very birth of temptations, and to be so formed to virtue that the very seeds of vice are rooted out, than to check by main force their growth and, having let oneself be caught by the first stirrings of the passions, to arm oneself and stand firm against their progress and overcome them; and that this second effect is more generous still than simply being endowed with an easy, affable nature, by itself averse to debauchery and vice — I do not think can be doubted. For this third and last sort of virtue seems to make a man innocent, but not virtuous; free from doing ill, but not very apt to do well. Considering also that this condition is so close a neighbour to imperfection and cowardice that I hardly know how to draw the boundary line between them. The very names of goodness and innocence have, for this reason, fallen into a certain contempt. I know well enough that several virtues — chastity, sobriety, temperance — may come to a man through personal defects. Constancy in danger, if it must be so called, the contempt of death, and patience in misfortunes can often be found in men through lack of judging such accidents rightly, through not grasping them for what they are. Want of comprehension and stupidity sometimes counterfeit virtuous effects, as I have often seen happen: men have been commended for what really deserved blame. An Italian lord once said this in my presence, to the disadvantage of his own nation: that the subtlety of the Italians and the vivacity of their conceptions were so great, and they foresaw the dangers and accidents that might befall them so far ahead, that it was not strange they were often, in war, observed providing for their safety even before they had seen the peril; that we French and the Spaniards, who were not so cunning, would go further, and had to be made to see and feel the danger before we would take the alarm — but even then we could not stick to it; while the Germans and Swiss, more gross and heavy, did not have the sense to look about them even when the blows were falling about their ears. He perhaps spoke this way only for mirth's sake; and yet it is most certain that in war, raw soldiers rush into dangers more recklessly than after they have been beaten about a bit*. (The original has eschauldex — scalded.)
"Haud ignarus . . . quantum nova gloria in armis, Et praedulce decus, primo certamine possit."
["Not unaware how much the fresh glory of arms and the sweetest honour can do in the first contest." — Aeneid, xi. 154.]
It is for this reason that, when we judge of a particular action, we have to consider the circumstances and the whole man by whom it was performed before we give it a name.

To take myself as an example: I have sometimes known my friends call that prudence in me which was sheer chance, and put down to courage and patience what was really judgment and opinion, attributing one title to me instead of another, sometimes to my advantage and sometimes the other way. For the rest, I am so far from having arrived at the first and most perfect degree of excellence, in which virtue is turned into a habit, that even of the second I have given no great proof. I have not been very busy to bridle the desires that have plagued me. My virtue is a virtue — or rather an innocence — of chance and accident. If I had been born with a more disordered temperament, I am afraid I should have made a sorry showing; for I have never noticed any great stability in my soul to resist passions, however slight their force. I do not know how to nurse quarrels and debates within my own bosom, and consequently owe myself no great thanks for being free from a number of vices:
"Si vitiis mediocribus et mea paucis Mendosa est natura, alioqui recta, velut si Egregio inspersos reprehendas corpore naevos:"
["If my nature is marred by only slight and few vices, and is otherwise sound, it is as if you should reproach moles on a fine body." — Horace, Sat., i. 6, 65.]

I owe it rather to my fortune than to my reason. She has caused me to be descended from a race famous for integrity, and from a very good father; I do not know whether he passed some of his temper on to me, or whether domestic example and the good upbringing of my infancy insensibly helped the work, or whether I was simply born that way:
"Seu Libra, seu me Scorpius adspicit Formidolosus, pars violentior Natalis horae, seu tyrannus Hesperiae Capricornus undae:"
["Whether the Balance, or dread Scorpio (the more violent over my natal hour), or Capricorn, tyrant of the Hesperian sea, looks down on me." — Horace, Od., ii. 17.]

but so it is, that I have a natural horror for most vices. The answer of Antisthenes to one who asked him what was the best apprenticeship — "to unlearn evil" — seems to point at this. I hold them in horror, I say, with a loathing so natural, and so much my own, that the same instinct and impression I brought with me from my nurse, I still retain, and no temptation whatever has had the power to make me change it. Not even my own discourses, which on certain things break out of the common track and might seem easily to license me for actions my natural inclination makes me hate. I will say a strange thing, but I will say it: I find myself, in many ways, more under restraint by my manners than by my opinions, and my desires less debauched than my reason. Aristippus put forward such bold opinions in favour of pleasure and riches that he set all the philosophers against him; but as for his manners — Dionysius the tyrant, having presented three beautiful women for him to choose from, he answered that he would have all three, and that Paris had got himself into trouble for preferring one over the other two — but having taken them home, he sent them back untouched. His servant, finding himself overburdened on the road with the money he was carrying after him, Aristippus ordered him to pour out and throw away as much as troubled him. And Epicurus, whose doctrines were so irreligious and effeminate, was in his life very laborious and devout; he wrote to a friend that he lived only on biscuit and water, begging him to send him a little cheese to keep by him for when he had a mind to make a feast. Must it be true that to be a perfectly good man one must be so by some hidden, natural, and universal property, without law, reason, or example? The debauches in which I have been engaged have not, thank God, been of the worst sort, and I have condemned them in myself — for my judgment was never infected by them; on the contrary, I accuse them more severely in myself than in anyone else. But that is all, for, as to the rest, I put up too little resistance and let myself lean too much to the other side of the scale, except that I moderate them, and prevent them from mixing with other vices, which for the most part will cling together if one is not careful. I have shortened and curtailed mine, to make them as single and as simple as I can:
"Nec ultra Errorem foveo."
["Nor do I push my error further." — Juvenal, viii. 164.]

As for the opinion of the Stoics, who say, "That the wise man, when he acts, acts by all the virtues together, though one is most apparent according to the nature of the action" (and here the analogy of a human body might serve them somewhat, for the action of anger cannot work unless all the humours assist it, though choler predominates) — if they want to draw a like consequence, that when the wicked man does wickedly he does it by all the vices together, I do not believe it, or else I do not understand them, for I find by experience the contrary. These are sharp, unsubstantial subtleties with which philosophy sometimes amuses itself. I follow some vices, but I flee others as much as a saint would. The Peripatetics also reject this indissoluble connection; and Aristotle is of opinion that a prudent and just man may be intemperate and inconstant. Socrates confessed to some who had detected a certain inclination to vice in his physiognomy that it was, in truth, his natural leaning, but that he had corrected it by discipline. And those who were familiar with the philosopher Stilpo said that, being born with an addiction to wine and women, he had by study rendered himself very abstinent from both.

What I have in me of good, I have, on the contrary, by the chance of my birth; and I hold it not by law, precept, or any other instruction. The innocence that is in me is a simple thing — little vigour and no art. Among other vices, I mortally hate cruelty, both by nature and by judgment, as the very extreme of all vices: so much so that I cannot see a chicken's neck pulled off without distress, and cannot endure without impatience the cry of a hare in my dog's teeth, though the chase is a violent pleasure of mine. Those who have to fight with sensuality readily make use of this argument to show that it is wholly vicious and unreasonable — that when it is at its height it overpowers us to such a degree that reason can have no access — and they cite our own experience in the act of love,
"Quum jam praesagit gaudia corpus, Atque in eo est Venus, ut muliebria conserat arva."

where they hold that pleasure so transports us that our reason cannot do its office while we are in such ecstasy and rapture. I know very well it can be otherwise, and that a man may sometimes, if he wishes, gain this point over himself — to bend his soul, even at the critical moment, to think of something else; but he has to bend it to that hard. I know one may triumph over the utmost effort of this pleasure: I have tried it on myself, and have not found Venus so imperious a goddess as many, much more virtuous men than I, declare. I do not consider it a miracle, as the Queen of Navarre does in one of the Tales of her Heptameron (which is a very pretty book of its kind), nor a thing of extreme difficulty, to pass whole nights, with all the convenience and liberty one could wish, with a long-coveted mistress, and yet keep the pledge first given to satisfy oneself with kisses and similar caresses, without pressing any further. The example of the pleasure of the chase, I think, would be more apt: where, though the pleasure is less, there is the higher excitement of unexpected joy, leaving no time for reason, taken by surprise, to prepare itself for the encounter — when, after a long quest, the beast suddenly starts up in a place where one perhaps least expected it; the shock and ardour of the shouts and cries of the hunters strike us so that it would be hard for those who love this lesser chase to turn their thoughts, at that instant, another way. The poets make Diana triumph over the torch and arrows of Cupid:
"Quis non malarum, quas amor curas habet, Haec inter obliviscitur?"
["Who, amid such delights, would not forget the anxious cares of love?" — Horace, Epod., ii. 37.]

To return to what I was saying: I am tenderly moved by the afflictions of others, and would readily cry for company, if, on any occasion at all, I could cry. Nothing draws tears from me except tears — and not only real and true ones, but whatever they are, feigned or painted. I do not much mourn the dead, and would envy them rather; but I greatly mourn the dying. The savages do not offend me so much by roasting and eating the bodies of the dead as those do who torment and persecute the living. Indeed, I cannot watch even the ordinary executions of justice, however reasonable, with a steady eye. Someone, to give evidence of Julius Caesar's clemency, says: "He was mild in his revenges. Having forced the pirates to surrender — those by whom he had earlier been taken prisoner and put to ransom — and forasmuch as he had threatened them with the cross, he did indeed condemn them to it, but only after they had been first strangled. He punished his secretary Philemon, who had attempted to poison him, with no greater severity than mere death." Without naming this Latin author, who dares to allege as a testimony of mercy the killing only of those by whom we have been offended, it is easy to guess that he was shocked by the horrid and inhuman examples of cruelty practised by the Roman tyrants.

For my part, even in justice itself, all that exceeds a simple death seems to me sheer cruelty — especially in us, who, having a regard for souls, ought to dismiss them in a good and calm condition; which cannot be when we have agitated them with insufferable torments. Not long ago a soldier, who was a prisoner, perceiving from a tower where he was shut up that people were beginning to gather at the place of execution and that the carpenters were busy putting up a scaffold, concluded straight away that the preparation was for him and made up his mind to kill himself. He could find no instrument to help him in his design except an old rusty cart-nail that fortune put in his hand; with this he first gave himself two great wounds about his throat, but finding these would not do, he gave himself a third in the belly, where he left the nail sticking up to the head. The first of his keepers who came in found him in this condition — still alive, but sunk down and exhausted by his wounds. So as to make use of the time before he died, they hurried to read his sentence; and when he heard that he was only condemned to be beheaded, he seemed to take new courage, accepted wine he had earlier refused, and thanked his judges for the unhoped-for mildness of their sentence; saying that he had decided to dispatch himself for fear of a more severe and unbearable death, having taken it, from the preparations he had seen on the spot, that they meant to torment him with some horrible execution; and that he felt delivered from death in having it changed from what he had feared.

I would advise that those examples of severity, by which it is meant to keep the people in their duty, should be exercised upon the dead bodies of criminals. To see them deprived of burial, to see them boiled and divided into quarters, would work nearly as much upon the crowd as the pain inflicted on the living — although in effect this last is little or nothing, as God himself says: "Who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do." And the poets dwell especially on the horrors of this picture as something worse than death:
"Heu! reliquias semiustas regis, denudatis ossibus, Per terram sanie delibutas foede divexarier."
["Alas! that the half-burnt remains of the king, with the bones exposed, should be foully dragged along the ground, smeared with gore." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 44.]

I happened to come by, one day at Rome, just as they were executing Catena, a notorious robber. He was strangled without any emotion in the spectators; but when they came to cut him in quarters, the hangman gave no blow that the people did not follow with a doleful cry and exclamation, as if each one had lent his sense of feeling to the wretched carcass. Those inhuman excesses should be exercised on the bark, not on the living wood. Artaxerxes, in nearly the same case, moderated the severity of the ancient laws of Persia, ordaining that the nobility who had committed a fault, instead of being whipped as they used to be, should be stripped only and have their clothes whipped for them; and that, whereas they used to have their hair torn out, they should only have their high-crowned tiara taken off. The very devout Egyptians thought they sufficiently satisfied divine justice by sacrificing hogs in effigy and representation — a bold invention, to pay God so essential a substance in mere picture and show.

I live in a time when we abound in incredible examples of this vice, through the licence of our civil wars; and we see nothing in ancient histories more extreme than what we have proof of every day. But I cannot, for all that, get used to it. I could hardly persuade myself, before I saw it with my own eyes, that there could be found souls so cruel and savage that, for the sole pleasure of murder, would commit it — would hack and lop off the limbs of others, sharpen their wits to invent unusual torments and new kinds of death, without hatred, without profit, for no other end than to enjoy the pleasing spectacle of the gestures and motions, the lamentable groans and cries of a man dying in anguish. For this is the utmost point to which cruelty can come:
"Ut homo hominem, non iratus, non timens, tantum spectaturus, occidat."
["That a man should kill a man, not being angry, not being in fear, only for the sake of the spectacle." — Seneca, Ep., 90.]

For my own part, I cannot, without grief, see so much as an innocent beast pursued and killed which has no defence and has done us no offence at all; and what often happens — that the stag we are hunting, finding himself weak and out of breath, and seeing no other remedy, surrenders himself to us his pursuers, imploring mercy by his tears —
"Questuque cruentus, Atque imploranti similis,"
["Who, bleeding, by his moans seems to beg for mercy." — Aeneid, vii. 501.]
has always been to me a very unpleasing sight; and I hardly ever take a beast alive that I do not at once turn out again. Pythagoras bought them from fishermen and fowlers to do the same:
"Primoque a caede ferarum, Incaluisse puto maculatum sanguine ferrum."
["I think it was the slaughter of wild beasts that first warmed up the steel of man, stained with blood." — Ovid, Met., xv. 106.]

Those natures that are bloodthirsty toward beasts show a natural proneness to cruelty. After the Romans had grown accustomed to spectacles of the slaughter of animals, they went on to those of the slaughter of men, of gladiators. Nature herself has, I fear, imprinted in man a kind of instinct toward inhumanity; nobody takes pleasure in seeing beasts play and caress one another, but everyone delights in seeing them tear and dismember each other. And so that I may not be laughed at for the sympathy I feel for them — theology itself enjoins us some favour on their behalf; and considering that one and the same master has lodged us together in this palace for his service, and that they, as well as we, are of his household, it has reason to enjoin upon us some affection and regard for them. Pythagoras borrowed the metempsychosis from the Egyptians, but it has since been received by several nations, and particularly by our Druids:
"Morte carent animae; semperque, priore relicta Sede, novis domibus vivunt, habitantque receptae."
["Souls do not die, but, having left their former seat, live in new dwellings, and are received and reside there." — Ovid, Met., xv. 158.]

The religion of our ancient Gauls held that souls, being eternal, never ceased to move from one body to another; and they mingled with this fancy some consideration of divine justice. For according to the deportments of the soul while it had been in Alexander, they said, God assigned it another body to inhabit, more or less painful, and suitable to its condition:
"Muta ferarum Cogit vincla pati; truculentos ingerit ursis, Praedonesque lupis; fallaces vulpibus addit: Atque ubi per varios annos, per mille figuras
Egit, Lethaeo purgatos flumine, tandem Rursus ad humanae revocat primordia formae:"

["He makes them bear the silent chains of brutes — the bloodthirsty souls he encloses in bears, the thieves in wolves, the deceivers in foxes; and when, through successive years and a thousand shapes, man has run his life, after their purging in Lethe's river, at last he calls them back to the original forms of human shape." — Claudian, In Ruf., ii. 482.]

If it had been brave, he lodged it in the body of a lion; if voluptuous, in a hog; if timorous, in a hart or a hare; if malicious, in a fox, and so for the rest, until — having purified it by this chastisement — it again entered the body of some other man:
"Ipse ego nam memini, Trojani tempore belli Panthoides Euphorbus eram."
["For I myself remember that, in the days of the Trojan war, I was Euphorbus, son of Panthus." — Ovid, Met., xv. 160; and see Diogenes Laertius, Life of Pythagoras.]
