Those troubled with the disease the doctors call hyposphagma — a suffusion of blood under the skin — see everything red and bloody. What do we know but that these humours, which alter the operations of sight, predominate in beasts and are normal with them? For we see some whose eyes are yellow, like us when we have jaundice, and others of a bloody colour; it is likely the colours of objects look different to them from what they look like to us. Which of the two will make a right judgment? For it is not said that the essence of things has a relation to man only. Hardness, whiteness, depth, and sharpness have reference to the service and knowledge of animals as well as ours, and nature has equally designed them for their use. When we press down on the eye, the body we look at appears longer and more drawn out — many animals have their eyes so pressed down; this length, then, may be the true form of that body, and not the one our eyes give it in their usual state. If we close the lower part of the eye, things appear double:
Bina lucernarum florentia lumina flammis... Et duplices hominum facies, et corpora bina.
["The lights of the lamps blossom in twin flames... and men appear with double faces and two bodies."]

If our ears are blocked, or the passage stopped with something, we receive sound quite otherwise than we usually do; animals whose ears are hairy, or have only a tiny hole instead of an ear, do not hear as we do but receive another kind of sound. We see at festivals and theatres that if a painted glass of a certain colour is set against the light of the torches, everything in the place appears green, yellow, or violet:

Et vulgo faciunt id lutea russaque vela, Et ferruginea, cum, magnis intenta theatris, Per malos vulgata trabesque, trementia pendent; Namque ibi consessum caveæ subter, et omnem Scenæ speciem, patrum, matrumque, deorumque Inficiunt, coguntque suo volitare colore:

["And yellow and red and dark-iron curtains commonly do this, when, stretched over the great theatres, spread on poles and beams, they hang trembling; for there they tinge the assembly below in the bowl and all the look of the stage — the fathers, mothers, and gods — and make them flit about in their own colour."]
It is likely that the eyes of animals — which we see are of various colours — produce the appearance of bodies in accord with those colours.

To make a right judgment, then, of the differences between the senses, we should first be agreed with the beasts, and second among ourselves — which we are not in the least, but enter into dispute every time one person hears, sees, or tastes something otherwise than another does, and we argue, as much as about anything else, about the diversity of the images the senses present to us. A child, by the ordinary course of nature, hears, sees, and speaks differently than a man of thirty; and he than one of sixty. The senses are duller and dimmer in some people, more open and quick in others. We receive things variously, depending on what we are and on how they appear to us. Those rings cut in the shape of feathers, called "endless feathers," no eye can take the measure of, nor keep from being deceived: on one side they seem to widen, on the other to narrow to a point, even as the ring is turned on the finger; yet by feel, they all seem of equal size. Now since our perception is so uncertain and contested, it is no wonder we are told that we may declare that snow appears white to us; but to affirm that it is in its own essence really so is more than we are able to justify. And this foundation once shaken, all the knowledge in the world must necessarily fall to ruin. What! Do our senses themselves hinder one another? A picture seems raised and embossed to the sight; in the handling it feels flat to the touch. Shall we say that musk, which delights the smell and offends the taste, is pleasant or not? There are herbs and unguents proper for one part of the body that are harmful to another; honey is pleasant to the taste but offensive to the sight. Those who, to assist their lust, used in ancient times to set magnifying-glasses in front of the members they were going to employ, so as to please themselves the more by that ocular swelling — to which of their senses did they give the prize? Was it the sight, which represented the parts as large and great as they could wish, or the touch, which represented them small and contemptible? Are they our senses that supply the subject with these different qualities, while the subjects themselves have only one? As we see in the bread we eat: it is nothing but bread, but by being eaten it becomes bones, blood, flesh, hair, and nails:
Ut cibus in membra atque artus cum diditur omnes, Disperit, atque aliam naturam sufficit ex se;
["As food, when it is distributed through all the limbs and joints, loses its former state and out of itself supplies a different nature."]

The moisture sucked up by the root of a tree becomes trunk, leaf, and fruit; and the air, being but one, is modulated in a trumpet into a thousand sorts of sounds. Are they our senses, I would like to know, that in the same way form these subjects into so many different qualities — or do the subjects really have them in themselves? And on this doubt, what can we determine about their true essence? Moreover, since the accidents of disease, of raving, or of sleep make things appear otherwise to us than they do to the healthful, the wise, and the awake, is it not likely that our right posture of health and understanding, and our natural humours, also have the means to give a being to things relative to their own condition, and accommodate things to themselves, just as the disordered states do? Is health any less capable of giving them an aspect than sickness is? Why does not the temperate man have his own form of objects, just as the intemperate does — and why may he not as well stamp them with his own character as the other does? The man whose mouth is out of taste says the wine is flat; the healthy man commends its flavour; the thirsty man, its briskness. Now since our condition always accommodates things to itself and transforms them according to its own posture, we cannot know what things truly are in themselves — since nothing comes to us but what is falsified and altered by the senses. Where the compass, the square, and the rule are crooked, all propositions drawn from them, and all buildings erected on those guides, must necessarily be defective too. The uncertainty of our senses makes uncertain everything they produce:

Denique ut in fabricâ, si prava est regula prima, Normaque si fallax rectis regionibus exit, Et libella aliquâ si ex parte claudicat hilum; Omnia mendose fieri, atque obstipa necessum est, Prava, cubantia, prona, supina, atque absona tecta; Jam ruere ut quædam videantur velle, ruantque Prodita judiciis fallacibus omnia primis; Sic igitur ratio tibi rerum prava necesse est, Falsaque sit, falsis quæcunque ab sensibus orta est.

["And so as in building, if the first measure is crooked, if the square is false in the right angles, and if the level limps in any part, everything must come out faulty, lopsided, leaning, sloping, sagging, and out of line — roofs that look like they want to fall, and do fall, all betrayed by faulty first judgments. Just so your reasoning about things must necessarily be crooked and false, if it has arisen from false senses."]

As to the rest, who can be fit to judge and to determine those differences? As we say in controversies of religion that we must have a judge inclined to neither side, free from all choice and affection — which cannot be among Christians — so it falls out here. For if he is old, he cannot judge of the sense of old age, being himself a party in the case; if young, the same exception applies; if healthy, sick, asleep, or awake, he is still the same incompetent judge. We would need someone exempt from all these states, as from things indifferent to him; and by this rule we would need a judge who never existed.

To judge of the appearances we receive of subjects, we ought to have a deciding instrument; to verify this instrument, we must have demonstration; to verify this demonstration, an instrument. And here we are back on the same wheel, no further along. Since the senses cannot settle our dispute, being themselves full of uncertainty, then reason must do it. But no reason can be set up except on the basis of another reason, and so we run back to infinity. Our fancy does not apply itself to things outside us, but only conceives them through the senses; and the senses do not comprehend a foreign subject, but only their own affections; so that fancy and appearance are not parts of the subject, but only of the passion and suffering of the sense — and this passion and the subject are different things. Therefore whoever judges by appearances is judging by something other than the subject. And to say that the passions of the senses convey to the soul the quality of foreign subjects by resemblance — how can the soul and the understanding be sure of this resemblance, having of itself no commerce with foreign subjects? Just as those who never knew Socrates cannot, when they see his portrait, say it is like him. Now whoever wants nevertheless to judge by appearances: if by all of them, that is impossible, because they hinder one another by their contrarieties and discrepancies, as we see by experience. Shall some select appearances govern the rest? You must verify this select group by another select group, the second by a third, and so it will never come to an end. Finally, there is no constant existence either of the objects' being or of our own: we, our judgments, and all mortal things are unceasingly running and rolling. And consequently nothing certain can be established from the one to the other, both the judging and the judged being in continual motion and change.

We have no communication with being, because all human nature is always in the middle, between being born and dying, giving only an obscure appearance and shadow, a weak and uncertain opinion of itself. And if perhaps you fix your thought on trying to apprehend your own being, it will be like grasping water — for the harder you clench your hand to squeeze and hold what is by its own nature flowing, the more you lose of what you would grasp and hold. So, since all things are subject to pass from one change to another, reason — which looks there for a real substance — finds itself deceived, unable to lay hold of anything that subsists and remains; for everything is either entering into being and has not yet arrived there, or is beginning to die before it is born. Plato said that bodies never had any existence, only birth — conceiving that Homer had made Ocean and Tethys father and mother of the gods, to show us that all things are in perpetual fluctuation, motion, and variation; the opinion, as he says, of all the philosophers before his time, except Parmenides alone, who would not allow things to have motion, and on whose power he sets a great value. Pythagoras held that all matter was flowing and unstable; the Stoics, that there is no present time, and that what we call so is nothing but the juncture and meeting of the future and the past; Heraclitus, that no man ever entered twice into the same river; Epicharmus, that he who borrowed money an hour ago no longer owes it now; and that he who was invited last night to come to dinner today comes nevertheless uninvited, since they are no longer the same men, but have become others; and that no mortal substance could be found twice in the same condition — for by the suddenness and quickness of the change, it disperses one moment and reunites the next; it comes and goes in such a way that what begins to be born never arrives at the perfection of being, since that birth is never finished and never stops, as being at an end, but is always shifting and changing from one seed to another. As human seed is first made, in the mother's womb, into a formless embryo; then delivered as a suckling infant; then becomes a boy, then a youth, then a man, and finally a decrepit old man — so that each successive age and generation is always destroying and spoiling the one before:
Mutat enim mundi naturam totius ætas, Ex alioque alius status excipere omnia debet; Nec manet ulla sui similis res; omnia migrant, Omnia commutat natura, et vertere cogit.

["For time changes the nature of the whole world, and one state of things must take over from another; nor does any thing remain like itself; all things migrate, nature transforms everything and forces it to change."]

"And yet we foolishly fear one kind of death, when we have already passed, and pass every day, so many others. For not only, as Heraclitus said, is the death of fire the generation of air, and the death of air the generation of water; but, more manifestly still, we can see it in ourselves: manhood dies and passes away when old age comes on; youth ends in the flower of a grown man's prime; infancy in youth; and our first age dies in infancy. Yesterday died in today, and today will die in tomorrow; nothing remains in the same state or is always the same thing. And that it is so, let this be the proof: if we are always one and the same, how does it come about that we are pleased with one thing now, and with another by and by? How is it that we love or hate contrary things, that we praise or condemn them? How is it that we have different affections, no longer holding the same feeling in the same thought? For it is not likely that, without change, we should take on other passions; and what undergoes change does not remain the same — and if it is not the same, it is not at all; rather, along with itself, being also unknowingly changes and alters, becoming always another thing from another. And consequently the natural senses cheat and deceive themselves, taking what only seems to be for what is, for want of really knowing what that-which-is is. But what is it then that truly is? That which is eternal — that is to say, that never had a beginning, nor ever shall have an ending, and to which time can bring no change. For time is a movable thing, and shows itself as if in a shadow, with a substance ever flowing and running, never standing stable and permanent; to which belong the words _before_ and _after_, _has been_ or _shall be_ — which at first sight clearly show that it is not a thing that is. For it would be a great folly and a manifest falsity to say that that _is_ which is not yet, or which has already ceased to be. And as for those words _present_, _instant_, _now_, on which it seems we chiefly support and ground our understanding of time — when reason looks closely at them, it immediately destroys them; for it divides and splits the now into _future_ and _past_, having of necessity to consider it divided in two. The same happens to nature, which is measured, as to time, which measures it; for she has nothing more subsisting and permanent than time does, but all things are either being born, bearing, or dying. So that it would be impious to say of God — who alone _is_ — that he _was_, or that he _shall be_; for those are terms of declension, transmutation, and vicissitude, of what cannot continue or remain in being. So we must conclude that God alone _is_ — not according to any measure of time, but according to an immutable and immovable eternity, not measured by time, not subject to any decline; before whom nothing was, and after whom nothing shall be, either newer or more recent; but a real being, who with one sole _now_ fills the for-ever; and that there is nothing that truly is but he alone — without our being able to say that he _has been_ or _shall be_; without beginning and without end." To this so religious conclusion of a pagan, I will only add this testimony from one of his own condition, to close this long and tedious discourse, which would supply me with endless matter: "What a vile and abject thing is man," says he, "if he does not raise himself above humanity!" It is a good word, and a profitable desire — but absurd all the same. For to make the handle bigger than the hand, the cubit longer than the arm, and to hope to stride further than our legs can reach, is both impossible and monstrous; just as it is for a man to rise above himself and his humanity. For he can see only with his eyes, and grasp only with his grip. He shall be exalted, if God will lend him an extraordinary hand; he shall exalt himself, by abandoning and renouncing his own proper means, and by allowing himself to be raised and elevated by means purely celestial. It belongs to our Christian faith, and not to Stoic virtue, to lay claim to that divine and miraculous metamorphosis.

chapters.title: Of judging of the death of another
paragraphs: When we judge another person's composure in dying — which, without doubt, is the most remarkable action of human life — we have to take care of one thing: that people very reluctantly believe themselves to have arrived at that hour. Few die thinking it is their last; and there is nothing in which the flattery of hope deludes us more. Hope never stops whispering in our ears, "Others have been much sicker without dying; your condition is not so desperate as people think; and, at the worst, God has done other miracles." This happens because we set too much value on ourselves; it seems as if the whole of things were in some measure to suffer by our dissolution, and that it pitied our condition — because our disturbed sight presents things to us wrongly, and we are of the opinion they need us as much as we need them. Like people at sea, to whom the mountains, fields, cities, sky, and earth all seem to be tossed at the same rate as they are:
"Provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt:"
["We sail out of port, and the lands and cities recede." — Aeneid, iii. 72.]
Did anyone ever see an old man who did not applaud the past and condemn the present time, laying the blame for his own misery and discontent on the world and the manners of men?
"Jamque caput quassans, grandis suspirat arator. Et cum tempora temporibus praesentia confert Praeteritis, laudat fortunas saepe parentis, Et crepat antiquum genus ut pietate repletum."

["Now the old ploughman, shaking his head, sighs, and comparing the present times with the past, often praises his parents' good fortune, and goes on about the ancient race as full of piety." — Lucretius, ii. 1165.]
We will have everything go down with us; from which it follows that we consider our death as a great thing, one that does not pass so easily, nor without the solemn consultation of the stars:
"Tot circa unum caput tumultuantes deos,"
["So many gods in tumult about one head." — Seneca, Suasor., i. 4.]

and we think of it the more in this way the more we value ourselves. "What! shall so much knowledge be lost, with so much damage to the world, without a particular concern on the part of the Fates? Does so rare and exemplary a soul cost no more to kill than one that is common and of no use to the public? This life, which protects so many others, on which so many other lives depend, which employs so vast a number of men in his service, which fills so many places — shall it drop off like one that hangs by a single thread?" None of us takes it sufficiently to heart that he is only one. Hence those words of Caesar to his pilot, more swollen than the sea that threatened him:
"Italiam si coelo auctore recusas, Me pete: sola tibi causa est haec justa timoris, Vectorem non nosse tuum; perrumpe procellas, Tutela secure mea."

["If you refuse to sail to Italy under the gods' authority, trust to mine; the only just cause you have to fear is that you do not know your passenger; break through the storms, secure in my protection." — Lucan, v. 579.]
And these:
"Credit jam digna pericula Caesar Fatis esse suis; tantusne evertere, dixit, Me superis labor est, parva quem puppe sedentem, Tam magno petiere mari;"

["Caesar now thought these dangers worthy of his destiny: 'What!' he said, 'is it for the gods so great a task to overthrow me, that they have to assail me with so great a sea while I sit in a poor little bark?'" — Lucan, v. 653.]
and the idle fancy of the public, that the sun bore on his face mourning for his death for a whole year:
"Ille etiam extincto miseratus Caesare Romam, Cum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine texit:"
["He too, Caesar being dead, pitying Rome, clothed his bright head in a dark cloud." — Virgil, Georg., i. 466.]
and a thousand of the like, by which the world lets itself be so easily imposed upon, believing that our interests touch the heavens, and that their infinity is concerned in our ordinary doings:
"Non tanta caelo societas nobiscum est, ut nostro fato mortalis sit ille quoque siderum fulgor."
["There is no such alliance between us and heaven that the brightness of the stars should also be made mortal by our death." — Pliny, Nat. Hist., ii. 8.]

Now, to judge of the constancy and resolution of a man who does not yet believe himself certainly in danger, though he really is, is not reasonable; and it is not enough that he die in this posture, unless he has deliberately put himself into it for this end. It usually happens that most men put a good face on the matter and speak with great indifference, to gain a reputation they hope, while still living, to enjoy. Of all whom I have seen die, fortune has disposed their countenances, and no design of theirs. And even among those who in ancient times have killed themselves, much depends on whether it was a sudden or a lingering death. That cruel Roman emperor would say of his prisoners that he would make them feel death; and if anyone killed himself in prison, "That fellow has made an escape from me." He would prolong death and make it felt by torments:
"Vidimus et toto quamvis in corpore caeso Nil anima lethale datum, moremque nefandae, Durum saevitiae, pereuntis parcere morti."
["We have seen in tortured bodies, amid all their wounds, none mortal to the soul — an inhuman fashion of dire cruelty, that means to kill, yet refuses to let the dying die." — Lucan, iv. 178.]

In plain truth, it is no such great matter for a man in health and a temperate state of mind to resolve to kill himself; it is easy enough to play the bold one before one comes to the point — so much so that Heliogabalus, the most effeminate man in the world, in the midst of his lowest sensualities, could plan to die delicately when he should be forced to it. That his death might not give the lie to the rest of his life, he had deliberately built a sumptuous tower, the front and base of which were covered with planks studded with gold and precious stones, from which to throw himself; and had cords woven of gold and crimson silk made, with which to strangle himself; and a sword with a blade of gold hammered out, to fall upon; and he kept poison in vessels of emerald and topaz, with which to poison himself, according as he should choose one of these ways of dying:
"Impiger . . . ad letum et fortis virtute coacta."
["Eager for death, and brave by a forced courage." — Lucan, iv. 798.]

Yet, in the case of this person, the effeminacy of his preparations makes it likely he would have thought better of it had he been put to the test. But of those who, with greater resolution, have made up their minds to kill themselves, we have to examine whether it was done with a single stroke that took away the leisure of feeling the effect; for it is a question whether, perceiving life little by little stealing away — the sentiment of the body mixing itself with that of the soul, and the means of repenting being offered — whether, I say, constancy and obstinacy in so dangerous a design could be maintained.

In the civil wars of Caesar, Lucius Domitius, captured in the Abruzzi, having poisoned himself, afterwards repented. In our own time it has happened that a certain person, resolved to die, did not strike deep enough at the first thrust — the sensibility of the flesh resisting his arm — and gave himself two or three more wounds, but could never bring himself to push it home. While Plautius Silvanus was on trial, Urgulania, his grandmother, sent him a dagger with which, being unable to kill himself, he had his servants cut his veins. Albucilla, in Tiberius's time, having, to kill himself, struck with too much tenderness, gave his adversaries the opportunity to imprison and put him to death in their own way. And that great leader Demosthenes, after his rout in Sicily, did the same; and C. Fimbria, having struck himself too feebly, begged his servant to finish him off. On the contrary, Ostorius, who could not use his own arm, disdained to employ his servant's for anything but to hold the dagger straight and firm, while he, bringing his throat to it, ran himself through. It is, in truth, a morsel to be swallowed without chewing, unless one is thoroughly resolved. And yet the emperor Hadrian made his physician mark and circle on his breast the mortal place where he was to stab the man to whom he had given orders to kill him. For this reason it was that Caesar, when asked what death he thought most desirable, answered, "The least premeditated and the shortest." If Caesar dared say it, it is no cowardice in me to believe it. "A short death," says Pliny, "is the sovereign good fortune of human life." People do not much care to recognise it. No one can be said to be resolute for death who fears to face it and cannot meet it with his eyes open. Those whom we see, in their criminal punishments, running to their death, hastening and pressing for their execution, do not do so out of resolution, but because they will not give themselves leisure to consider it; it is not being dead that troubles them, but dying:
"Emori nolo, sed me esse mortuum nihil aestimo:"
["I have no mind to die, but I think nothing of being dead." — Epicharmus, in Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 8.]
It is a degree of constancy that, by experience, I find I can arrive at — like those who plunge into dangers as into the sea, with their eyes shut.

There is nothing, in my opinion, more illustrious in the life of Socrates than that he had thirty whole days to ruminate on the sentence of his death — to digest it all that time with the most assured hope, without anxiety and without change, and with a series of words and actions rather careless and indifferent than in any way stirred or disturbed by the weight of such a thought.

That Pomponius Atticus, to whom Cicero writes so often, being sick, had Agrippa, his son-in-law, and two or three more of his friends called to him and told them that, having found all the means tried for his recovery to be in vain, and that all he did to prolong his life prolonged and increased his pain, he was resolved to put an end to both; he asked them to approve of his determination, or at least not to waste their labour in trying to dissuade him. Now, having chosen to destroy himself by abstinence, his disease was thereby cured; the remedy he had taken to kill himself restored him to health. His physicians and friends, rejoicing at so happy an outcome and coming to congratulate him, found themselves very much deceived — it being impossible for them to make him alter his purpose. He told them that since he must one day die, and was now so far along the road, he would save himself the labour of beginning again another time. This man, having considered death at leisure, was not only not discouraged at its approach, but actively sought it; for being content that he had entered the combat, he made it a point of bravery to see the end of it. It is far beyond not fearing death to taste and relish it.

The story of the philosopher Cleanthes is very like this: he had his gums swollen and rotten; his physicians advised him to great abstinence; having fasted two days, he was so much better that they pronounced him cured and allowed him to return to his ordinary diet. He, on the contrary, already finding some sweetness in this faintness, refused to be persuaded to go back, but resolved to push on and finish what he had so far advanced.

Tullius Marcellinus, a young Roman, having a mind to anticipate the hour of his fate, to be rid of a disease that troubled him more than he was willing to endure (though his physicians had assured him of a certain — if not immediate — cure), called a council of his friends to deliberate about it. Of these, some — out of unmanliness — gave him the counsel they would have taken themselves; others, out of flattery, gave him the counsel they thought he would most like; but a Stoic said this to him: "Do not concern yourself, Marcellinus, as if you were deliberating about a matter of importance; it is no great matter to live — your servants and the beasts live; but it is a great thing to die handsomely, wisely, and firmly. Just think how long you have been doing the same things: eat, drink, sleep; drink, sleep, eat. We endlessly wheel in the same circle. Not only intolerable accidents, but even satiety of living, can incline a man to want to die." Marcellinus did not need a man to advise, but a man to help. His servants were afraid to meddle in the business; but this philosopher made them understand that domestics fall under suspicion even when it is in doubt whether the master's death was voluntary or not, and that it would be as bad an example to hinder him as to kill him, for —
"Invitum qui servat, idem facit occidenti."
["He who saves a man against his will, does as much as if he killed him." — Horace, De Arte Poet., 467.]

He then told Marcellinus that it would not be unfitting — as what is left on the table after we have eaten is given to those waiting at it — so, life being ended, to distribute something to those who have been our servants. Now Marcellinus was of a free and liberal spirit; he therefore divided a certain sum of money among his servants and comforted them. As to the rest, he had no need of steel or of blood; he resolved to walk out of this life and not to run out of it, not to escape from death but to taste it. And to give himself leisure to deal with it, having given up all manner of nourishment, the third day following — after having had himself sprinkled with warm water — he fainted away by degrees, and, as he himself declared, not without a certain pleasure.

In fact, those who have known these faintings, brought on by weakness, say that they feel no pain at all in them, but rather a kind of delight, as in the passage into sleep and rest. These are studied and digested deaths.

But so that Cato may furnish the full example of virtue, it seems as if his good destiny — which gave him the leisure to confront and struggle with death — put his ill one into the hand that gave himself the blow, seeing that he had courage in the danger to deepen it rather than let it slacken. And had I had to depict him in his supreme station, I should have done it in the posture of tearing out his bloody bowels, rather than with his sword in his hand, as did the sculptors of his time; for this second murder was much more fierce than the first.

chapters.title: That our mind hinders itself
paragraphs: It is a pleasant fancy to imagine a mind exactly balanced between two equal desires: without doubt it could never settle on either, for the choice and application would betray an inequality of estimation; and were we set between a bottle and a ham, with an equal appetite to drink and to eat, there would be no remedy but to die of thirst and hunger. To get around this problem, the Stoics, when asked where the election in the soul between two indifferent things comes from — that makes us, out of a great number of crowns, take one rather than another, when they are all alike and there is no reason to incline us to such a preference — answer that this movement of the soul is extraordinary and irregular, coming into us by some foreign, accidental, fortuitous impulse. It might rather, I think, be said that nothing presents itself to us in which there is not some difference, however slight; and that, either by sight or touch, there is always some choice which, however imperceptibly, tempts and attracts us. So whoever assumes a length of pack-thread of equal strength all the way through — it is simply impossible it should break, for where would you have the breaking to begin? And that it should break all at once is not in nature. Whoever should also throw in here the geometrical propositions which, by the certainty of their demonstrations, conclude the contained to be greater than the container, the centre to be as great as its circumference, and which discover two lines forever approaching each other and yet never able to meet — and the philosopher's stone, and the squaring of the circle, where reason and effect are so opposite — might perhaps find some argument to back up this bold saying of Pliny:
"Solum certum nihil esse certi, et homine nihil miserius aut superbius."
["It is only certain that nothing is certain, and that nothing is more miserable, or more proud, than man." — Nat. Hist., ii. 7.]

chapters.title: That our desires are augmented by difficulty
paragraphs: There is no reason that does not have its contrary, say the wisest of the philosophers. I was just now ruminating on the excellent saying one of the ancients gives as a reason for the contempt of life: "No good can bring pleasure unless it is one for the loss of which we are prepared beforehand."
"In aequo est dolor amissae rei, et timor amittendae,"
["The grief of losing a thing, and the fear of losing it, are equal." — Seneca, Ep., 98.]

meaning by this that the enjoyment of life cannot be truly pleasant to us if we are in fear of losing it. It might however be said, on the contrary, that we hug and embrace this good so much the more keenly, and with so much greater affection, by how much we see it less secure and fear it being taken from us. For it is plain — as fire burns with greater fury when cold comes to mix with it — that our will is more obstinate by being opposed:
"Si nunquam Danaen habuisset ahenea turris, Non esses, Danae, de Jove facta parens;"
["If a brazen tower had not held Danae, you would not, Danae, have been made a mother by Jove." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 27.]
and there is nothing naturally so contrary to our taste as satiety, which comes from ease; nor anything that so much whets it as rarity and difficulty:
"Omnium rerum voluptas ipso, quo debet fugare, periculo crescit."
["The pleasure of all things grows by the same danger that should deter us from them." — Seneca, De Benef., vii. 9.]
"Galla, nega; satiatur amor, nisi gaudia torquent."
["Galla, refuse me; love is glutted by joys that are not attended with trouble." — Martial, iv. 37.]

To keep love breathing, Lycurgus made a decree that married couples in Lacedaemon should never come together except by stealth, and that to be caught in bed together would be as great a shame as to be caught with others. The difficulty of assignations, the danger of being surprised, the shame of the morning,
"Et languor, et silentium, Et latere petitus imo Spiritus:"
["And languor, and silence, and sighs drawn from deep within." — Horace, Epod., xi. 9.]

these are what give the sauce its piquancy. How many very wantonly pleasant games spring from the most decent and modest language in writings about love? Pleasure itself wants to be heightened by pain; it is much sweeter when it smarts, when it leaves the skin rippled. The courtesan Flora said she never lay with Pompey but that she left him wearing the marks of her teeth.

"Quod petiere, premunt arcte, faciuntque dolorem Corporis, et dentes inlidunt saepe labellis . . . Et stimuli subsunt, qui instigant laedere ad ipsum, Quodcunque est, rabies unde illae germina surgunt."

["What they have sought they press close, causing bodily pain; teeth fix on lips, kisses leave their mark: hidden goads urge them to wound the very part from which that madness rises." — Lucretius, iv. 1077.]

And so it is in everything: difficulty gives all things their value. The people of the March of Ancona more readily make their vows to St James, those of Galicia to Our Lady of Loreto; they make a great fuss at Liège about the baths of Lucca, and in Tuscany about those of Aspa; there are few Romans to be seen in the fencing school at Rome, which is full of Frenchmen. That great Cato also, as much as the rest of us, grew weary of his wife while she was his, and longed for her when she was in another man's possession. I once had to turn an old horse out to pasture, because he was unmanageable when he smelt a mare: ease quickly sated him as to his own, but for strange mares — and the first that passed along his fence — he would fall again to his pressing neighings and his furious heats, as before. Our appetite scorns and passes by what it has in possession, to run after what it does not have:
"Transvolat in medio posita, et fugientia captat."
["He passes over what lies in his path, and chases after what flees from him." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 108.]
To forbid us anything is to make us have a mind to it:
"Nisi tu servare puellam Incipis, incipiet desinere esse mea:"
["Unless you begin to guard your mistress, she will soon stop being mine." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 47.]
to give it up to us entirely is to breed in us contempt. Want and abundance fall into the same difficulty:
"Tibi quod superest, mihi quod desit, dolet."
["Your superfluities trouble you, and what I lack troubles me." — Terence, Phorm., i. 3, 9.]

Desire and fulfilment afflict us equally. The harshness of mistresses is hard to bear, but ease, to tell the truth, is harder still — since discontent and anger spring from the value we set on the thing desired, and stir love into life, while satiety breeds disgust; it is a blunt, dull, stupid, tired, slothful passion:
"Si qua volet regnare diu, contemnat amantem."
["She who would long retain her power, let her treat her lover with disdain." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 33.]
"Contemnite, amantes: Sic hodie veniet, si qua negavit heri."
["Be scornful, lovers: she who refused you yesterday will come today." — Propertius, ii. 14, 19.]

Why did Poppaea invent the use of a mask to hide the beauties of her face, but to enhance them in the eyes of her lovers? Why have women veiled, even down to the heels, those beauties that everyone wants to show and that everyone wants to see? Why do they cover with so many hindrances, one on top of another, the parts where our desire — and their own — has its principal seat? And to what serve those huge bastion farthingales with which our ladies fortify their hips, but to whet our appetite and to draw us on by removing the goal further from us?
"Et fugit ad salices, et se cupit ante videri."
["She flies to the willows, and yet wants to be seen before she does." — Virgil, Eclog., iii. 65.]
"Interdum tunica duxit operta moram."
["The hidden robe has at times held back love." — Propertius, ii. 15, 6.]

What use is the artifice of this virgin modesty, this grave coldness, this severe look, this professing to be ignorant of things they know better than we, who instruct them in them — but to increase in us the desire to overcome, to control, to trample underfoot at pleasure all this ceremony and all these obstacles? For there is not only pleasure but, on top of that, glory in conquering and corrupting that soft sweetness and childish modesty, and reducing a cold and matronlike gravity to the mercy of our burning desires. It is a glory, they say, to triumph over modesty, chastity, and temperance; and whoever talks ladies out of these qualities betrays both them and himself. We are to believe that their hearts tremble with fright, that the very sound of our words offends the purity of their ears, that they hate us for talking so, and only yield to our pressing by a kind of compulsion. Beauty, all-powerful as it is, has not the means to make itself relished without the help of these little arts. Look at Italy, where there is the most beauty for sale, and the finest, and see how it is forced to have recourse to extrinsic means and other artifices to make itself charming — and yet, in truth, whatever it does, being venal and public, it remains feeble and languishing. So too in virtue itself: of two equal effects, we look upon the one as the finer and worthier in which more trouble and risk have been set before us.

It is an effect of divine Providence to allow the holy Church to be afflicted, as we see her, with so many storms and troubles — by this opposition to rouse pious souls, and to wake them from that drowsy lethargy into which, through so long a tranquillity, they had sunk. If we should set the loss we have suffered, in the number of those who have gone astray, against the benefit we have had in being brought to breathe again, and in having our zeal and strength revived by reason of this opposition, I do not know whether the gain would not overtop the damage.

We thought to tie the nuptial knot of our marriages more firm and fast by taking away all means of dissolving it; but the knot of the will and affection is so much the more slackened and loosened the closer the knot of constraint is drawn. And on the contrary, what kept marriages at Rome so long in honour and inviolate was the liberty everyone had to break them at will. They kept their wives the better because they could part with them if they wished; and, in the full liberty of divorce, five hundred years and more passed before anyone made use of it.
"Quod licet, ingratum est; quod non licet, acrius urit."
["What is allowed, gives no pleasure; what is forbidden, sharpens the appetite." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19.]

We might bring in here the opinion of an ancient writer on this point: "That executions rather whet than dull the edge of vices; that they do not breed any care of doing well — that being the work of reason and discipline — but only a care not to be caught in doing ill":
"Latius excisae pestis contagia serpunt."
["The plague-sore, once lanced, spreads its contagion all the more." — Rutilius, Itinerar., i. 397.]
I do not know that this is true; but I know by experience that civil government was never reformed by such means; the order and regulation of manners depend on some other expedient.

The Greek histories make mention of the Argippians, neighbours of Scythia, who live without rod or stick for any offence; where not only does no one attempt to attack them, but whoever can flee to them is safe, by reason of their virtue and sanctity of life, and no one dares lay hands on them — and they have applications made to them to settle the disputes that arise between men of other countries. There is a certain nation where the enclosures of the gardens and fields they want to preserve are made only of a string of cotton; and, so fenced, are more firm and secure than by our hedges and ditches.
"Furem signata sollicitant . . . aperta effractarius praeterit."
["Things sealed up tempt the thief; the housebreaker passes by open doors." — Seneca, Epist., 68.]

Perhaps the openness of my house, among other things, has been a means of preserving it from the violence of our civil wars: defence invites attack, and defiance provokes an enemy. I disabled the soldiers' design by stripping the exploit of danger and of all the military glory that usually serves them as pretext and excuse — for whatever is done bravely is always done honourably, in a time when justice is dead. I render the conquest of my house cowardly and base; it is never shut to anyone who knocks; my gate has no other guard than a porter, and he by ancient custom and ceremony — who does not so much serve to defend it as to offer it with more decorum and grace. I have no other guard or sentinel than the stars. A gentleman would play the fool to make a show of defence if he were not really in a condition to defend himself. He who lies open on one side lies open everywhere. Our ancestors did not think of building frontier garrisons. The means of assaulting — without battery or army, I mean — and of surprising our houses, increases every day more and more beyond the means to guard them; men's wits are generally bent that way; in invasion everyone is concerned; in defence, only the rich. Mine was strong for the time when it was built; I have added nothing to it of that kind, and would be afraid that its strength might turn against me; besides which, we have to bear in mind that a time of peace would require it to be dismantled. There is a danger of never being able to retake it, and it would be very hard to hold; for in intestine quarrels, your own man may be of the party you fear, and where religion is the pretext, even one's nearest relations become unreliable, with some colour of justice. The public exchequer will not maintain our domestic garrisons; they would exhaust it. We ourselves do not have the means to do it without ruin — or, what is more inconvenient and harmful, without ruining the people. The condition of my loss would scarcely be worse. As to the rest, you there lose everything; and even your friends would more readily blame your lack of vigilance, your lack of foresight, your ignorance of and indifference to your own affairs, than pity you. That so many garrisoned houses have been undone, while mine remains, makes me apt to believe that they were lost only by being guarded; this gives an enemy both an invitation and a colour of reason; all defence shows the face of war. Let whoever wishes come to me in God's name; but I shall not invite them. This is the retirement I have chosen for my repose from war. I try to withdraw this corner from the public storm, as I also do another corner in my soul. Our war may take whatever forms it likes, multiply and diversify itself into new parties; for my part, I do not stir. Among so many garrisoned houses, I alone of those of my rank, so far as I know, in France, have trusted purely to Heaven for the protection of mine, and have never removed plate, deeds, or hangings. I will neither fear nor save myself by halves. If a full acknowledgment earns the divine favour, it will stay with me to the end; if not, I have still gone on long enough to make my continuance remarkable and worth recording. How? Why, it has been thirty years that I have lived this way.

chapters.title: Of glory
paragraphs: There is the name, and there is the thing. The name is a sound that denotes and signifies the thing; the name is no part of the thing or of its substance — it is a foreign piece attached to the thing, on the outside. God, who is all fullness in Himself and the height of all perfection, cannot grow or add anything to Himself within; but His name can be magnified and increased by the blessing and praise we attach to His outward works. That praise, since we cannot incorporate it into Him (He being incapable of any further good), we attach to His name, which is the part of Him nearest to us. So glory and honour belong to God alone, and nothing is more contrary to reason than to chase after them for ourselves: poor and needy within, our essence being imperfect and in constant need of improvement, that is where we ought to direct all our effort. We are hollow and empty; it is not with wind and voice that we are to fill ourselves; we need more solid substance to repair us. A man starving with hunger would be very simple to seek a gay garment before a good meal: we are to look after what we most need. As our ordinary prayer puts it:
"Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus."

We lack beauty, health, wisdom, virtue, and the other essential qualities; outward ornaments should be looked after only when the necessities are provided for. Theology treats this subject amply and far more fittingly than I can, but I am not much versed in it.

Chrysippus and Diogenes were the earliest and most committed advocates of contempt for glory; they argued that of all pleasures none is more dangerous, none more to be avoided, than the pleasure that comes from the approval of others. And experience does in fact show us many hurtful treacheries in it. Nothing poisons princes so much as flattery, and nothing makes it easier for the wicked to gain credit and favour with them; no procuring is so apt and so commonly used to corrupt the chastity of women as flattering them with praise of themselves. The first charm the Sirens used to lure Ulysses is of this kind:
"Deca vers nous, deca, o tres-louable Ulysse, Et le plus grand honneur don't la Grece fleurisse."
["Come over to us, come, much-praised Ulysses, greatest ornament and pride of Greece." — Homer, Odyssey, xii. 184.]
These philosophers said that all the glory in the world was not worth a man of sense lifting a finger to obtain:
"Gloria quantalibet quid erit, si gloria tantum est?"
["What is glory, however glorious, if it is only glory?" — Juvenal, Sat., vii. 81.]

I say this of glory taken on its own; for it often brings other goods along with it that are quite reasonably wanted. It earns us goodwill and makes us less exposed to insults and slights from others, and so on. It was also one of the main doctrines of Epicurus: his sect's precept, Conceal your life, which forbids encumbering oneself with public business and office, presupposes contempt for glory — the world's approval of the actions we perform in public. Anyone who tells us to hide ourselves, to have no concern but for ourselves, who would not have us known to others, would still less have us honoured and praised; and so he advises Idomeneus not to regulate his actions by common opinion at all, except so far as needed to avoid the practical inconveniences that the contempt of men might bring upon him.

These arguments are, in my view, very sound and reasonable; but we are, I don't quite know how, double in ourselves, which is why we don't believe what we believe and cannot disengage from what we condemn. Look at the last words of Epicurus, dying: they are grand and worthy of such a philosopher, and yet they contain some hint of self-commendation and of that very humour he had spent his life denouncing. Here is the letter he dictated just before his last gasp:
"EPICURUS TO HERMACHUS, health.

"As I am passing the happy and last day of my life, I write this — at the same time afflicted by such pain in my bladder and bowels that nothing could be greater, but it was repaid by the pleasure that the memory of my discoveries and doctrines brought to my soul. Now, as the affection you have always borne, from your infancy, towards me and philosophy demands, take on the protection of Metrodorus's children."

That is the letter. And the reason I interpret his "pleasure of soul concerning his discoveries" as carrying a reference to the reputation he hoped to leave behind is the form of his will: in it he orders Amynomachus and Timocrates, his heirs, to defray every January the costs of celebrating his birthday as Hermachus should direct, and the expense of entertaining the philosophers, his friends, on the twentieth of each moon, who should assemble in honour of his memory and of Metrodorus.

Carneades took the opposite view: he held that glory was to be desired for its own sake, just as we love our posthumous descendants for their own sake, even though we will have no knowledge or enjoyment of them. This opinion has not failed to be the more widely followed, as is usually the case with views that fit our inclinations. Aristotle gives glory first place among external goods, and avoids as extreme vices either the immoderate pursuit or the immoderate avoidance of it. I think that if we still had the books Cicero wrote on this subject, we should find pretty stories there, for he was so possessed by this passion that, if he had dared, I think he could happily have gone the whole way the others went — saying that virtue itself is not to be valued except for the honour that always attends it:
"Paulum sepultae distat inertiae Celata virtus:"
["Virtue concealed differs little from dead sloth." — Horace, Od., iv. 9, 29.]
An opinion so false that I am sorry it could ever enter the mind of a man who was honoured with the name of philosopher.

If this were true, men need only be virtuous in public; we would have no further reason to keep the operations of the soul — the true seat of virtue — regular and in order, except insofar as they come to the knowledge of others. Is it then a matter only of slyly and circumspectly doing wrong? "If you knew," says Carneades, "of a serpent lurking in a place where, with no warning, someone is about to sit down, by whose death you stood to gain, you do wrong if you do not warn him of the danger; and so much the more because the act would be known to no one but you." If we do not take the rule of right-doing from ourselves, if impunity passes with us for justice, to how many kinds of wickedness will we abandon ourselves every day? I do not find what Sextus Peduceus did — faithfully returning the treasure that C. Plotius had committed to his sole secrecy and trust (a thing I have often done myself) — so very commendable; I should have thought doing otherwise an execrable baseness. And I think it useful in our day to recall the example of P. Sextilius Rufus, whom Cicero accuses of having entered upon an inheritance against his conscience, though not against the law — indeed by the law's own determination; and of M. Crassus and Hortensius, who, because of their authority and power, were called in by a stranger to share in a forged will (so that he could secure his own part), and were content not to have a hand in the forgery while not refusing to take their share. Safe enough, if they could shelter themselves from accusations, witnesses, and the law's notice:
"Meminerint Deum se habere testem, id est (ut ego arbitror) mentem suam."
["Let them remember they have God as witness — that is (as I interpret it), their own conscience." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 10.]

Virtue is a very vain and frivolous thing if it derives its standing from glory; and it is no use trying to give it a station of its own, separate from fortune — for what is more accidental than reputation?
"Profecto fortuna in omni re dominatur: ea res cunctas ex libidine magis, quam ex vero, celebrat, obscuratque."
["Fortune rules in everything; it celebrates or obscures things more out of its own caprice than out of truth." — Sallust, Catilina, c. 8.]

Arranging it so that one's actions are known and seen is purely the work of fortune; it is chance that hands us glory, according to its own whim. I have often seen her go before merit, and often far outstrip it. Whoever first compared glory to a shadow knew better than he realised: both are eminently empty things. Glory, like a shadow, sometimes goes before the body and sometimes stretches out far beyond it. Those who instruct gentlemen to use their courage only for the sake of honour:
"Quasi non sit honestum, quod nobilitatum non sit;"
["As if a thing were not virtuous unless it were famous." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 10.]

what do they teach but never to risk anything unobserved, and to check carefully whether there are witnesses present to bring back the news of their courage? Yet a thousand occasions for good action arise that cannot be noticed. How many brave individual acts are buried in the crowd of a battle? Anyone who takes it on himself to watch another's conduct in such confusion is not very busy fighting himself, and the testimony he gives of his comrades' behaviour is evidence against his own:
"Vera et sapiens animi magnitudo, honestum illud, quod maxime naturam sequitur, in factis positum, non in gloria, judicat."
["True and wise greatness of soul judges that bravery, which most follows nature, consists in deeds rather than in glory." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 19.]

All the glory I claim from my life is that I have lived it quietly — quietly, not according to Metrodorus, or Arcesilaus, or Aristippus, but according to myself. Since philosophy has not found any road to tranquillity that works for everyone in common, let each man look for it on his own.

What do Caesar and Alexander owe the boundless grandeur of their reputations to but fortune? How many men has she snuffed out at the start of their progress, of whom we know nothing, who brought as much courage to the task as they did, if bad luck had not cut them off in their first sortie? Among so many great dangers I do not remember reading anywhere that Caesar was ever wounded; a thousand men have fallen in less dangerous moments than the least of those he went through. An infinite number of brave actions must be performed without witness and lost before one of them counts for anything. A man is not always on top of a breach or at the head of an army, in his general's sight, as if on a stage. He is often surprised between the hedge and the ditch; he has to risk his life over a chicken coop; he has to dislodge four ragged musketeers from a barn; he has to spur out alone from his troop and attempt something solo, as necessity demands. And anyone who watches will find, I believe, that the least glamorous occasions are always the most dangerous, and that in the wars of our own time more good men have been lost on small occasions, in some dispute over a paltry little fort, than in places of great importance where their courage could have been honourably employed.

The man who thinks his death was wasted unless it falls on some signal occasion, instead of illustrating his death, deliberately obscures his life, letting many perfectly fitting occasions for risking himself slip through his hands; and every fitting one is illustrious enough — every man's conscience is sufficient trumpet to him.
"Gloria nostra est testimonium conscientiae nostrae."
["Our glory is the testimony of our conscience." — Corinthians, i. 1.]

The man who is good only that he may be seen to be good, that he may be the better esteemed once it is known, who will only do well on condition that his virtue is known to men — that is a man from whom not much service is to be expected:

"Credo ch'el reste di quel verno, cose Facesse degne di tener ne conto; Ma fur fin'a quel tempo si nascose, Che non a colpa mia s'hor non le conto Perche Orlando a far l'opre virtuose Piu ch'a narrar le poi sempre era pronto; Ne mai fu alcun' de'suoi fatti espresso, Se non quando ebbe i testimonii appresso."

["The rest of the winter, I believe, was spent in deeds worthy of being recounted; but they were so concealed at the time that it is no fault of mine if I cannot tell them now, for Orlando was always more eager to do brave deeds than to narrate them, and none of his actions were ever made known except those that had witnesses present." — Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, xi. 81.]

A man must go to war out of duty, and expect the reward that never fails brave and worthy actions, however private — or even virtuous thoughts: the satisfaction a well-set conscience feels in itself when it acts well. A man must be valiant for his own sake, for the advantage of having his courage lodged in a firm and secure place against the assaults of fortune:
"Virtus, repulsae nescia sordidae, Intaminatis fulget honoribus, Nec sumit, aut ponit secures Arbitrio popularis aurae."
["Virtue, knowing no base rebuff, shines in untainted honours, and neither takes nor lays down dignities at the mere caprice of the popular breeze." — Horace, Od., iii. 2, 17.]

It is not for outward show that the soul has to play its part, but for ourselves inside, where no eyes can pierce but our own; there she defends us from the fear of death, of pain, of shame itself; there she arms us against the loss of our children, our friends, and our fortunes; and when the chance offers, she leads us into the hazards of war:
"Non emolumento aliquo, sed ipsius honestatis decore."
["Not for any profit, but for the honour of honesty itself." — Cicero, De Finib., i. 10.]
This profit is far greater, and far more worth wanting and hoping for, than honour and glory, which are nothing but a favourable judgment passed on us.

A dozen men have to be called out of a whole nation to judge a question of an acre of land; and the judgment of our inclinations and our actions — the most difficult and most important matter there is — we refer to the voice and verdict of the crowd, mother of ignorance, injustice, and inconstancy. Is it reasonable that a wise man's life should depend on the judgment of fools?
"An quidquam stultius, quam, quos singulos contemnas, eos aliquid putare esse universos?"
["Can anything be more foolish than to think that those you despise one by one amount to something taken all together?" — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 36.]
Whoever makes it his business to please them will have plenty to do and never be done; it is a target that can never be aimed at, let alone hit:
"Nil tam inaestimabile est, quam animi multitudinis."
["Nothing is so impossible to gauge as the minds of the multitude." — Livy, xxxi. 34.]
Demetrius said pleasantly of the voice of the people that he made no more account of what came from above than of what came from below. Cicero says more:
"Ego hoc judico, si quando turpe non sit, tamen non esse non turpe, quum id a multitudine laudatur."
["My view is that even if a thing is not foul in itself, it nevertheless cannot help becoming so when commended by the multitude." — Cicero, De Finib., ii. 15.]

No art, no exercise of wit, could steer our steps so as to follow so wandering and irregular a guide. In this windy confusion of vulgar rumours and opinions pushing us around, no path worth anything can be chosen. Let us not set ourselves so floating and shifting a goal; let us follow reason steadily; let public approval follow us along if it likes, and since it depends entirely on fortune, we have no more reason to expect it by any other route than that. Even if I were not inclined to follow the right road because it is right, I would still follow it, having found by experience that, at the end of the reckoning, it is usually the happiest and the most useful.
"Dedit hoc providentia hominibus munus, ut honesta magis juvarent."
["Providence has given men this gift, that honourable things are also the most pleasing." — Quintilian, Inst. Orat., i. 12.]

The old mariner said this to Neptune in a great tempest: "O God, you will save me if you will, and if you choose you will destroy me; but whatever happens, I will hold my rudder straight." I have seen in my time a thousand pliant, half-bred, ambiguous men — none of whom anyone doubted was more worldly-wise than I — lose themselves, where I have saved myself:
"Risi successus posse carere dolos."
["I have laughed to see cunning fail of its success." — Ovid, Heroid., i. 18.]

Paulus Aemilius, setting out on his glorious expedition to Macedonia, charged the people of Rome above all things not to talk about his actions during his absence. The licence of opinions is a great disturbance to great affairs; not everyone has Fabius's firmness against common, hostile, and unjust tongues — he preferred to let his authority be carved up by the vain fancies of men rather than perform his charge less well in order to keep a favourable reputation and the people's applause.
There is some natural sweetness, I don't know what, in hearing oneself praised — but we are far too fond of it:
"Laudari metuam, neque enim mihi cornea fibra est; Sed recti finemque extremumque esse recuso Euge tuum, et belle."
["I would fear to be praised — my heart is not made of horn — but I refuse to admit that 'Excellent! Beautifully done!' are the proper aim and end of virtue." — Persius, i. 47.]

I care not so much what I am in others' opinion as what I am in my own; I would be rich on my own account, not by borrowing. Strangers see only events and outward appearances; anyone can put a good face on it when their insides are trembling with terror — they do not see my heart, they see my face. People are right to deplore the hypocrisy that is in war, for what is easier for an old soldier than to dodge in moments of danger and counterfeit bravery when he has no more heart than a chicken? There are so many ways to avoid putting one's person at risk that we have deceived the world a thousand times before we are actually committed to real danger; and even then, finding ourselves under an unavoidable need to do something, we manage for that moment to hide our fears by putting on a good face, though our hearts pound. Whoever had Plato's ring, which makes whoever wears it invisible when turned palm-inward, would find that a great many people would often hide themselves when they ought most to appear, and would regret being placed in so honourable a post where necessity forces them to be bold.
"Falsus honor juvat, et mendax infamia terret Quem nisi mendosum et mendacem?"
["False honour pleases, lying infamy terrifies — whom else but the guilty and the sickened?" — Horace, Ep., i. 16, 89.]

So we see how all judgments founded on outward appearances are extraordinarily uncertain and questionable, and that there is no surer testimony than each man's to himself. In these things, how many soldiers' boys are companions of our glory? The man who holds steady in an open trench — what is he doing more than the fifty poor sappers who clear the way for him and cover it with their own bodies for fivepence a day?
"Non quicquid turbida Roma Elevet, accedas; examenque improbum in illa Castiges trutina: nec te quaesiveris extra."
["Do not assent if turbulent Rome disparages something; do not correct a false balance by that scale; do not seek yourself outside yourself." — Persius, Sat., i. 5.]

Spreading our names through many mouths is what we call making them great; we want them well received there, and want this circulation to redound to their advantage — which is the only excusable element in the design. But the excess of this disease goes so far that many want a name no matter what kind. Trogus Pompeius says of Herostratus, and Livy of Manlius Capitolinus, that they were more ambitious for a great reputation than for a good one. Very common — we are more anxious that men should speak of us than how they speak of us; it is enough for us that our names are often mentioned, in whatever manner. It looks as though to be known is in some sense to have one's life and its duration held in others' keeping. I, for my part, hold that I exist only in myself; and as for that other life of mine that lies in the knowledge of my friends — considered nakedly and simply in itself — I know perfectly well that I feel no pleasure or enjoyment from it except through the vanity of a fantastic opinion; and once I am dead, I shall feel it still less, and shall meanwhile lose any real advantages that sometimes accidentally follow from it.

I shall have no more handle by which to grasp reputation, nor any by which reputation can grasp me; to expect my name to be advanced by it — in the first place, I have no name properly my own. Of the two I have, one is shared by my whole family, and indeed by others as well: there are two families in Paris and Montpellier whose surname is Montaigne, another in Brittany, and one in Xaintonge, De La Montaigne. The shifting of a single syllable would be enough to tangle our affairs, and I shall share their glory while perhaps they share my discredit; and besides, my ancestors used to be surnamed Eyquem, a name a family well known in England today still bears. As to my other name, anyone may take it who likes, and so I might end up doing honour to a porter in my own stead. And even if I had a distinction all my own, what is there to distinguish, when I am no more? Can it point out and favour nothingness?
"Non levior cippus nunc imprimit ossa? Laudat posteritas! Nunc non e manibus illis, Nunc non a tumulo fortunataque favilla, Nascentur violae?"
["Does the tomb press less heavily on my bones? Does posterity praise me? Not from my shade, not from my tomb, not from the lucky ash will violets grow." — Persius, Sat., i. 37.]

I have spoken of this elsewhere. As for the rest: in a great battle where ten thousand men are maimed or killed, there are not fifteen who get noticed; it must take some real eminence, or some consequence of great importance that fortune adds to it, to make a private action stand out — not just of a musketeer, but even of a great captain. To kill a man, or two, or ten; to expose yourself bravely to the worst peril of death — that is indeed something for each of us, since we risk everything; but from the world's perspective they are things so ordinary, and so many of them are seen every day, and there must be so many of the same kind in succession to produce any notable effect, that we cannot expect any particular fame from it:
"Casus multis hic cognitus, ac jam Tritus, et a medio fortunae ductus acervo."
["The accident is known to many, and now stale; drawn from the middle of fortune's heap." — Juvenal, Sat., xiii. 9.]

Of the many thousands of brave men who have died sword in hand in France in the last fifteen hundred years, not a hundred have come to our knowledge. The memory not just of the commanders, but of the battles and victories themselves, is buried and gone; the fortunes of more than half the world, for want of any record, do not stir from their place and vanish without leaving any duration. If I had unknown events in my possession, I think I could easily outdo what is recorded, in every kind of example. Is it not strange that even of the Greeks and Romans, with all their writers and witnesses, with so many rare and noble exploits, so few have come down to us?
"Ad nos vix tenuis famae perlabitur aura."
["To us scarcely a thin rumour drifts down." — Aeneid, vii. 646.]

It will be a great thing if, a hundred years from now, it is remembered in general that in our day there were civil wars in France. The Lacedaemonians, before going into battle, sacrificed to the Muses, so that their actions might be well and worthily written up; they regarded it as a divine and uncommon favour that brave deeds should find witnesses able to give them life and memory. Do we expect that at every musket-shot we take, at every danger we run, there should be a clerk standing by to record it? And besides, a hundred clerks may write them down whose commentaries will last no longer than three days and never come to anyone's eye. We do not have a thousandth part of the ancient writings; it is fortune that gives them a shorter or longer life, according to her favour, and one may reasonably doubt whether what we have is not the worst — never having seen the rest. People do not write histories of trivial matters: you must have been a general in the conquest of an empire or a kingdom, you must have won fifty-two pitched battles, always with the smaller army, as Caesar did. Ten thousand brave men and many great captains lost their lives valiantly in his service whose names lasted no longer than their wives and children lived:
"Quos fama obscura recondit."
["Whom an obscure reputation conceals." — Aeneid, v. 302.]

Even those whom we see acquit themselves well — three months or three years after they are gone, no more is said of them than if they had never lived. Anyone who considers fairly, and in due proportion, what kind of men and what kind of actions sustain glory in the records of history will find that very few actions and very few persons of our time have any rightful claim there. How many worthy men have we known who outlived their own reputation, who saw and endured the honour and glory most justly earned in their youth extinguished in their very presence? And for three years of this fantastic, imaginary life, we are to throw away our true and essential life, and pledge ourselves to a perpetual death! The wise propose a nobler and juster end in so important an enterprise:
"Recte facti, fecisse merces est: officii fructus, ipsum officium est."
["The reward of doing well is to have done it; the fruit of a service is the service itself." — Seneca, Ep., 8.]

It might be excusable in a painter or another craftsman, or in a rhetorician or grammarian, to try to make himself a name through his works; but acts of virtue are too noble in themselves to seek any reward other than their own value — and certainly not in the vanity of human judgments.

If, however, this false opinion is so useful to the public that it keeps men in their duty; if the people are stirred up by it to virtue; if princes are moved to see the world bless the memory of Trajan and curse that of Nero; if it strikes them to see the name of that great brute, once so terrible and dreaded, freely cursed and reviled by every schoolboy — then by all means let it grow, and be nursed and cherished among us as much as possible. Plato too, bending his whole effort towards making his citizens virtuous, advises them not to despise the people's good opinion and esteem, and says it happens, by a certain divine inspiration, that even the wicked, in word and opinion alike, can rightly distinguish the virtuous from the wicked. Plato and his master are both remarkable, bold artificers in adding divine operations and revelations wherever human force runs out:
"Ut tragici poetae confugiunt ad deum, cum explicare argumenti exitum non possunt:"
["As the tragic poets fly to some god when they cannot work out the resolution of the plot." — Cicero, De Nat. Deor., i. 20.]

It was perhaps for this reason that Timon, mocking him, called him the great manufacturer of miracles. Since men, by their inadequacy, cannot pay themselves enough in real coin, let counterfeit be added on top. It is a method all legislators have used; there is no government that does not have some mixture either of ceremonial pomp or of false belief, serving as a curb to keep the people in their duty. That is why most of them have fabulous origins, enriched with supernatural mysteries — and why bastard religions have gained credit and been countenanced by men of understanding. It is why Numa and Sertorius, to give their men a better opinion of them, fed them this foolery: one claimed that the nymph Egeria, the other that his white hind, brought him all his counsels from the gods. The authority Numa gave to his laws under the patronage of this goddess, Zoroaster, lawgiver of the Bactrians and Persians, gave to his under the name of the god Oromasdes; Trismegistus, lawgiver of the Egyptians, under that of Mercury; Zamolxis, lawgiver of the Scythians, under that of Vesta; Charondas, lawgiver of the Chalcidians, under that of Saturn; Minos, lawgiver of the Cretans, under that of Jupiter; Lycurgus, lawgiver of the Spartans, under that of Apollo; and Draco and Solon, lawgivers of the Athenians, under that of Minerva. And every government has a god at the head of it — the others falsely, that one truly, which Moses set over the Jews at their departure out of Egypt. The religion of the Bedouins, as the Sire de Joinville reports, among other things enjoined a belief that the soul of one of them who died for his prince passed into another body, happier, more beautiful, and stronger than the former — by which they much more readily ventured their lives:
"In ferrum mens prona viris, animaeque capaces Mortis, et ignavum est rediturae parcere vitae."
["Their minds are eager for the sword, their souls capable of death; it is cowardly to spare a life that will be renewed." — Lucan, i. 461.]
A very comforting belief, however mistaken. Every nation has many such examples of its own; but the subject would require a treatise of its own.
To add a word to what has gone before, I would advise the ladies no longer to call by the name of honour what is merely their duty:
"Ut enim consuetudo loquitur, id solum dicitur honestum, quod est populari fama gloriosum;"
["As custom puts it, that alone is called honest which is glorious in public report." — Cicero, De Finibus, ii. 15.]

Their duty is the target; their honour is only the outer rind. Nor would I have them give this excuse as their reason for refusing — I assume that their intentions, their desires, and their wills (things in which their honour is not at all involved, since nothing of them appears outwardly) are much better regulated than the acts:
"Quae quia non liceat, non facit, illa facit:"
["She who only refuses because it is forbidden, consents." — Ovid, Amor., iii. 4, 4.]

The offence, before God and in the conscience, would be as great in the desire as in the deed; and besides, the acts are so private and secret in themselves that they could easily be kept from the knowledge of others — in which the honour consists — were it not for some other respect to their duty, and the affection they bear for chastity in itself. A woman of honour will far rather lose her honour than wound her conscience.

chapters.title: Of presumption
paragraphs: There is another kind of glory — having too good an opinion of our own worth. It is a thoughtless self-love that flatters us, and represents us to ourselves as other than we truly are; like the passion of love, which lends beauties and graces to its object, and makes those caught up in it, with corrupted judgment, consider the thing they love other than it is and more perfect than it is.

I would not, however, for fear of erring on this side, that a man should fail to know himself properly, or think himself less than he is. The judgment ought in all things to keep its rights; it is only reasonable that he should discern in himself, as in others, what truth places before him. If he is Caesar, let him boldly think himself the greatest captain in the world. We are nothing but ceremony: ceremony carries us along and we leave behind the substance of things; we hold onto the branches and let go the trunk and the body. We have taught the ladies to blush when they hear that named which they are not at all afraid to do; we dare not call our members by their right names, yet are not afraid to put them to every kind of debauchery. Ceremony forbids us to express in words what is lawful and natural, and we obey it; reason forbids us to do what is unlawful and wrong, and nobody obeys it. I find myself here hampered by the laws of ceremony, for it permits a man neither to speak well of himself nor ill; we will leave it there for now.

Those whom fortune (call it good or ill) has set in some prominent station can show by their public actions what they are; but those she has only employed in the crowd, of whom no one will say a word unless they speak for themselves, are to be excused if they take the liberty of speaking about themselves to people who have an interest in knowing them — on the precedent of Lucilius:
"Ille velut fidis arcana sodalibus olim Credebat libris, neque si male cesserat, usquam Decurrens alio, neque si bene: quo fit, ut omnis, Votiva pateat veluri descripta tabella Vita senis;"

["He used formerly to confide his secret thoughts to his books, as to tried friends, and resorted to no other refuge, in good times or ill: so it comes about that the old man's whole life is laid out there as on a votive tablet." — Horace, Sat., ii. 1, 30.]
He always committed his actions and his thoughts to paper, and portrayed himself there exactly as he found himself to be:
"Nec id Rutilio et Scauro citra fidem; aut obtrectationi fuit."
["Nor was this thought a breach of good faith or a thing damaging to Rutilius or Scaurus." — Tacitus, Agricola, c. 1.]

I remember, then, that from my infancy I was observed to carry myself in a way, I don't know quite how, that smacked of pride and arrogance.
