One could perhaps imagine so vast a disproportion of measure that the pleasure might justly excuse the sin, as we say happens with utility — not only when the pleasure is accidental and outside the sin, as in theft, but in the very act of sinning, or in the enjoyment of women, where the temptation is violent and, it is said, sometimes not to be overcome.

Being the other day in Armagnac, on the estate of a relative of mine, I saw a peasant whom everyone nicknamed "the thief". This is how he told the story of his life: that being born a beggar, and finding that he would not be able, by the sweat of his brow, to free himself from poverty, he resolved to become a thief, and by means of his bodily strength had practised this trade all through his youth in great safety. For he always made his harvest and his vintage in other men's grounds — but a great way off, and in such quantities that it seemed unbelievable that one man could carry away so much on his shoulders in one night. Furthermore, he was careful to spread out and divide the damage so that the loss was of less importance to any one man in particular. He is now grown old, and rich for a man of his station, thanks to his trade, which he openly confesses to everyone. And to make his peace with God, he says he is daily ready by good offices to make restitution to the heirs of those he has robbed; and if he doesn't finish (which he can't do all at once), he will leave the rest in charge to his heirs, in proportion to the wrong he, and only he, knows he has done each one. By this account, true or false, the man looks on theft as a dishonest action and hates it, but less than he hates poverty, and so simply repents; but to the extent he has thus made restitution, he does not repent. This is not the habit which incorporates us into vice and conforms even our understanding to it; nor is it the impetuous whirlwind that troubles and blinds our soul by gusts and, for the time, hurries us, judgment and all, into the power of vice.

I customarily do thoroughly whatever I do, and take but one step on it; I rarely have any movement that hides itself or steals away from my reason, and that doesn't proceed in the matter by the consent of all my faculties, without division or internal sedition. My judgment gets all the blame or all the praise; and the blame, once it has, it keeps; for from my infancy on, it has always been one and the same — the same inclination, the same turn, the same force. And as for general convictions, I fixed myself from childhood in the place where I resolved to stay. There are sins that are impetuous, prompt, and sudden — let us set them aside. But in these other sins, so often repeated, deliberated, contrived — whether sins of complexion or of profession and vocation — I cannot conceive that they should have lodged themselves so long in the same resolution unless the reason and conscience of the man who has them is steady in wanting to have them; and the repentance he claims is inspired in him on a sudden is very hard for me to imagine or shape. I don't follow the opinion of the Pythagorean sect, "that men take up a new soul when they go to the images of the gods to receive their oracles" — unless they mean that it must indeed be extrinsic, new, and lent for the time; our own showing so little sign of purification and cleanness fit for such an office.

They act quite contrary to the Stoic precepts, who command us to correct the imperfections and vices we are aware of in ourselves but forbid us to disturb the repose of our soul on their account: these people make us believe they have great grief and remorse within them, but they show nothing of amendment, correction, or interruption. It cannot be a cure if the malady isn't entirely discharged; if repentance were placed on the scale of the balance, it would outweigh sin. I know no quality so easy to counterfeit as devotion, if men do not conform their behaviour and life to the profession; its essence is hidden and obscure, the appearance easy and showy.

For my own part, I may desire in general to be other than I am; I may condemn and dislike my whole form, and beg of Almighty God for an entire reformation, and pray that he will please to pardon my natural infirmity. But I ought not to call this repentance, it seems to me, any more than my dissatisfaction at not being an angel or Cato. My actions are regular and conformable to what I am and to my condition; I can do no better; and repentance does not properly touch things that are not in our power — sorrow does. I imagine an infinite number of natures more elevated and well-ordered than mine; and yet I do not for that reason improve my faculties, any more than my arm or will grow stronger and more vigorous from my conceiving someone else's to be so. If our conceiving and wishing for a nobler way of acting than ours should produce repentance for our own way, we should have to repent of our most innocent actions, since we may well suppose that in a more excellent nature they would have been carried out with greater dignity and perfection — and we wish that ours had been so. When I look back on the conduct of my youth and compare it with my old age, I find that I have generally behaved with equal regularity in both, according to my understanding: that is all my resistance can do. I do not flatter myself: in the same circumstances I should do the same things again. It is not a patch but rather a universal tincture with which I am stained. I know no repentance that is superficial, half-hearted, ceremonial; it must sting me all over before I can call it that, and must prick my bowels as deeply and as universally as God sees into me.

As for business, many excellent opportunities have escaped me for want of good management; and yet my decisions were sound enough, given what was before me — they tend always to choose the easiest and safest course. I find that in my past resolves I have proceeded with discretion, according to my own rule and according to the state of the subject proposed; and I should do the same a thousand years from now in like cases. I am not considering what the matter is now, but what it was then, when I was deliberating on it: all the force of advice consists in the time; the occasions and the things shift and change continually. In my life I have made some important mistakes, not for want of good understanding but for want of good luck. There are secret, unforeseen parts in the matters we have in hand — especially in the nature of men — silent conditions that make no show, unknown sometimes even to those who possess them, that spring up and start on the occasion. If my prudence could not penetrate them or foresee them, I do not blame it: it has its commission only within its limits. If the event proves too hard for me, and takes the side I refused, there is no help for it; I do not blame myself, I accuse my fortune and not my work. That cannot be called repentance.

Phocion, having given the Athenians an advice that was not followed, and the affair turning out contrary to his opinion, someone said to him, "Well, Phocion, are you happy that things have gone so well?" — "I am very happy," he replied, "that this has happened so well, but I do not repent giving the other advice." When friends of mine come to me for advice, I give it candidly and clearly, without sticking — as nearly everyone else does — at the risk that the thing might turn out contrary to my opinion and that I might be reproached for my counsel. I am quite indifferent on that score; the fault will be theirs for having consulted me, and I could not refuse them that office.

I, for my own part, can rarely blame anyone but myself for my mistakes and misfortunes; for in truth I seldom ask the advice of another, except by way of polite ceremony, or where I need information, special expertise, or facts. But in things where I need only judgment, the reasons of others may serve to back up my own, but have little power to dissuade me from it; I hear them all with civility and patience, but to my recollection, I have never used any but my own. To me, others' reasons are only flies and atoms, confusing and distracting my will. I lay no great weight on my own opinions; but I lay just as little on those of others, and fortune rewards me accordingly: if I get little advice, I give little too. I am seldom consulted, and even more seldom believed, and I know no business, public or private, that has been mended or bettered by my advice. Even those whom fortune had in some way put under my direction have more willingly let themselves be governed by other counsels than mine. And as a man who is as jealous of my repose as of my authority, I am better pleased that it should be so; in leaving me there, they fall in with what I profess, which is to settle and contain myself wholly within myself. I take pleasure in being uninterested in other men's affairs, and disengaged from being their guarantor and responsible for what they do.

In all affairs that are past, however they turned out, I have very little regret; for this consideration sets me at ease — that they were bound to fall out as they did, in the great revolution of the world, and in the chain of Stoic causes. Your fancy cannot, by wish and imagination, move a single tittle without the great current of things reversing both the past and the future.

As for the rest, I detest that incidental repentance which old age brings with it. The man who said long ago that he was obliged to age for having weaned him from pleasure was of a different mind than I am; I will never think myself indebted to impotence for any good it may do me:
"Nec tam aversa unquam videbitur ab opere suo providentia, ut debilitas inter optima inventa sit."
["Nor can Providence ever seem so averse to her own work that debility should be reckoned among the best of things." — Quintilian, Instit. Orat., v. 12.]

Our appetites are rare in old age; a profound satiety seizes us after the act: in this I see nothing of conscience; chagrin and weakness imprint in us a drowsy and rheumatic virtue. We must not let ourselves be so wholly carried away by natural changes that we let our judgments be imposed on by them. Youth and pleasure did not formerly so far prevail with me that I could not still discern the face of vice in pleasure; nor does the distaste years have brought me now so prevail with me that I cannot discern pleasure in vice. Now that I am no longer in my flourishing age, I judge of these things as well as if I were.
["Old though I am, for ladies' love unfit, / The power of beauty I remember yet." — Chaucer.]

I, who examine it narrowly and strictly, find my reason just the same as it was in my most licentious age — except, perhaps, that it is weaker and more decayed by being grown older. And I find that the pleasure it refuses me on account of my bodily health, it would no more refuse me now, on account of the health of my soul, than at any time before. I do not reckon it the more valiant for not being able to combat; my temptations are so broken and mortified that they are not worth its opposition; holding out my hands, I repel them. Were one to set the old concupiscence before it, I fear it would have less power to resist than before. I cannot see that in itself it now judges anything otherwise than it did before, or that it has gained any new light. Therefore, if there is any convalescence in me, it is an enchanted one. Miserable kind of remedy, to owe one's health to one's disease! It is not for our misfortune to perform this office, but for the good fortune of our judgment. Persecutions and afflictions are not what move me — they make me curse them: that is for people who can only be roused with a whip. My reason is much freer in prosperity, and much more distracted and put to it to digest pains than pleasures. I see best in a clear sky; health admonishes me more cheerfully and to better purpose than sickness. I did all that lay in me to reform and regulate myself away from pleasures at a time when I had health and vigour to enjoy them; I should be ashamed and envious if the misery and misfortune of my old age were to have credit over my good, healthy, sprightly, and vigorous years, and that men should estimate me not by what I have been but by what I have ceased to be.

In my opinion, it is happy living, not (as Antisthenes said) happy dying, that human felicity consists in. I have not made it my business to fix the monstrous addition of a philosopher's tail onto the head and body of a libertine; nor do I want this wretched remainder to give the lie to the pleasant, sound, and long part of my life: I would present myself uniformly throughout. If I were to live my life over again, I should live it just as I have lived it; I neither complain of the past nor fear the future; and if I am not much deceived, I am the same within as I am without. It is one main obligation I owe to my fortune, that the succession of my bodily estate has gone according to the natural seasons; I have seen the grass, the blossom, the fruit, and now I see the withering — happily, however, because naturally. I bear the infirmities I have the better, because they didn't come till I had reason to expect them, and also because they make me remember with greater pleasure the long happiness of my past life. My wisdom may have been just the same in both ages, but it was more active and of better grace while young and lively than now, when it is broken, peevish, and uneasy. So I reject these casual and painful reformations. God must touch our hearts; our consciences must amend of themselves by the help of our reason, not by the decay of our appetites; pleasure is not in itself pale or discoloured, only to be discerned by dim and decayed eyes.

We ought to love temperance for its own sake, and because God has commanded it and chastity; but what we are reduced to by catarrhs, and what I owe to the stone, is neither chastity nor temperance. A man cannot boast he despises and resists pleasure if he cannot see it, if he doesn't know what it is, if he cannot make out its graces, its force, and its most alluring beauties. I know both the one and the other, and may therefore the better say so. But it seems to me that our souls in old age are subject to more troublesome maladies and imperfections than in youth; I said the same when I was young and was reproached for having no beard, and I say it now that my grey hairs give me some authority. We call the difficulty of our humours and our distaste for present things wisdom; but in truth we do not so much forsake our vices as exchange them — and, in my opinion, for worse. Besides a foolish and feeble pride, an impertinent prating, surly and unsociable humours, superstition, and a ridiculous desire for riches when we have lost the use of them, I find there more envy, injustice, and malice. Age leaves more wrinkles in the mind than it does on the face; and souls are never, or very rarely, seen that in growing old do not smell sour and musty. Man moves all together, both toward his perfection and his decay. Observing the wisdom of Socrates and several circumstances of his condemnation, I dare to believe that he in some way deliberately, by collusion, contributed to it, since at the age of seventy he might fear to see the lofty motions of his mind cramped and his accustomed lustre obscured. What strange metamorphoses do I see age make every day in many of my acquaintances! It is a potent malady, and one that naturally and imperceptibly steals into us; a great deal of study and great precaution are needed to avoid the imperfections it loads us with, or at least to slow their progress. I find that, in spite of all my entrenchments, it gets foot by foot upon me; I resist as best I can, but I do not know what at last it will reduce me to. But come what may, I am content for the world to know, when I have fallen, from what I fell.

chapters.title: Of three commerces
paragraphs: We must not rivet ourselves so fast to our humours and temperaments: our chief ability is to know how to apply ourselves to different employments. It is to be, but not to live, to keep oneself tied and bound by necessity to a single course; the bravest souls are those that have in them the most variety and pliancy. Here is an honourable testimony of the elder Cato:
"Huic versatile ingenium sic pariter ad omnia fuit, ut natum ad id unum diceres, quodcumque ageret."
["His gifts were so pliable to every use that you would have said he had been born only for whatever he happened to be doing." — Livy, xxxix. 49.]

If I had the liberty to fashion myself in my own mode, there is no manner so graceful that I would so fix myself to it as not to be able to disengage from it. Life is an unequal, irregular, and multiform motion. It is not to be a friend to oneself, much less a master, but a slave, to be incessantly led by the nose by one's self, and to be so fixed in one's previous inclinations that one cannot turn aside or wrench one's neck out of the collar. I say this now in this part of my life when I find I cannot easily disengage myself from the importunity of my own soul, which cannot ordinarily occupy itself but in things of limited range, nor employ itself except entirely and with all its force. On the lightest subject thrown to it, it expands and stretches itself to that degree that it employs its utmost powers on it; so that idleness is a very painful labour to me, and very damaging to my health. Most men's minds need foreign matter to exercise and enliven them; mine has rather a need of it to sit still and rest:
"Vitia otii negotio discutienda sunt,"
["The vices of idleness must be shaken off by business." — Seneca, Ep. 56.]

— for its chief and hardest study is to study itself. Books are a sort of employment for it that draws it away from that study. With the first thoughts that take possession of it, it begins to bustle and test its vigour in every direction, exercising its powers of handling — now testing its strength, now fortifying, moderating, and arranging itself by way of grace and order. It has of its own enough to rouse its faculties: nature has given it, as it has given everyone else, matter enough of its own to take advantage of, and subjects fit enough on which it may either invent or judge.

Meditation is a strong and full study for those who can effectively taste it and apply themselves to it; I would rather shape my soul than furnish it. There is no employment, either feebler or stronger, than that of entertaining one's own thoughts, depending on what kind of soul one has; the greatest men make it their whole business,
"Quibus vivere est cogitare;"
["For whom to live is to think." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 28.]

— nature has therefore favoured it with this privilege, that there is nothing we can do for so long, nor any action we more often and easily give ourselves up to. It is the business of the gods, says Aristotle, and the source of both their beatitude and ours.

The main use of reading, for me, is that by its various objects it rouses my reason and exercises my judgment — not my memory. Few conversations hold me without effort and strain. It is true that beauty and elegance of speech take with me as much as, or more than, the weight and depth of the subject; and since I am apt to be sleepy in all other kinds of talk and give only the rind of my attention, it often happens that in such poor and pitiful conversations — mere chatter — I either make drowsy, unmeaning answers, unbecoming a child and ridiculous, or, more foolishly and rudely still, keep an obstinate silence. I have a pensive way that withdraws me into myself; and along with that, a heavy and childish ignorance of many very ordinary things — by which two qualities I have earned this, that people can truly tell five or six tales as ridiculous about me as about any other man whatever.

But, to proceed with my subject, this difficult constitution of mine makes me very particular about the company I keep with men: I must select and pick them out for my purpose; and it unfits me for common society. We live and have to deal with the public; if their conversation is troublesome to us, if we disdain to apply ourselves to ordinary and vulgar souls (and the ordinary and vulgar are often as regular as those of the finest thread, and all wisdom is folly that does not accommodate itself to the common ignorance), we must give up meddling either with other people's affairs or our own; for business, both public and private, has to do with such people. The least forced and most natural motions of the soul are the finest; the best employments are those least strained. My God, what a good office wisdom does those whose desires it limits to their power! That is the most useful knowledge: "according to what a man can," was Socrates' favourite saying and motto. A motto of great solidity.

We must moderate and adapt our desires to the nearest and easiest things to obtain. Is it not a foolish whim of mine to separate myself from a thousand people to whom my fortune has joined me, and without whom I cannot live, and cleave to one or two who are outside my circle — or rather a fantastic desire for something I cannot obtain? My gentle and easy manners, enemies of all sourness and harshness, may easily enough have saved me from being envied or hated; to be loved, I won't say, but no man ever gave less occasion to be hated. Yet the coldness of my conversation has, reasonably enough, deprived me of the goodwill of many, who may be excused if they interpret it in another and worse sense.

I am very capable of contracting and maintaining rare and exquisite friendships; for since I so greedily seize on the acquaintances that suit my liking, I throw myself with such violence on them that I hardly fail to stick fast and to leave an impression wherever I hit — as I have often happily proven. In ordinary friendships I am somewhat cold and shy, because my motion is not natural when not under full sail. Besides, my fortune having in my youth given me a taste for one sole and perfect friendship, has, in truth, made others somewhat distasteful to me, and stamped too deeply on my mind that friendship is a beast of company, as the ancient said, but not of the herd. I also have a natural difficulty in communicating myself by halves, with the qualifications and the servile, jealous prudence required in the company of numerous and imperfect friendships — and we are mostly thrust onto these in this age of ours, when we cannot talk about the world except either with danger or in falsehood.

Yet I see clearly enough that anyone who has the conveniences of life (I mean the essential conveniences) for his end, as I do, should avoid these difficulties and this delicacy of humour as much as the plague. I would praise a soul of several storeys, that knows both how to stretch itself and to slacken — that finds itself at ease in every condition fortune leads it into; that can talk with a neighbour about his building, his hunting, his quarrels; that can chat with a carpenter or a gardener with pleasure. I envy those who can render themselves familiar with the meanest of their followers and talk with them in their own way; and I dislike Plato's advice, that men should always speak in a magisterial tone to their servants, men or women, without sometimes being playful and familiar; for besides the reasons I have given, it is inhumane and unjust to put such great value on this pitiful prerogative of fortune. The polities where less disparity is permitted between masters and servants seem to me the most equitable. Others study how to raise and elevate their minds; I, how to humble mine and to bring it low; it is only vicious in its expansion:
"Narras et genus AEaci, Et pugnata sacro bella sub Ilio Quo Chium pretio cadum Mercemur, quis aquam temperet ignibus, Quo praebente domum, et quota, Pelignis caream frigoribus, taces."

["You tell us long tales about the race of Aeacus, and the battles fought under sacred Ilium; but what to give for a cask of Chian wine, who will prepare the warm bath, in whose house, and when I may escape the Pelignian cold — that you do not tell us." — Horace, Od., iii. 19, 3.]

Thus, as the Lacedaemonian valour needed moderation, and the sweet and harmonious sound of flutes to soften it in battle, lest they should rush themselves into rashness and fury — whereas other nations commonly use harsh and shrill sounds, and loud and imperious cries, to incite and heat the soldier's courage to the last degree — so too, in my opinion, contrary to the usual method, in the conduct of our minds we have for the most part more need of lead than of wings, of temperance and composure than of ardour and agitation. But, above all, I think it egregiously foolish to put on the grave airs of a man of lofty mind among those who are nothing of the sort: forever to speak in print (as if by the book),
"Favellare in puma di forchetta."
["To talk with the point of a fork," i.e. affectedly.]

You must let yourself down to those you converse with, and sometimes affect ignorance; lay aside power and subtlety in common talk; to preserve decorum and order, that is enough — nay, crawl on the earth, if they so wish.

The learned often stumble at this stone; they will always be parading their pedantic science and strewing their books everywhere; in our day they have so filled the cabinets and the ears of ladies with them that if the ladies have lost the substance, they at least retain the words; so that in any kind of talk, on whatever subject, however mean and common, they speak and write in a new and learned way,
"Hoc sermone pavent, hoc iram, gaudia, curas, Hoc cuncta effundunt animi secreta; quid ultra? Concumbunt docte;"

["In this language they express their fears, their anger, their joys, their cares; in this they pour out all the secrets of their souls; what more? They lie with their lovers learnedly." — Juvenal, vi. 189.]

— and quote Plato and Aquinas on matters the first man they meet could settle as well. The learning that cannot penetrate their souls hangs still upon the tongue. If people of quality would be persuaded by me, they should be content to set out their own proper and natural treasures: they conceal and cover their beauties under others that are not theirs. It is great folly to put out one's own light and shine by a borrowed lustre; they are buried under "de capsula totae" — completely out of their box. It is because they don't sufficiently know themselves or do themselves justice: the world has nothing fairer than them; it's for them to honour the arts and to paint painting itself. What need have they of anything but to live loved and honoured? They have and know but too much for that purpose: they need only rouse and warm a little the faculties they have of their own. When I see them tampering with rhetoric, law, logic, and other such drugs — so improper and unnecessary for their business — I begin to suspect that the men who fill them with such notions do it that they may govern them on that account; for what other excuse can I find? It is enough that, without our instruction, they can compose the graces of their eyes for gaiety, gravity, or sweetness, and season a refusal with sharpness, suspense, or favour; they need no one else to interpret what we say in their service. With this knowledge, they command with a switch, and rule both the tutors and the schools. But if, nevertheless, it angers them to give place to us in anything whatever, and they will out of curiosity have their share in books, poetry is a diversion proper for them: a wanton, subtle, dissembling, prating art, all pleasure and all show, like themselves. They may also extract several commodities from history. From philosophy, out of its moral part, they may select such instructions as will teach them to judge of our humours and conditions, to defend themselves from our treacheries, to regulate the ardour of their own desires, to manage their liberty, to lengthen the pleasures of life, and gently to bear the inconstancy of a lover, the rudeness of a husband, the encroachment of years and wrinkles, and the like. This is the utmost I would allow them in the sciences.

There are some particular natures that are private and retired; my natural way is suited to communication and apt to lay me open. I am all without and in sight, born for society and friendship. The solitude that I love myself and recommend to others is chiefly nothing other than to withdraw my thoughts and affections into myself: to restrain and check, not my steps, but my own cares and desires; resigning all foreign solicitude, and avoiding to death servitude and obligation, and not so much the crowd of men as the crowd of business. Local solitude, to tell the truth, rather gives me more room and sets me more at large; I more readily throw myself onto affairs of state and of the world when I am alone. At the Louvre and in the bustle of the court, I fold myself within my own skin; the crowd pushes me back onto myself; and I never entertain myself so wantonly, with so much licence, or so particularly, as in places of respect and ceremonious caution. Our follies do not make me laugh; it is our wisdom that does. I am not by nature an enemy of court life; I have spent part of mine there, and am of a temperament cheerfully to frequent great company, provided it be at intervals and at my own time. But this delicacy of judgment I'm speaking of perforce ties me to solitude. Even at home, amid a numerous family and in a house frequently visited, I see people enough, but rarely such as I delight to converse with; and I there reserve, both for myself and others, an unusual liberty: there is in my house no such thing as ceremony, ushering, or seeing people down to the coach, and other such troublesome ceremonies as our politeness enjoins (O servile and importunate custom!). Everyone there governs himself by his own method; let whoever wishes speak his thoughts; I sit mute, meditating and shut up in my closet, without any offence to my guests.

The men whose society and familiarity I covet are those they call sincere and able men; and the image of these makes me disrelish the rest. It is, rightly understood, the rarest of our forms, and a form we chiefly owe to nature. The end of this commerce is simply intimacy, frequenting and conferring, the exercise of souls, without any other fruit. In our conversations, all subjects are alike to me; whether there is weight or depth or not, it is all one; there is always grace and pertinency; everything in them is tinted with a mature and constant judgment, and mixed with goodness, freedom, gaiety, and friendship. It is not only in talking of the affairs of kings and state that our wits show their force and beauty, but every bit as much in private conferences. I know my men by their silences and their smiles, and discover them better, perhaps, at table than in council. Hippomachus said very well that he could tell good wrestlers just by seeing them walk in the street. If learning chooses to step into our talk, it shall not be rejected — not magisterial, imperious, and obtrusive, as it commonly is, but subordinate and docile itself: we are there only to pass the time. When we want to be instructed and preached at, we will go look for that on its throne; let it humble itself to us for the moment. For useful and profitable as it is, I imagine we can, when need be, manage well enough without it, and do our business without its help. A well-born soul, practised in the conversation of men, will of herself render herself sufficiently agreeable; art is nothing but the counterpart and register of what such souls produce.
The conversation of beautiful and honourable women is also a sweet commerce to me:
"Nam nos quoque oculos eruditos habemus."
["For we too have eyes that are versed in the matter." — Cicero, Paradox, v. 2.]

If the soul has not so much to enjoy in this commerce as in the first, the bodily senses, which participate more here, bring it to a level next to it — though, in my opinion, not equal to it. But it is a commerce in which one must stand a little on his guard, especially someone like me in whom the body can do much. I scalded myself in my youth at it, and suffered all the torments that poets say befall those who fling themselves into love without order and judgment. It is true that that whipping has made me wiser since:
"Quicumque Argolica de classe Capharea fugit, Semper ab Euboicis vela retorquet aquis."
["Whoever of the Greek fleet escaped the Caphareus rocks ever takes care to steer clear of the Euboean sea." — Ovid, Trist., i. 1, 83.]

It is folly to fix all one's thoughts upon it and engage in it with a furious and indiscreet affection; but on the other hand, to engage there without love and without inclination, like an actor, to play a common part, putting in nothing of one's own but words, is to provide for one's safety, but in as cowardly a way as one who would abandon his honour, profit, or pleasure for fear of danger. For it is certain that from such a practice, those who set it on foot can expect no fruit that can please or satisfy a noble soul. A man must, in good earnest, have desired what he, in good earnest, expects to take pleasure in enjoying; I say this even though fortune should unjustly favour their dissembling — which often happens, because there is no woman, however ugly as the devil, who does not think herself worthy to be loved, and who does not prefer herself before other women, whether for her youth, the colour of her hair, or her graceful walk (for there are no more universally ugly women than there are universally beautiful ones; and such Brahmin virgins as have nothing else to recommend them, the people being assembled by the common crier for the purpose, come out into the marketplace to expose their marriageable parts to public view, to try whether these at least may not be tempting enough to get them a husband). Consequently there is not one of them who does not readily let herself be overcome by the first vow her suitor makes to serve her. Now from this common, everyday treachery of the men of our day, that must follow which we already see by experience: either women rally together and separate themselves off, to avoid us, or else they discipline themselves on the example we give them, play their parts in the farce as we do ours, and give themselves up to the sport without passion, care, or love;
"Neque affectui suo, aut alieno, obnoxiae;"
["Subject neither to their own affections nor to those of others." — Tacitus, Annal., xiii. 45.]

believing, with the persuasion of Lysias in Plato, that they may with more profit and convenience surrender themselves to us the less they love us. Then it will turn out as in comedies, where the audience has as much pleasure as the actors, or more. For my part, I no more acknowledge a Venus without a Cupid than a mother without children: they are things that mutually lend and owe their essence to each other. Thus this cheat recoils on him who is guilty of it; it does not cost him much, indeed, but he also gets little or nothing by it. Those who have made Venus a goddess have noted that her chief beauty was incorporeal and spiritual; but the Venus these people hunt after is not even human, nor indeed brutal — the very beasts will not accept it so coarse and so earthbound. We see that imagination and desire often heat and stir them before the body does; we see in both sexes that, in the herd, they have choice and particular preference in their affections, and that they have among themselves a long commerce of goodwill. Even those whom old age denies the practice of their desire still tremble, whinny, and twitter for love; we see them, before the act, full of hope and ardour; and when the body has played its game, still please themselves with the sweet remembrance of the past delight; some swell with pride after they have performed; others, tired and sated, still express a triumphal joy by their cries. He whose only business is to discharge his body of a natural necessity does not need to trouble others with such elaborate preparations: it is not meat for a gross, coarse appetite.

Since I have no desire that anyone should think me better than I am, I will say this here about the errors of my youth. Not only because of the danger of impairing my health (and yet I could not be so careful but that I had two light mishaps), but also out of a feeling of contempt, I have seldom given myself up to common and mercenary embraces. I would heighten the pleasure by difficulty, by desire, and a certain kind of glory; and I was of Tiberius's mind, who in his amours was as much taken with modesty and birth as with any other quality; and of the courtesan Flora's humour, who never lent herself to less than a dictator, a consul, or a censor, and took pleasure in the dignity of her lovers. Doubtless pearls and gold tissue, titles and train, add something to it.

For the rest, I had a great esteem for wit — provided the person was not objectionable. For, to tell the truth, if one or the other of these two attractions had to be absent, I would rather have lost the understanding part, which has its use in better things; but in the matter of love, a subject mainly concerning the senses of sight and touch, something can be done without the graces of the mind; without the graces of the body, nothing. Beauty is the true prerogative of women, and so peculiarly their own that ours, though it naturally requires a different sort of feature, is never at its best except when youthful and beardless — a sort of confused image of theirs. They say that those who serve the Grand Signior on account of beauty, who are an infinite number, are at the latest dismissed by the age of twenty-two. Reason, prudence, and the offices of friendship are better found among men, and that is why they govern the affairs of the world.

These two engagements are accidental and depend on others; the one is troublesome by its rarity, the other withers with age, so that they could never have been sufficient for the business of my life. That of books, which is the third, is far more certain, and far more our own. It yields the other advantages to the first two, but has the constancy and ease of its service as its own share. It goes step by step with me my whole course, and everywhere it stands by me; it comforts me in old age and in solitude; it eases me of the troublesome burden of idleness, and delivers me at any hour from company I dislike; it blunts the point of griefs, if they are not extreme and have not got total possession of my soul. To divert myself from a troublesome fancy, I have only to run to my books; they at once fix me on them and chase the other out of my thoughts; and they don't mutiny at seeing that I have recourse to them only for want of other, more real, natural, and lively comforts; they always receive me with the same kindness. He may well walk on foot, they say, who leads his horse in his hand; and our James, King of Naples and Sicily, who, handsome, young, and healthy, had himself carried about on a barrow, stretched out on a pitiful mattress, in a poor robe of grey cloth and a cap of the same, yet attended by a royal train, litters, led horses of all sorts, gentlemen and officers — even he represented thereby a tender and unsteady authority: "The sick man has no cause to complain who has his cure in his sleeve." In the experience and practice of this maxim, which is a very true one, lies all the benefit I get from books. In fact, I make no more use of them, so to speak, than those who know them not. I enjoy them as misers do their money, in knowing that I may enjoy them whenever I please; my mind is satisfied with this right of possession. I never travel without books, in peace or in war; and yet sometimes I pass several days, even months, without looking at them. I'll read by and by, I say to myself, or tomorrow, or whenever I please; and meanwhile time slips away without inconvenience. For it is unimaginable how much I please myself and rest content in this thought, that I have them by me to divert myself with whenever I am so disposed, and in remembering what a refreshment they are to my life. It is the best provision I have yet found for this human journey, and I very much pity men of understanding who lack it. I more readily accept any other kind of diversion, however slight, because this one can never fail me.

When at home, I more often visit my library, from which I overlook at once all the concerns of my household. It is situated at the entrance of my house, and I see from there beneath me my garden, courtyard, and back court, and nearly every part of the building. There I turn over now one book, then another, on various subjects, without method or design. Sometimes I meditate; sometimes I record, and dictate as I walk to and fro, such whimsies as these I am setting down for you. It is on the third storey of a tower, of which the ground room is my chapel, the second a chamber with a withdrawing room and closet where I often lie to be more retired; and above is a great wardrobe. This used to be the most useless part of the house. I pass there most of the days of my life, and most of the hours of those days. I am never there at night. Beside it is a cabinet handsome enough, with a fireplace very conveniently contrived, and plenty of light; and were I not more afraid of the trouble than the expense — the trouble that frightens me from all business — I could easily add on either side, on the same floor, a gallery a hundred paces long and twelve wide, having found walls already raised for some other design to the requisite height. Every place of retirement requires a walk: my thoughts go to sleep if I sit still; my fancy doesn't move by itself the way it does when my legs move it; and all those who study without a book are in the same condition. The shape of my study is round, and there is no more open wall than is taken up by my table and chair, so that the rest of the circle presents me a view of all my books at once, ranged on five rows of shelves around me. It has three noble and free prospects, and is sixteen paces across. I am not so continually there in winter, for my house stands on an eminence, as its name implies, and no part of it is so exposed to the wind and weather as this — which pleases me the better, for being of more difficult access and a little remote, both for the sake of exercise and as being there more withdrawn from the crowd. There I am in my kingdom, and there I endeavour to make myself an absolute monarch, and to sequester this one corner from all society — conjugal, filial, and civil. Elsewhere I have only verbal authority, of a confused essence. That man, in my opinion, is very wretched who hasn't somewhere at home where he can be by himself, where he can entertain himself alone, or hide from others. Ambition plagues her converts well enough by keeping them always in show, like the statue in a public square:
"Magna servitus est magna fortuna."
["A great fortune is a great slavery." — Seneca, De Consol. ad Polyb., c. 26.]

They cannot even be private in the water-closet. I have found nothing so severe in the austerity of life that our monks practise as what I have observed in some of their communities — namely, by rule, to have a perpetual society of place, and many persons present at every act whatever; and I think it much more bearable to be always alone than never to be so.

If anyone tells me that it is to undervalue the Muses to use them only for sport and to pass away the time, I shall tell him he does not know as well as I do the value of the sport, the pleasure, and the pastime; I can hardly help adding that any other end is ridiculous. I live from day to day, and, with reverence be it spoken, I live only for myself: there all my designs end. I studied, when young, for show; later, to make myself a little wiser; and now for my diversion — but never for profit. A vain and prodigal humour I once had for this kind of furniture, not just for supplying my own need but for ornament and outward show, I have since quite cured myself of.

Books have many charming qualities for those who know how to choose them; but every good has its ill; it's a pleasure that is not pure and clean, any more than others — it has its drawbacks, and great ones. The soul, it is true, is exercised in it; but the body, the care of which I must on no account neglect, remains meanwhile inactive, and grows heavy and sombre. I know no excess more harmful to me, nor more to be avoided, in this my declining age.
These have been my three favourite and particular occupations; I am not speaking here of those I owe the world by civil obligation.

chapters.title: Of diversion
paragraphs: I was once employed in consoling a lady who was truly afflicted. Most of their mournings are artificial and ceremonious:
"Uberibus semper lacrymis, semperque paratis, In statione subatque expectantibus illam, Quo jubeat manare modo."
["A woman has always a fountain of tears ready to gush forth whenever she wishes to make use of them." — Juvenal, vi. 272.]

A man goes the wrong way to work when he opposes this passion; for opposition only irritates it and makes them more obstinate in their sorrow; the trouble is sharpened by argument. We see, in ordinary conversation, that something I have casually let drop, if anyone takes it up to contradict it, I defend with the best arguments I have — and far more so a thing in which I had a real interest. Besides, by doing so you enter roughly on your operation; whereas the first approach of a physician to his patient should be gracious, cheerful, and pleasing; never did any ill-looking, morose physician achieve anything. On the contrary, then, a man should at first favour their grief and show some approval of their sorrow. By this rapport you earn the credit to go further, and by an easy and imperceptible gradation fall into discourses more solid and more proper for their cure. I, whose main aim was to fool the company who had their eyes on me, took it into my head only to palliate the disease. And indeed I have found by experience that I have an unlucky hand at persuading. My arguments are either too sharp and dry, or pressed too roughly, or not driven home enough. After I had applied myself to her grief for some time, I did not attempt to cure her by strong and lively reasons, either because I had none at hand, or because I thought I could do my business better another way. Nor did I make use of any of the methods of consolation philosophy prescribes: that what we complain of is no evil, according to Cleanthes; that it is a slight evil, according to the Peripatetics; that to bemoan oneself is an action neither commendable nor just, according to Chrysippus; nor Epicurus's, more suited to my way, of shifting one's thoughts from afflicting things to pleasing ones; nor of bundling all these together to be used as the occasion calls, according to Cicero. But by gently bending my discourse, and digressing little by little, sometimes to subjects nearer, sometimes more remote from the purpose, as she gave me more or less attention, I imperceptibly led her away from that sorrowful thought, and kept her calm and in good humour while I stayed there. I made use of diversion. Those who came after me in the same service found no improvement in her, for I had not gone to the root.

I may, perhaps, have glanced elsewhere at some kind of public diversion. And the practice of military diversion, which Pericles used in the Peloponnesian war, and a thousand others in other places — to draw the enemy's forces out of their own country — is too common in history to need mention. It was an ingenious device by which Monseigneur d'Hempricourt saved both himself and others in the city of Liège, into which the Duke of Burgundy, who was besieging it, had made him enter to carry out the articles of their promised surrender. The people, assembled by night to deliberate on it, began to mutiny against the agreement, and several of them resolved to fall upon the commissioners, whom they had in their power. He, sensing the gusts of this first popular storm coming to break upon his lodgings, suddenly sent out to them two of the citizens (some of whom were with him) with new and milder terms to be proposed in their council, terms he had improvised then and there to meet his need. These two diverted the first tempest, carrying the enraged crowd back to the town hall to hear and consider what they had to say. The deliberation was short; a second storm arose as violent as the first. Whereupon he dispatched four new mediators of the same standing to meet them, protesting that he had now better conditions to present, ones that would entirely satisfy them; by this means the tumult was again calmed, and the people once more turned back to the council chamber. In short, by this dispensation of distractions, one after another, diverting their fury and dissipating it in frivolous consultations, he at last laid it to sleep until day broke — which was his principal aim.

This other story is of the same kind. Atalanta, a virgin of exceeding beauty and wonderful build of body, to disengage herself from the crowd of a thousand suitors who sought her hand, made this proposal: that she would accept as her husband whoever could equal her in running, on condition that those who failed should lose their lives. There were plenty who thought the prize well worth the risk, and who suffered the cruel penalty of the contract. Hippomenes, about to make his trial after the rest, addressed himself to the goddess of love, imploring her help; she, granting his request, gave him three golden apples, and instructed him how to use them. The race begun, as Hippomenes saw his mistress pressing hard upon him, he, as if by chance, let fall one of the apples; the maiden, taken with its beauty, did not fail to step out of her way to pick it up:
"Obstupuit Virgo, nitidique cupidine pomi Declinat cursus, aurumque volubile tollit."
["The virgin, astonished and drawn by the glittering apple, halts her course and seizes the rolling gold." — Ovid, Metam., x. 666.]

He did the same when he saw his chance with the second and the third, until by so diverting her, and making her lose so much ground, he won the race. When physicians cannot stop a catarrh, they divert and turn it into some other less dangerous part. And I find this is also the most ordinary practice for the diseases of the mind:
"Abducendus etiam nonnunquam animus est ad alia studia, sollicitudines, curas, negotia: loci denique mutatione, tanquam aegroti non convalescentes, saepe curandus est."

["The mind must sometimes be drawn off to other studies, thoughts, cares, business; and finally cured by change of place, as sick persons who are not recovering must be." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 35.]
It is to little effect to directly jostle a man's infirmities; we don't make him bear the attack, nor repel it; we only make him decline and evade it.

This other lesson is too high and too difficult: it is for men in the first rank of knowledge to insist purely on the thing, to consider and judge it; it belongs to only one Socrates to meet death with an ordinary countenance, to grow acquainted with it and to sport with it. He seeks no consolation from outside the thing itself; dying appears to him a natural and indifferent accident; it is there that he fixes his sight and his resolution, without looking elsewhere. The disciples of Hegesias, who starved themselves to death — drawn to it by his fine lectures, and in such numbers that King Ptolemy ordered him forbidden to entertain his followers with such homicidal doctrines — did not consider death in itself, nor judge of it; that is not where they fixed their thoughts; they were running toward and aiming at a new state of being.

The poor wretches we see brought to the scaffold, full of ardent devotion, and in it, as much as they can, employing all their senses — their ears in hearing the instructions given them, their eyes and hands lifted toward heaven, their voices in loud prayers, with a vehement and continual emotion — do, no doubt, things very commendable and proper for such a need; we must commend them for their devotion, but not properly for their constancy: they shun the encounter, they divert their thoughts from the consideration of death, as children are diverted with some toy when the surgeon is about to prick them with his lancet. I have seen some who, casting their eyes on the dreadful instruments of death set out around them, have fainted, and furiously turned their thoughts another way. Those who are to pass over a fearful precipice are advised either to shut their eyes or look another way.

Subrius Flavus, being ordered by Nero's command to be put to death by the hand of Niger, both of them great captains, when they led him to the place appointed for his execution, seeing the grave that Niger had had hollowed for him to be put into ill-made, said, turning to the soldiers who guarded him, "This is not even according to military discipline." And to Niger, who exhorted him to keep his head firm: "Just strike as firmly," he said. And he saw very well what would follow when he said so; for Niger's arm trembled so that he had to strike several blows at his head before he could cut it off. This man seems to have had his thoughts rightly fixed on his subject.

He who dies in battle, with his sword in his hand, does not then think about death; he feels it and considers it not; the ardour of the fight diverts his thought another way. A worthy man of my acquaintance, falling as he was fighting a duel and feeling himself nailed to the earth by nine or ten thrusts from his enemy, was urged on all sides to think of his conscience; but he later told me that, though he heard well enough what they said, it didn't move him at all, and that he thought of nothing but how to disengage and take his revenge. He afterwards killed his man in that very duel. He who brought to L. Silanus the sentence of death did him a very great kindness: for, having received Silanus's answer that he was well prepared to die but not by base hands, he ran upon him with his soldiers to force him; and as Silanus, unarmed as he was, obstinately defended himself with his fists and feet, the messenger made him lose his life in the struggle — in doing so dispelling and diverting, in a sudden and furious rage, the painful apprehension of the lingering death he had been designed for.

We always think of something else; either the hope of a better life comforts and supports us, or the hope of our children's worth, or the future glory of our name, or the leaving behind of this life's evils, or the vengeance that threatens those who are the cause of our death — these console us:
"Spero equidem mediis, si quid pia numina possunt, Supplicia hausurum scopulis, et nomine Dido Saepe vocaturum . . . . Audiam; et haec Manes veniet mihi fama sub imos."

["I hope, however, if the pious gods have any power, you will drink your punishment among the rocks, and will call on the name of Dido; I shall hear, and this report will come to me below." — Aeneid, iv. 382, 387.]

Xenophon was sacrificing, with a crown on his head, when someone came to tell him of the death of his son Gryllus, killed in the battle of Mantinea: at the first shock of the news, he threw his crown to the ground; but, learning from the rest of the report the manner of so brave and valiant a death, he picked it up again and put it back on his head. Epicurus himself, at his death, consoles himself with the usefulness and eternity of his writings:
"Omnes clari et nobilitati labores fiunt tolerabiles;"
["All labours that are illustrious and famous become bearable." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 26.]

— and the same wound, the same fatigue, is not, says Xenophon, so intolerable to a general of an army as to a common soldier. Epaminondas took his death much more cheerfully when he had been told that the victory remained with him:
"Haec sunt solatia, haec fomenta summorum dolorum;"
["These are the sedatives and salves of the greatest pains." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 23.]

— and such circumstances divert, amuse, and turn our thoughts from the consideration of the thing in itself. Even the arguments of philosophy are always edging and glancing along the matter, scarcely rubbing its crust. The greatest man of the first philosophical school, and superintendent over all the rest, the great Zeno, frames this syllogism against death: "No evil is honourable; but death is honourable; therefore death is no evil." Against drunkenness this: "No one entrusts his secrets to a drunkard; but everyone entrusts his secrets to a wise man; therefore a wise man is no drunkard." Is this hitting the bull's-eye? I love seeing that these great and leading souls cannot rid themselves of our company: perfect as they are, they are still simply men.

Revenge is a sweet passion, of great and natural impression; I see that well enough, though I have no experience of it. Not long ago, to divert a young prince from it, I did not tell him he must, to one who had struck him on the one cheek, turn the other, for the sake of charity; nor did I set out to represent for him the tragic events poetry attributes to that passion. I left that aside; and I busied myself making him relish the beauty of a contrary picture: representing to him what honour, esteem, and goodwill he would gain by clemency and good nature, I diverted him to ambition. That is how a man is to deal in such cases.

If your passion of love is too violent, disperse it, they say — and they speak truly, for I have often tried it with good results: break it into several desires, and let one be regent over the rest if you like; but, lest it tyrannize and lord it over you, weaken and dilute it by dividing and diverting it:
"Cum morosa vago singultiet inguine vena,"
["When you are tormented with fierce desire, satisfy it with the first person who presents herself." — Persius, Sat., vi. 73.]
"Conjicito humorem collectum in corpora quaeque,"
[Lucretius, vi. 1062, to the same effect.]
— and take care of it in time, lest it become troublesome to deal with once it has seized you:
"Si non prima novis conturbes vulnera plagis, Volgivagaque vagus venere ante recentia cures."
["Unless you cure old wounds with new." — Lucretius, iv. 1064.]

I was once wounded with a violent displeasure, and one more justified than violent; I might perhaps have lost myself in it had I trusted to my own strength alone. Needing a powerful diversion to disengage me, by art and study I made myself fall in love, which my youth assisted; love relieved me and rescued me from the trouble friendship had got me into. It is the same with everything else: a violent fancy has seized me; I find it a quicker way to change it than to subdue it; I substitute, if not a contrary one, at least another, in its place. Variety always relieves, dissolves, and dissipates.

If I am not able to contend with it, I escape from it; and in avoiding it, I slip out of the way and double back; shifting place, business, and company, I lose myself in the crowd of other thoughts and fancies, where it loses my trace and I escape.

Nature proceeds in the same way, by the benefit of inconstancy; for time, which she has given us as the sovereign physician of our passions, works chiefly in this — that by supplying our imagination with other and new things, it loosens and dissolves the first apprehension, however strong. A wise man sees his friend dying at the end of twenty-five years little less than he did in the first year, and, according to Epicurus, not less at all; for he attributed no relief from afflictions either to their foresight or their antiquity. But so many other thoughts cross this one that it languishes and tires at last.

Alcibiades, to divert the run of common gossip, cut off the ears and tail of his beautiful dog and turned him out into the public place, so that, giving the people this occasion to prate about it, they would let his other actions alone. I have also seen, for this same purpose of diverting people's opinions and conjectures and shutting their mouths, some women conceal their real affections under feigned ones; but I have also seen some who in pretending have let themselves be truly caught, and have abandoned their original true affection for the feigned one. From whom I learned that those who find their affections well placed are fools to consent to this disguise, since the public and favourable reception is reserved for the pretended lover. One may consider him a fellow of very little address and less wit if he doesn't in the end put himself in your place, and put you in his: that is precisely to cut out and stitch up a shoe for another to slip on.

A small thing will turn and divert us, because a small thing holds us. We do not much consider subjects in the gross, or singly; it is little and superficial circumstances, or images, that strike us — the outward useless rinds peeling off from the subjects themselves:
"Folliculos ut nunc teretes aestate cicadae Linquunt."
["As we find the husks grasshoppers leave behind them in summer." — Lucretius, v. 801.]

Even Plutarch himself laments his daughter for the little apish tricks of her infancy. The memory of a parting, of a particular grace in some action, of a last recommendation, troubles us. The sight of Caesar's robe troubled all of Rome — more than his death had done. Even the sound of names ringing in our ears, as "my poor master," "my faithful friend," "alas, my dear father," or "my sweet daughter," afflict us. When these repetitions hurt me, and I look at it a little more closely, I find it is no more than a grammatical and verbal complaint; I am only wounded by the word and tone, just as the exclamations of preachers often work more on their audience than their reasons do, and as the pitiful eyes of a beast killed for our service do — without my weighing or going into the meantime the true and solid essence of my subject:
"His se stimulis dolor ipse lacessit."
["With these spurs, grief provokes itself." — Lucretius, ii. 42.]
These are the foundations of our mourning.

The obstinacy of my stone, particularly in the bladder, has sometimes thrown me into such long suppressions of urine, for three or four days together, and so close to death, that it would have been folly to hope to escape it — and it was rather much more to be wished for, considering the miseries I endured in those cruel fits. Oh, that good emperor, who had criminals tied up to die for want of urination, was a great master in the hangman's science! Finding myself in this condition, I considered by how many slight causes and objects imagination kept the regret of life alive in me; of what atoms the weight and difficulty of this dislodging was compounded in my soul; to how many idle and frivolous thoughts we give way in so great a matter; a dog, a horse, a book, a glass — every kind of thing was considered in my loss; to others, their ambitious hopes, their money, their knowledge — no less foolish considerations than mine, in my opinion. I look on death carelessly when I look on it in general, as the end of life. I rule over it in the gross; but in detail, it dominates me; the tears of a footman, the disposing of my clothes, the touch of a friendly hand, a common consolation, discourages and softens me. So too the complaints in tragedies stir our souls with grief; and the laments of Dido and Ariadne move even those who don't believe them, in Virgil and Catullus. It is the mark of an obstinate and obdurate nature to be unmoved by any feeling, as is reported as a marvel of Polemon; but then he did not even change countenance at the bite of a mad dog that tore away the calf of his leg; and no wisdom goes so far as to grasp, by judgment alone, so vivid and entire a cause of sorrow that it does not allow it to be increased by its presence, when eyes and ears get their share — parts that can only be moved by vain accidents.

Is it reasonable that the arts themselves should take advantage of our natural stupidity and weakness? An orator, says rhetoric, in the farce of his pleading shall be moved by the sound of his own voice and his feigned emotions, and shall let himself be imposed on by the passion he is representing; he will imprint in himself a true and real grief by means of the part he is playing, in order to transmit it to the judges, who are less affected than he is; just like those hired at funerals to assist in the ceremony of sorrow, who sell their tears and mourning by weight and measure: for although they perform in a borrowed manner, nevertheless, by habituating and setting their countenances in the occasion, it is most certain that they often are really affected with actual sorrow. I was, with several other friends of his, one of those who conveyed the body of Monsieur de Grammont to Soissons from the siege of La Fère, where he was killed; and I noticed that in every place we passed through, we filled the people we met with lamentations and tears purely by the solemn pomp of our convoy — for the dead man's name was not even known there. Quintilian reports having seen comedians so deeply engaged in a mourning part that they were still weeping in the dressing room, and that, having undertaken to stir up passion in another, they have so espoused it themselves as to be infected by it, not only to the point of tears, but with pallor and the bearing of men really overwhelmed with grief.

In a country near our mountains, the women play "Priest Martin," for as they enlarge the regret for the dead husband by the remembrance of his good and agreeable qualities, they also at the same time make a register of and publish his imperfections — as if to enter into some compromise with themselves, and divert themselves from compassion to disdain. With much better grace than we do, who, when we lose an acquaintance, strive to give him new and false praises, and make him quite another thing once we have lost sight of him than he appeared to us when we did see him — as if regret were an instructive thing, or as if tears, by washing our understanding, cleared it. For my part, I henceforth renounce all favourable testimonies people may give of me, not because I shall deserve them, but because I shall be dead.

Ask a man, "What interest do you have in this siege?" — "The interest of example," he will say, "and of common obedience to my prince: I claim no profit from it; and as for glory, I know how small a share can fall to a private man like me; I have here neither passion nor quarrel." And yet you shall see him the next day quite another man, chafing and red with fury, ranged in the line of battle for the assault; it is the glitter of so much steel, the fire and noise of our cannon and drums, that have infused this new rigidity and fury into his veins. A frivolous cause, you will say. How a cause? There needs none to stir up the mind; a mere whim, without body and without subject, will rule it and agitate it. Let me think about building castles in Spain — my imagination supplies me with conveniences and pleasures by which my soul is really tickled and pleased. How often do we torment our mind with anger or sorrow by such shadows, and engage ourselves in fantastic passions that damage both soul and body! What astonished, fleeting, confused grimaces this raving puts on our faces! what sallies and stirrings, both of limbs and voices, it inspires us with! Does it not seem that this individual man has visions in the middle of the crowd he is dealing with, or that some internal demon is persecuting him? Ask yourself where the object of this change is: is there anything besides ourselves in nature that emptiness sustains, that emptiness has power over? Cambyses, having dreamt that his brother would one day be king of Persia, put him to death — a beloved brother, in whom he had always confided. Aristodemus, king of the Messenians, killed himself out of a fancy of ill omen, from I don't know what howling of his dogs; and King Midas did as much on account of some foolish dream he had had. It is to price life at its just value, to abandon it for a dream. And yet hear the soul triumph over the miseries and weakness of the body, and over its being exposed to every attack and alteration: truly, it has reason to speak so!
"O prima infelix finger ti terra Prometheo! Ille parum cauti pectoris egit opus Corpora disponens, mentem non vidit in arte; Recta animi primum debuit esse via."

["O wretched clay, first fashioned by Prometheus! In his attempt, how little wisdom he showed! In framing bodies, he did not apply his art to forming the mind, which should have been his first care." — Propertius, iii. 5, 7.]

chapters.title: Upon some verses of Virgil
paragraphs: The more profitable our thoughts are — the fuller and more solid — the more cumbersome and heavy they also become: vice, death, poverty, disease are weighty and grievous subjects. A soul should be schooled to bear up under evils and to argue with them, trained in the rules of living and believing well, and roused up often to exercise itself in this noble study. But for an ordinary soul this has to happen in intervals, and in moderation, or it will grow stupefied if always kept at it. When I was young I had to keep prodding myself, reminding myself, to hold to my duty: cheerfulness and good health, they say, do not go well with grave serious meditations. I am now in another state. The conditions of age keep reminding me, pressing me toward wisdom, preaching at me. I have fallen from an excess of liveliness into an excess of severity, which is much more troublesome — and for that reason I now and then deliberately let myself slip into a bit of disorder and occupy my mind with wanton and youthful thoughts to give it a holiday. Lately I have grown too reserved, too heavy, too ripe; the years read me daily lectures on coldness and temperance. This body of mine avoids disorder and dreads it: it is the body's turn now to lead the mind toward reformation; it governs in its turn, and more rudely and imperiously than the mind ever did; it lets me have no hour to myself, sleeping or waking, but is always preaching death, patience, repentance. I now defend myself against temperance as I used to defend myself against pleasure; it draws me too far back, even into a kind of stupidity. I will be master of myself in all things; wisdom too has its excesses, and stands as much in need of moderation as folly does. So, lest I wither, dry up, and overload myself with prudence, in the intervals and truces my infirmities allow me:
"Mens intenta suis ne seit usque malis."
["That my mind not be forever fixed on its ills." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 1, 4.]

I gently turn aside and avert my eyes from the stormy clouded sky in front of me — which, thank God, I look at without fear, but not without meditation and study — and amuse myself in the memory of my better years:
"Animus quo perdidit, optat, Atque in praeterita se totus imagine versat."
["The mind longs for what it has lost, and throws itself wholly into images of the past." — Petronius, c. 128.]

Let childhood look forward and age look back: was that not what Janus' double face meant? Let the years drag me along if they must, but let it be backward. As long as my eyes can still make out that pleasant season now expired, I will turn them that way from time to time; though it has fled from my blood and my veins, I will not let its image be uprooted from my memory:
"Hoc est Vivere bis, vita posse priore frui."
["It is to live twice, to be able to enjoy one's former life again." — Martial, x. 23, 7.]

Plato directs that old men should attend the exercises, dances, and sports of the young, that they may take joy in others for the bodily energy and beauty that is no longer in themselves, and recall the grace and comeliness of that blossoming age; and he wants the prize at these recreations to be awarded to whichever young man has most pleased the company. I used to mark the cloudy gloomy days as exceptional; now those are my ordinary days, and the extraordinary ones are the clear and bright. I am ready to leap for joy, as at some unusual favour, when nothing in particular goes wrong. Tickle me how you like, I cannot squeeze a smile out of this wretched body. I am cheerful only in fancy and dreaming, by some trick to divert the melancholy of age; but in truth that calls for another remedy than a dream. A feeble contest of art against nature. It is great folly to draw out and anticipate human troubles, as everyone does; I would rather be old for a shorter time than be old before I really am. I seize on even the smallest occasions of pleasure I can come across. I know, by hearsay, several sorts of prudent pleasures, genuinely such, and glorious too; but the reputation of them has no hold over me strong enough to give me an appetite for them. I do not so much want them magnanimous, magnificent, and pompous as I want them sweet, easy, and ready to hand:
"A natura discedimus; populo nos damus, nullius rei bono auctori."
["We depart from nature and give ourselves over to the crowd, who has nothing good to teach." — Seneca, Ep., 99.]
My philosophy is in action, in natural and immediate practice, very little in fancy: what if I should take pleasure in cracking nuts or whipping a top?
"Non ponebat enim rumores ante salutem."
["He did not put rumours ahead of his own health." — Ennius, in Cicero, De Offic., i. 24.]

Pleasure is a quality of very little ambition; it thinks itself rich enough by itself, without any boost in reputation, and is best pleased when retired from view. A young man ought to be whipped who sets himself up as a connoisseur of wines and sauces; at that age there was nothing I valued less or knew less. Now I am beginning to learn. I am very much ashamed of it — but what am I to do? I am more ashamed and vexed at the occasions that drive me to it. It is for us to dote and trifle the time away, and for young men to mind their reputation and stand on nice points; they are heading out into the world and the world's opinion, while we are retiring from it:
"Sibi arma, sibi equos, sibi hastas, sibi clavam, sibi pilam, sibi natationes, et cursus habeant: nobis senibus, ex lusionibus multis, talos relinquant et tesseras;"
["Let them keep for themselves the arms, horses, spears, clubs, ball games, swimming, and races; and out of all those sports leave to us old men cards and dice." — Cicero, De Senec., c. 16.]

the laws themselves send us home. I can do no less for this wretched state into which my age has thrown me than furnish it with toys to play with, as you do for a child; and in truth that is what we become. Wisdom and folly will both have plenty to do, taking turns to prop me up and ease me through this calamity of age:
"Misce stultitiam consiliis brevem."
["Mix a brief interval of folly with your counsels." — Horace, Od., iv. 12, 27.]
I accordingly avoid the lightest little pricks; the things that once would not have scratched the skin now go right through me. My body is so naturally inclining toward ill:
"In fragili corpore odiosa omnis offensio est;"
["In a fragile body every shock is hateful." — Cicero, De Senec., c. 18.]
"Mensque pati durum sustinet aegra nihil."
["And the sick mind can bear no hard exertion." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 5, 18.]
I have always been very tender about offences; I am much more tender now, and exposed all over.
"Et minimae vires frangere quassa valent."
["Little force suffices to break what was already cracked." — Ovid, De Tris., iii. 11, 22.]

My judgment restrains me from kicking and grumbling at the inconveniences nature commands me to endure, but it does not take away my feeling them. I, whose only aim is to live and be merry, would run from one end of the world to the other to find one good year of pleasant cheerful tranquillity. A melancholy dull tranquillity may be enough for me, but it numbs me and stupefies me; I am not content with it. If there is any person, any little knot of good company, in country or city, in France or anywhere else, resident or on the move, who can take to my humour and whose humour I can take to, let them whistle and I will come running and furnish them with essays in flesh and bone:

Since it is the privilege of the mind to rescue itself from old age, I urge mine to do so with all the power I have. Let it stay green meanwhile and flourish if it can, like mistletoe on a dead tree. But I fear it is a traitor; it has contracted such a close brotherhood with the body that it leaves me at every turn to go follow the body in its need. I wheedle it apart in vain; I try in vain to wean it off this correspondence, to no effect; I quote Seneca and Catullus to it, and ladies and royal masques. If its companion has the stone, it seems to have it too; even those faculties most peculiarly its own cannot then perform their functions but appear stupefied and asleep. There is no liveliness in what it produces if the body is not in equal measure lively too.

Our schoolmasters are to blame, when they hunt for the causes of the soul's exceptional movements, that besides ascribing them to divine ecstasy, love, martial fury, poetry, or wine, they have not also assigned a share to health: a boiling, vigorous, full, easeful health, such as the greenness of youth and a sense of safety used to give me by fits. That fire of liveliness and gaiety throws into the mind flashes that are brighter and livelier than our natural light, and is, of all enthusiasms, the most jovial — if not the most extravagant.
So it is no wonder if the opposite state dulls and clogs my spirit, and produces the opposite effect:
"Ad nullum consurgit opus, cum corpore languet;"
["It rises to no effort; it languishes with the body." — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 125.]

and yet my mind expects me to be grateful for the fact that, as it would make out, it gives much less consent to this stupidity than is usual in men of my age. While we are in a truce, at least, let us drive incommodities and difficulties out of our exchanges:
"Dum licet, obducta solvatur fronte senectus:"
["While we can, let us banish old age from the brow." — Herodotus, Ep., xiii. 7.]
"Tetrica sunt amcenanda jocularibus."
["Sour things should be sweetened with pleasant ones." — Sidonius Apollinaris, Ep., i. 9.]
I love a gay civil wisdom and steer clear of all sourness and austerity of manner; any forbidding bearing is suspect to me:
"Tristemque vultus tetrici arrogantiam:"
["The gloomy arrogance of a crabbed face." — Anonymous.]
"Et habet tristis quoque turba cinaedos."
["An austere countenance sometimes covers a debauched mind." — Idem.]

I am very much of Plato's opinion, that easy or harsh humours are strong indications of the soul's good or ill disposition. Socrates had a steady countenance — but serene and smiling, not sourly austere like the elder Crassus, whom nobody ever saw laugh. Virtue is a pleasant and gay quality.

I know very well that few will quarrel with the licence of my writings who do not have more to quarrel with in the licence of their own thoughts. I conform myself well enough to their inclinations, but I offend their eyes. It is a fine humour they have, to strain Plato's writings and twist his supposed intimacies with Phaedo, Dion, Stella, and Archeanassa:
"Non pudeat dicere, quod non pudet sentire."
["Let us not be ashamed to say what we are not ashamed to think."]
