Even the most contemplative and prudent man, when I imagine him in this posture, I hold an impudent fellow for pretending to be prudent and contemplative; these are the peacock's feet that lower his pride:
"Ridentem dicere verum Quid vetat?"
["What prevents one from telling the truth with a smile?" — Horace, Sat., i. 1, 24.]

Those who banish serious thoughts from their sports, says someone, are like a man who dares not adore the statue of a saint unless it is covered with a veil. We eat and drink, indeed, as the beasts do; but these are not actions that obstruct the soul's functions; in these we keep our advantage over them. This other action subjects every other thought, and by its imperious authority makes an ass of all Plato's divinity and philosophy; and yet no one complains of it. In every other thing a man may keep some decorum; all other operations submit to the rules of decency; this one cannot, even in imagination, appear anything but vicious or ridiculous. Find out, if you can, any serious, discreet procedure in it. Alexander said that what chiefly let him know he was mortal was this act and sleeping; sleep stifles and suppresses the soul's faculties, and the company of women likewise dissipates and exhausts them. Without a doubt, it is a mark not only of our original corruption but of our vanity and deformity.

On the one hand, nature pushes us into it, having fixed the most noble, useful, and pleasant of all her functions to this desire; and on the other, leaves us to accuse it and shun it, as if it were insolent and indecent, to blush at it, and to recommend abstinence. Are we not brutes to call brutish the work that begets us? Peoples of so many differing religions have agreed on various rites — sacrifices, lamps, burning incense, fasts, offerings — and among others in condemning this act; all opinions tend that way, besides the widespread custom of circumcision, which can be looked on as a punishment. We have perhaps reason to blame ourselves for being guilty of so foolish a production as man, and to call the act and the parts that perform the act shameful (mine, in truth, are now shameful and pitiful). The Essenes, whom Pliny speaks of, sustained their country for several ages without nurse or baby-clothes, by the arrival of strangers who, taking up this odd humour, kept coming to join them; a whole nation resolved to hazard total extermination rather than engage in female embraces, and to lose the succession of men rather than beget one. They say that Zeno only had to do with a woman once in his life, and then out of civility, that he might not seem too obstinately to scorn the sex.
[Diogenes Laertius, vii. 13. What is said there, however, is that Zeno seldom had commerce with boys, lest he be thought a complete misogynist.]

Everyone avoids seeing a man born; everyone runs to see him die. To destroy a man, a spacious field is sought out in the face of the sun; but to make one, we creep into as dark and private a corner as we can; it is a man's duty to withdraw bashfully from the light to create, but it is glory and the fountain of many virtues to know how to destroy what we have made — the one being an injury, the other a favour. For Aristotle says that to do anyone a kindness, in a certain phrase of his country, is to kill him. The Athenians, to couple the disgrace of these two actions, having to purify the isle of Delos and justify themselves to Apollo, banned both births and burials within its precincts:
"Nostri nosmet paenitet."
["We are ashamed of ourselves." — Terence, Phormio, i. 3, 20.]

There are nations that won't be seen to eat. I know a lady, of the best quality, who is of the same opinion — that chewing disfigures the face and takes away much from a lady's grace and beauty, and so unwillingly appears at a public table with an appetite. And I know a man too who cannot endure to see another eat, nor himself to be seen eating; he is more shy of company when putting in than putting out. In the Turkish empire there are a great number of men who, to excel others, never let themselves be seen when they take their meal; who only eat once a week; who cut and gash their faces and limbs; who never speak to anyone — fanatical people who think to honour their nature by denaturing themselves, who value themselves on their contempt of themselves, and propose to grow better by being worse. What monstrous animal is this, who is a horror to himself, to whom his delights are a grief, and who weds himself to misfortune? There are people who conceal their life:
"Exilioque domos et dulcia limina mutant,"
["And they exchange their homes and sweet thresholds for exile." — Virgil, Georg., ii. 511.]

and withdraw from the sight of other men; who avoid health and cheerfulness as dangerous and prejudicial qualities. Not only many sects but many peoples curse their birth and bless their death; and there is a place where the sun is cursed and darkness adored. We are only ingenious in using ourselves ill; it is the real quarry our wits fly at; and the intellect, when misapplied, is a dangerous tool!
"O miseri! quorum gaudia crimen habent!"
["O wretched men, whose pleasures are a crime!" — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 180.]

Alas, poor man! you have enough inevitable inconveniences without increasing them by your own invention, and are wretched enough by nature without being so by art. You have real and essential deformities enough without forging imaginary ones. Do you think you are too much at ease unless half your ease is uneasy? Do you find that you have not performed all the necessary offices nature has laid on you, and that she is idle in you, unless you bind yourself to other new ones? You don't stick at infringing her universal and undoubted laws; but you stick to your own particular and fantastic rules, and the more particular, uncertain, and contradictory they are, the more you employ your whole care on them. The laws of your parish occupy you and bind you; those of God and the world don't concern you. Just run over the examples of this kind a little; your life is full of them.

While the verses of these two poets treat wantonness as reservedly and discreetly as they do, they discover it, it seems to me, much more openly. Ladies cover their necks with netting, priests cover several sacred things, painters shadow their pictures to give them more lustre; and they say that the sun and wind strike more violently by reflection than in a straight line. The Egyptian wisely answered the man who asked him what he had under his cloak: "It is hid under my cloak," he said, "so that you may not know what it is." But there are certain other things that people hide only to show them. Listen to that other, who speaks plainer:
"Et nudum pressi corpus ad usque meum:"
["And pressed her naked body to mine." — Ovid, Amor., i. 5, 24.]

it seems to me he unmans me. Let Martial turn up Venus as high as he can, he cannot show her so naked. He who says everything that is to be said gluts and disgusts us; he who is afraid to express himself draws us on to guess more than is meant. There is a treachery in this kind of modesty, and especially when, like these two, they half open so fair a path to imagination. Both the action and the description ought to taste of theft.

The more respectful, more timorous, more coy, secret love of the Spaniards and Italians pleases me. I don't know who of old wished his throat as long as a crane's, so he could the longer taste what he swallowed; this would have been better wished for as to this quick precipitous pleasure, especially in such natures as mine, that have the fault of being too prompt. To stay its flight, and put off the moment with preambles — every glance, every bow, every word, every sign passes between them for favour and reward. Wouldn't it be excellent thrift in a man who could dine on the steam of the roast? It is a passion that mixes with very little solid substance — far more vanity and feverish raving; and we should serve it and pay it accordingly. Let us teach the ladies to set a better value and esteem on themselves, to amuse us and fool us; we deliver the last charge at the first attack; the French impetuosity will always show itself. By spinning out their favours and giving them out in small parcels, even miserable old age will find some little share of reward, according to its worth and merit. He who finds no pleasure but in the having, who wins nothing unless he sweeps the stakes, who takes no pleasure in the chase but only in the quarry, ought not to enrol himself in our school: the more steps and degrees there are, the higher and more honourable the topmost seat. We should take pleasure in being led to it, as in magnificent palaces, by various porticoes and passages, long pleasant galleries, and many turnings. This arrangement of things would turn to our advantage; we would stay there longer and love longer; without hope and without desire we get nowhere. Our conquest and entire possession is what they ought infinitely to dread; once they surrender themselves wholly to the mercy of our fidelity and constancy, they run a mighty hazard — these are virtues very rare and hard to be found. As soon as the ladies are ours, we are no longer theirs:
"Postquam cupidae mentis satiata libido est, Verba nihil metuere, nihil perjuria curant;"
["Once their desire is satisfied, they fear no oaths and care nothing for promises." — Catullus, lxiv. 147.]

And Thrasonides, a young man of Greece, was so in love with his own passion that, having gained his mistress's consent, he refused to enjoy her, so as not to extinguish and stupefy through fruition the restless ardour he was so proud of and fed himself on. Costliness is a good sauce to a dish: just see how much the manner of greeting peculiar to our nation has, by its easiness, made kisses — which Socrates says are so powerful and dangerous for stealing the heart — of no esteem at all. It is a displeasing custom, and injurious to the ladies, that they have to lend their lips to every fellow with three footmen at his heels, however ill-favoured he may be in himself:
"Cujus livida naribus caninis Dependet glacies, rigetque barba . . . Centum occurrere malo culilingis:" — Martial, vii. 94.

and even we ourselves are scarcely the better for it; for the way the world is divided, for three beautiful women we must kiss fifty ugly ones; and to a tender stomach like those of my age, an ill kiss costs more than a good one is worth.

In Italy they passionately court even their common women, who sell themselves for money, and justify it by saying: "There are degrees of enjoyment, and by this service we secure for ourselves the fullest; the women sell only their bodies; the will is too free and too much its own to be put up for sale." So they say it is the will they are courting, and they have reason. It is indeed the will we are to serve and gain by our wooing. I abhor to imagine to myself a body without affection; and this madness is, I think, cousin to that of the boy who would needs pollute the beautiful statue of Venus made by Praxiteles; or that of the furious Egyptian who violated the dead corpse of a woman he was embalming — which gave rise to the law then made in Egypt that the bodies of beautiful young women and those of good quality should be kept three days before being delivered to those whose office it was to bury them. Periander did more strangely, extending his conjugal affection (more regular and lawful) to the enjoyment of his wife Melissa after she was dead. Doesn't it look like a lunatic humour in the Moon, that, since she could not otherwise enjoy her darling Endymion, she laid him asleep for several months, and pleased herself with the enjoyment of a boy who stirred only in his sleep? I likewise say that we love a body without soul or sentiment when we love a body without its consent and desire. Not all enjoyments are alike: some are hectic and languishing; a thousand other causes besides goodwill may procure us this favour from the ladies; it is not a sufficient testimony of affection; treachery may lurk there as elsewhere; they sometimes go to it by halves:
"Tanquam thura merumque parent Absentem marmoreamve putes:"
["As if they were preparing frankincense and wine . . . you would think her absent or made of marble." — Martial, xi. 103, 12 and 59, 8.]

I know some who would rather lend that than their coach, and who only impart themselves that way. You have to examine whether your company pleases them on any other account, or, as some strong-chined groom, for that only; what degree of favour and esteem you have with them:
"Tibi si datur uni, Quem lapide illa diem candidiore notat."
["That is enough, if that day alone is given to you which she marks with a whiter stone." — Catullus, lxviii. 147.]
What if they eat your bread with the sauce of a more pleasing imagination?
"Te tenet, absentes alios suspirat amores."
["She holds you in her arms; her sighs are for other, absent lovers." — Tibullus, i. 6, 35.]
What? Have we not seen one in our own day who made use of this act for the purpose of a most horrid revenge, killing and poisoning, as he did, a worthy lady by that means?

Those who know Italy will not think it strange that for this subject I look no further for examples; that nation may be called the regent of the world in this. They have more generally good-looking women, and fewer ugly ones, than we do; but for rare and excellent beauties we have as many as they. I think the same of their wits: of the common sort, they have evidently far more — brutishness is incomparably rarer there; but in individual characters of the highest stamp, we owe them nothing. If I should carry the comparison further, I might say, on the other hand, that as to valour, it is, by comparison, common and natural with us; but sometimes we see them possessed of it to a degree that surpasses the greatest examples we can produce. The marriages of that country are defective in this: their custom commonly imposes so harsh and slavish a law on the women that the most distant acquaintance with a stranger is as capital an offence as the most intimate; so that, since all approaches are necessarily made substantial, and since it all comes to one account, they have no hard choice to make; and once they have broken down the fence, we can safely presume they take fire:
"Luxuria ipsis vinculis, sicut fera bestia, irritata, deinde emissa."
["Lust, like a wild beast, made fiercer by its chains, then breaks loose." — Livy, xxxiv. 4.]
They must be given a little more rein:
"Vidi ego nuper equum, contra sua frena tenacem, Ore reluctanti fulminis ire modo":
["I saw, the other day, a horse struggling against his bit, rush off like a thunderbolt." — Ovid, Amor., iii. 4, 13.]

the desire for company is calmed by giving it a little liberty. We are very much in the same case: they are extreme in constraint, we in licence. It is a good custom we have in France that our sons are received into the best families, to be entertained and brought up as pages, in a kind of school of nobility; and it is looked on as a discourtesy and an affront to refuse this to a gentleman. I have noticed (for, as many families, so many differing forms) that the ladies who have been strictest with their maids have had no better luck than those who allowed them greater liberty. There should be moderation in these things; a great deal of their conduct must be left to their own discretion, for, in the end, no discipline can curb them throughout. But it is also true that the woman who comes off with flying colours from a school of liberty brings with her grounds for more confidence than she who comes away sound from a severe and strict school.

Our fathers dressed up their daughters' looks in bashfulness and fear (their courage and desires being the same); we dress ours in confidence and assurance. We understand nothing of the matter. We must leave it to the Sarmatian women, who may not lie with a man until they have killed another in battle with their own hands. As for me, who have no other title left to such things but by the ears, it is enough if, according to the privilege of my age, they keep me on their counsel. I advise them, then, and us men too, to abstinence; but if the age we live in will not endure it, at least to modesty and discretion. For, as in the story of Aristippus, who, speaking to some young men who blushed at seeing him go into a scandalous house, said "The vice is in not coming out, not in going in," let her who has no care for her conscience have at least some regard for her reputation; and though she is rotten within, let her carry a fair outside at least.

I commend a gradual delay in bestowing their favours. Plato declares that, in all sorts of love, easiness and promptness are forbidden to the one being courted. It is a sign of eagerness, which they ought to disguise with all the art they have, so rashly, so wholly, and so over-hand to surrender themselves. In carrying themselves in an orderly, measured way in the granting of their last favours, they much better stir our desires and hide their own. Let them still fly before us, even those who have most mind to be overtaken; they conquer us better by fleeing, as the Scythians did. To tell the truth, according to the law nature has imposed on them, it is not properly for them either to will or to desire; their part is to suffer, obey, and consent; and for this nature has given them a perpetual capacity, where ours is only by fits and uncertain. They are always fit for the encounter, that they may always be ready when we are — "Pati natae." ["Born to suffer." — Seneca, Ep., 95.] And whereas nature has ordered that our appetites be made manifest by a prominent demonstration, she has wanted theirs to be hidden and concealed within, and has furnished them with parts unfit for ostentation, and simply defensive. Such proceedings as the following must be left to Amazonian licence: Alexander marching his army through Hyrcania, Thalestris, queen of the Amazons, came with three hundred light horse of her own sex, well mounted and armed, having left the rest of a very great army that followed her behind the neighbouring mountains, to pay him a visit; where she publicly told him in plain terms that the fame of his valour and victories had brought her there to see him, and to make him an offer of her forces to assist him in the pursuit of his enterprises; and that, finding him so handsome, young, and vigorous, she — who was also perfect in all those qualities — advised that they should lie together, so that from the most valiant woman in the world and the bravest man then living, some great and wonderful issue might spring for the time to come. Alexander thanked her for everything else; but to give time for the accomplishment of her last demand, he detained her thirteen days in that place, which were spent in royal feasting and merriment, for the welcome of so courageous a princess.

We are, almost throughout, unjust judges of their actions, as they are of ours. I confess the truth when it tells against me, as well as when it is on my side. It is an abominable intemperance that drives them so often to change, and that will not let them limit their affection to any one person whatever; as is evident in that goddess to whom so many changes and so many lovers are attributed. But it is also true that it is contrary to the nature of love if it is not violent, and contrary to the nature of violence if it is constant. And those who marvel and exclaim and make such a fuss to find out the causes of this frailty in them, as if it were unnatural and not to be believed — how is it that they do not notice how often they are themselves guilty of the same, without any astonishment or miracle at all? It would perhaps be stranger to see the passion fixed; it is not a simply corporeal passion. If there is no end to avarice and ambition, there is doubtless no more to desire; it still lives after satiety; and it is impossible to prescribe either constant satisfaction or an end to it; it always goes beyond its possession. By this means inconstancy is perhaps in some sort more pardonable in them than in us; they may plead, as well as we do, the inclination to variety and novelty common to us both; and secondly, that, without us, they buy a cat in a sack. Joanna, queen of Naples, had her first husband, Andreas, hanged at the bars of her window in a halter of gold and silk woven with her own hand, because in matrimonial performance she found neither his parts nor his abilities answered the expectation she had conceived from his stature, beauty, youth, and activity, by which she had been caught and deceived. They may say that there is more work in doing than in suffering; and so, on their side they are always at least provided for necessity, whereas on ours it may fall out otherwise. For this reason Plato wisely made a law that, before marriage, to determine the fitness of the persons, the judges should see the young men who applied for it stripped naked, and the women only to the girdle. When they come to try us, perhaps they do not find us worthy of their choice:
"Experta latus, madidoque simillima loro Inguina, nec lassa stare coacta manu, Deserit imbelles thalamos."
["After every endeavour to arouse him to action, she quits the barren couch." — Martial, vii. 58.]
It is not enough that a man's will be good; weakness and insufficiency are lawful grounds for breaking a marriage,
"Et quaerendum aliunde foret nervosius illud, Quod posset zonam solvere virgineam:"
["And one must look elsewhere for a more vigorous lover, one who could undo her virgin girdle." — Catullus, lxvii. 27.]
why not? And, by her own measure, an amorous intelligence more licentious and active —
"Si blando nequeat superesse labori."
["If his strength be unequal to the pleasant task." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 127.]
But is it not great impudence to offer our imperfections and weaknesses where we want to please and leave a good opinion and esteem of ourselves? For the little I am able to do now:
"Ad unum Mollis opus."
["Fit but for once." — Horace, Epod., xii. 15.]
I would not trouble a woman I am to revere and fear:
"Fuge suspicari, Cujus undenum trepidavit aetas Claudere lustrum."
["Do not suspect a man whose eleventh lustrum is closed." — Horace, Od., ii. 4, 12 — actually it limits this to the eighth.]

Nature should be satisfied to have made this age miserable, without also making it ridiculous. I hate to see it, for one poor inch of pitiful vigour that visits but thrice a week, strut and put itself forward with as much eagerness as if it were about to perform mighty feats — a true flax-flame; and laugh to see it so boil and bubble, and then in a moment so frozen and out. This appetite ought to belong only to the flower of beautiful youth: don't trust it to second that indefatigable, full, constant, magnanimous ardour you think is in you, for it will certainly leave you in a pretty corner; but rather transfer it to some tender, bashful, ignorant boy, who still trembles at the rod and blushes:
"Indum sanguineo veluti violaverit ostro Si quis ebur, vel mista rubent ubi lilia multa Alba rosa."
["As Indian ivory streaked with crimson, or white lilies mixed with the damask rose." — Aeneid, xii. 67.]
Whoever can wait till morning without dying of shame to see the disdain in the fair eyes of her who knows so well his fumbling incompetence,
"Et taciti fecere tamen convicia vultus,"
["Though she says nothing, her looks betray her anger." — Ovid, Amor., i. 7, 21.]

has never had the satisfaction and glory of having cudgelled them till they were weary, by the vigorous performance of one heroic night. When I have seen any one vexed with me, I have not at once accused her fickleness; I have been in doubt whether I did not have more reason to complain of nature; she has doubtless treated me very uncivilly and unkindly:
"Si non longa satis, si non bene mentula crassa Nimirum sapiunt, videntque parvam Matronae quoque mentulam illibenter:"

[The first verse is from an epigram in the Veterum Poetarum Catalecta, and the two others from an epigram in the same collection (Ad Matronas). They state Montaigne's charge against nature in terms not easily translated, indicated in the passage above.]
and done me a most enormous injury. Every limb I have, as much as any other, is equally my own, and none other more properly makes me a man than this.

I owe my whole picture to the public. The wisdom of my instruction lies in liberty, in truth, in essence: scorning to introduce those little, made-up, common, and provincial rules into the catalogue of its real duties — duties all natural, general, and constant, of which civility and ceremony are daughters indeed, but illegitimate. We are sure to have the vices of appearance, once we have had those of essence; once we have done with these, we run full tilt at the others, if it must be so; for there is danger that we shall invent new offices to excuse our negligence toward the natural ones, and to confound them. To show this — is it not seen that in places where faults are crimes, crimes are only faults; that in nations where the laws of decency are most rare and most lax, the primitive laws of common reason are best observed? The countless multitude of so many duties stifles and dissipates our care. The application of ourselves to light and trivial things diverts us from those that are necessary and just. Oh, how easily and plausibly these superficial men take their way, compared to ours! These are shadows with which we paper one another over; but we do not pay; we only inflame the reckoning to be made with that great judge who tucks up our rags and tatters above our shameful parts, and does not flinch from viewing us all over, even to our inmost and most secret filth. It would be a useful decency of our maidenly modesty if it could keep him from this discovery. In short, whoever could reclaim man from such a scrupulous verbal superstition would do the world no great disservice. Our life is divided between folly and prudence; whoever writes about it only what is reverend and canonical will leave more than half of it behind. I do not excuse myself to myself; and if I did, it would be rather for my excuses I would excuse myself than for any other fault. I excuse myself of certain humours, which I think stronger in number than those on my side. With that consideration, I will say further (since I wish to please everyone, hard as that will be):
"Esse unum hominem accommodatum ad tantam morum ac sermonum et voluntatum varietatem,"
["That one man should accommodate himself to such a variety of manners, discourses, and wills." — Q. Cicero, De Pet. Consul, c. 14.]

that they ought not to condemn me for putting forward, as authorities, things received and approved by so many ages; and that there is no reason that for want of rhyme they should refuse me the liberty they grant even to churchmen of our nation and time — and these among the most notable. Here are two of their lively verses:
"Rimula, dispeream, ni monogramma tua est."
"Un vit d'amy la contente et bien traicte:"
[St Gelais, Œuvres Poétiques, p. 99, ed. Lyons, 1574.]

and how many others. I love modesty; and it is not out of judgment that I have chosen this scandalous way of speaking; nature has chosen it for me. I don't commend it, any more than other forms that go against common use; but I excuse it, and by both general and particular circumstances soften the accusation against it.
But to go on. Where, too, can it come from, that usurpation of sovereign authority you take to yourself over the women, who favour you at their own expense,
"Si furtiva dedit mira munuscula nocte,"
["If, in the stealthy night, she has made strange little gifts." — Catullus, lxviii. 145.]

such that you presently take up the interest, coolness, and authority of a husband? It is a free contract — why do you not then keep to it, as you would have them do? There is no prescription on voluntary matters. It is against the form, but it is true that in my time I have conducted this bargain, as much as the nature of it would permit, as conscientiously and with as much colour of justice as any other contract; and that I never pretended any other affection than what I really had, and have truthfully acquainted them with its birth, vigour, and decline, its fits and lulls. A man does not always hold on at the same rate. I have been so sparing of my promises that I think I have done better than my word. They have found me faithful even to the service of their inconstancy, a confessed and sometimes repeated inconstancy. I never broke with them while I had any hold at all; and whatever cause they have given me, never broke with them to hatred or contempt; for such intimacies, however scandalously obtained, do oblige one to some goodwill. I have sometimes shown, at their tricks and evasions, a little indiscreet anger and impatience; for I am naturally subject to rash emotions, which, light and short as they are, often spoil my market. When they have consulted my judgment, I have never stuck at giving them sharp paternal counsels, and pinching them to the quick. If I have left them any cause to complain of me, it is rather of finding in me a love foolishly conscientious by comparison with modern usage than anything else. I have kept my word in things from which I might easily have been dispensed; they have sometimes surrendered themselves with reputation, and on terms that they would have been willing enough should be broken by the conqueror. I have, more than once, made pleasure, at its greatest height, give way to the interest of their honour; and where reason urged me, have armed them against myself, so that they conducted themselves more decorously and securely by my rules, when they frankly referred themselves to them, than they would have done by their own. I have ever, as much as I could, taken on myself alone the hazard of our assignations, to clear them; and have always contrived our meetings after the hardest and most unusual manner, as less suspected and, in my opinion, more accessible. They are most open where they think themselves most securely shut up; things least feared are least forbidden and observed. One may more boldly venture what nobody thinks you would venture, which by its difficulty becomes easy. Never did any man make his approaches more impertinently obvious; this way of loving is more according to discipline, but how ridiculous it is to our people, and how ineffective, no one knows better than I; yet I shall not repent of it; I have nothing more there to lose:
"Me tabula sacer Votiva paries, indicat uvida Suspendisse potenti Vestimenta maris deo:"
["The holy wall, by my votive tablet, shows that I have hung up my wet clothes in honour of the mighty god of the sea." — Horace, Od., i. 5, 13.]
it is now time to speak out. But as I might perhaps say to another, "You are talking idly, my friend; the love of your time has little dealing with faith and integrity":
"Haec si tu postules Ratione certa facere, nihilo plus agas, Quam si des operam, ut cum ratione insanias:"
["If you seek to make these things certain by reason, you will get no further than if you tried to be sanely mad." — Terence, Eun., act i., sc. 1, v. 16.]

on the contrary, also, if it were for me to begin over again, it would certainly be by the same method and the same progress, however fruitless it might be for me; folly and inability are commendable in an uncommendable action. The further I go from their humour in this, the closer I come to my own. As for the rest, in this traffic I did not let myself be wholly carried away; I pleased myself in it, but did not forget myself. I kept entire, for their service and my own, the little sense and discretion nature has given me: a little emotion, but no dotage. My conscience too was engaged in it, even to debauch and licentiousness; but as to ingratitude, treachery, malice, and cruelty, never. I would not purchase the pleasure of this vice at any price, but content myself with its proper and simple cost:
"Nullum intra se vitium est."
["Nothing is a vice in itself." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]

I almost equally hate a stupid sluggish laziness and a toilsome painful employment; the one pinches, the other puts me to sleep. I like wounds as well as bruises, and cuts as well as dull blows. I found in this commerce, when I was most able for it, a just moderation between these extremes. Love is a sprightly, lively, gay agitation; I was neither troubled nor afflicted with it, but heated, and indeed disordered; a man must stop there; it hurts nobody but fools. A young man asked the philosopher Panaetius if it was becoming for a wise man to be in love. "Let the wise man look to that," he answered, "but as for you and me, who are not so, let us not engage in so stirring and violent an affair, which enslaves us to others and makes us contemptible to ourselves." He spoke true: we are not to trust a thing so precipitous in itself to a soul that has not the wherewithal to withstand its assaults and to disprove in practice the saying of Agesilaus, that prudence and love cannot live together. It is a vain employment, true, unbecoming, shameful, and illegitimate; but carried on in this manner, I look on it as wholesome, fit to enliven a drowsy soul and to rouse a heavy body; and, as an experienced physician, I would prescribe it for a man of my form and condition, as soon as any other recipe, to rouse him and keep him in vigour till well advanced in years, and to put off the approaches of age. While we are still in the suburbs, and while the pulse still beats:
"Dum nova canities, dum prima et recta senectus, Dum superest lachesi quod torqueat, et pedibus me Porto meis, nullo dextram subeunte bacillo,"

["While my white hair is new, while old age is still upright-shouldered, while there is still something for Lachesis to spin, while I can walk on my own legs and need no staff to lean upon." — Juvenal, iii. 26.]

we have need to be prodded and tickled by some such sharp incentive as this. Just see what youth, vigour, and gaiety it inspired in good Anacreon; and Socrates, then older than I am, speaking of an amorous object:

"Leaning," said he, "my shoulder to her shoulder and my head to hers, as we were reading together in a book, I felt, without dissembling, a sudden sting in my shoulder like the biting of an insect, which I still felt above five days afterwards; and a continual itching crept into my heart." So a merely accidental touch, and that of a shoulder, heated and altered a soul cooled and enervated by age, and the strictest liver of all mankind. And, indeed, why not? Socrates was a man, and would not be, nor seem, anything else. Philosophy does not contend against natural pleasures, provided they are moderate, and only preaches moderation, not total abstinence; the power of its resistance is exerted against those that are adulterate and strange. Philosophy says that the appetites of the body ought not to be heightened by the mind, and ingeniously warns us not to stir up hunger by being already full; not to stuff, instead of merely filling, the belly; to avoid all enjoyments that may bring us to want, and all meats and drinks that bring thirst and hunger; just as in the service of love, philosophy prescribes that we take such an object as may simply satisfy the body's need, and does not stir the soul, which ought only barely to follow and assist the body without mixing in the affair. But have I not reason to hold that these precepts, which in my opinion are somewhat over-strict, only concern a body in its best plight, and that in a body broken by age, as in a weak stomach, it is excusable to warm and support it by art, and by the mediation of fancy to restore the appetite and cheerfulness it has lost of itself?

May we not say that there is nothing in us, during this earthly imprisonment, that is purely either corporeal or spiritual; and that we injuriously break up a man alive; and that it seems only reasonable we should carry ourselves at least as favourably toward the use of pleasure as we do toward that of pain? Pain was, for example, vehement, even to perfection, in the souls of the saints by penitence; the body there naturally had a share, by right of union, and yet could have had little part in the cause; and yet they were not content for the body merely to follow and assist the afflicted soul: they have afflicted it with grievous and special torments, so that by the emulation of one another, the soul and body might plunge man into a misery the more salutary the more severe. In the same way, is it not injustice, in bodily pleasures, to subdue and keep down the soul, and say that it must therein be dragged along as to some forced, servile obligation and necessity? Rather, it is the soul's part to hatch and cherish them, there to present herself and to invite them — the authority of ruling belonging to her; just as it is also her part, in my opinion, in the pleasures proper to her, to inspire and infuse into the body all the feeling it is capable of, and to study how to make them sweet and useful to it. For it is good reason, as they say, that the body should not pursue its appetites to the prejudice of the mind; but why is it not also reasonable that the mind should not pursue hers to the prejudice of the body?

I have no other passion to keep me in breath. What avarice, ambition, quarrels, lawsuits do for others who, like me, have no particular vocation, love would do for me much more conveniently; it would give me back vigilance, sobriety, grace, and the care of my person; it would steady my countenance, so that the grimaces of old age — those deformed and dismal looks — would not come to disgrace it; it would put me again on sound and wise studies, by which I might make myself more loved and esteemed, clearing my mind of the despair of itself and of its use, and reintroducing it to itself; it would divert me from a thousand troublesome thoughts and melancholy humours that idleness and the ill posture of our health load us with at this age; it would warm again, at least in dreams, the blood that nature is abandoning; it would hold up the chin, and a little stretch the nerves, the vigour and cheerfulness of that poor man who is going full drive toward his ruin. But I very well understand that it is a thing hard to recover; by weakness and long experience, our taste has become more delicate and nice; we ask the most when we bring the least, and are hardest to choose when we least deserve to be accepted; and knowing ourselves for what we are, we are less confident and more distrustful. Nothing can assure us of being loved, considering our condition and theirs. I am ashamed to see myself in the company of those young wanton creatures:
"Cujus in indomito constantior inguine nervus, Quam nova collibus arbor inhaeret."
["In whose unbridled loins the vigour holds firmer than the young tree on the hills." — Horace, Epod., xii. 19.]
Why should we go and insinuate our misery into their gay and sprightly humour?
"Possint ut juvenes visere fervidi. Multo non sine risu, Dilapsam in cineres facem."
["That ardent youths may see, not without much laughter, a burning torch worn to ashes." — Horace, Od., iv. 13, 21.]

They have strength and reason on their side; let us give way; we have no business there. And these blossoms of springing beauty will not let themselves be handled by such numbed hands or dealt with by mere material means; for as the old philosopher answered one who jeered him because he could not gain the favour of a young girl he was making love to: "Friend, the hook won't stick in such soft cheese." It is a commerce that requires reciprocity and correspondence; the other pleasures we receive can be acknowledged by recompenses of another nature, but this one is not to be paid except in the same coin. In earnest, in this sport, the pleasure I give tickles my imagination more than what they give me does; now, the man has nothing of generosity in him who can receive pleasure where he confers none — it must be a mean soul that owes everything, and is content to maintain relations with people to whom he is a continual burden. There is no beauty, grace, or privacy so exquisite that a gentleman ought to want it at that rate. If they can only be kind to us out of pity, I had much rather die than live on charity. I would have the right to ask, in the style I heard them beg in Italy, "Fate ben per voi," or after the manner Cyrus exhorted his soldiers, "Whoever loves himself, let him follow me." "Consort yourself," someone will say, "with women of your own condition, whom a like fortune will make easier to your desire." Oh, ridiculous and insipid composition!
"Nolo Barbam vellere mortuo leoni."
["I will not pluck the beard from a dead lion." — Martial.]

Xenophon lays it as an objection and accusation against Menon, that he never made love to any but old women. For my part, I take more pleasure in just seeing the just and sweet mingling of two young beauties, or only thinking of it in my fancy, than in being myself an actor in some pitiful and imperfect conjunction;
[Which Cotton renders, "Than to be myself an actor in the second with a deformed creature."]
I leave that fantastic appetite to the Emperor Galba, who was only for old curried flesh; and to this poor wretch:
"O ego Di faciant talem to cernere possim, Caraque mutatis oscula ferre comis, Amplectique meis corpus non pingue lacertis!"
[Ovid, who (Ex Ponto, i. 4, 49) writes to his wife, "O may the gods grant that I might see you so, and bring dear kisses to your changed locks, and embrace your withered body in my arms."]

Among chief deformities I count forced and artificial beauties. Hemon, a young boy of Chios, thinking by fine dressing to get the beauty that nature had denied him, came to the philosopher Arcesilaus and asked him if it were possible for a wise man to be in love. "Yes," he replied, "provided it be not with a painted and adulterated beauty like yours."
[Diogenes Laertius, iv. 36. The question was whether a wise man could love him. Cotton has "Emonez, a young courtesan of Chios."]

Ugliness of a confessed antiquity is to me less old and less ugly than another that is polished and plastered up. Shall I say it, at the risk of having my throat cut? Love, in my opinion, is not properly and naturally in its season except in the age next to childhood,
"Quem si puellarum insereres choro, Mille sagaces falleret hospites, Discrimen obscurum, solutis Crinibus ambiguoque vultu:"
["Whom if you should place in a company of girls, a thousand sharp-eyed strangers would fail to tell him from them, with his loose locks and ambiguous look." — Horace, Od., ii. 5, 21.]

nor beauty either; for whereas Homer extends it as far as the budding of the beard, Plato himself has noted this as rare. The reason why the sophist Bion so pleasantly called the first appearing hairs of adolescence "Aristogitons" and "Harmodiuses" is well known. In virility I find it already somewhat out of date, though not as much as in old age;
"Importunus enim transvolat aridas Quercus."
["For it rudely passes over withered oaks." — Horace, Od., iv. 13, 9.]

and Marguerite, queen of Navarre, like a woman, very generously extends the advantage of women, ordaining that it is time at thirty to convert the title "fair" into "good." The shorter the authority we give to love over our lives, the better for us. Just look at his bearing — he is a beardless boy. Who does not know how, in his school, things proceed contrary to all order? Study, exercise, and usage are their ways to insufficiency; there novices rule:
"Amor ordinem nescit."
["Love knows no rule." — St Jerome, Letter to Chromatius.]

Without question his conduct is much more graceful when mixed with inadvertency and trouble; missteps and ill successes give him point and grace. Provided it is sharp and eager, it doesn't much matter whether it is prudent or not. Just see how he goes reeling, tripping, and playing; you put him in the stocks when you guide him by art and wisdom; and he is robbed of his divine liberty when put into those hairy, callous clutches.

As to the rest, I often hear the women set out this exchange as entirely spiritual, and disdain to consider the part the senses play in it; everything there serves; but I can say that I have often seen us excuse weaknesses in their understanding in favour of their outward beauty, but never yet seen that, in favour of mind, however mature and full, any of them would hold out a hand to a body even slightly in decline. Why does some one of them not take it into her head to make that noble Socratic bargain between body and soul, purchasing a philosophical and spiritual intelligence, and generation, at the price of her thighs, which is the highest price she can get for them? Plato ordains in his Laws that he who has done any signal and advantageous exploit in war may not be refused, throughout the campaign, his age or ugliness notwithstanding, a kiss or any other amorous favour from any woman whatever. What he thinks so just in honour of military valour — why may it not be the same in honour of any other good quality? And why does not some woman take a fancy to gain over her companions the glory of this chaste love? I may well say chaste:
"Nam si quando ad praelia ventum est, Ut quondam in stipulis magnus sine viribus ignis, Incassum furit:"
["For when they sometimes engage in love's battle, his sterile ardour blazes up only as a fire of straw." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 98.]
the vices that are stifled in the thought are not the worst.
To conclude this notable commentary, which has escaped me in a torrent of babble, a torrent sometimes impetuous and harmful,

"Ut missum sponsi furtivo munere malum Procurrit casto virginis a gremio, Quod miserae oblitae molli sub veste locatuat, Dum adventu matris prosilit, excutitur, Atque illud prono praeceps agitur decursu Huic manat tristi conscius ore rubor."

["As when an apple, sent by a lover as a secret gift to his mistress, falls from the chaste virgin's bosom, where she had quite forgotten it; when, starting at her mother's coming in, it is shaken out and rolls headlong over the floor before her eyes, a conscious blush covers her face." — Catullus, lxv. 19.]

I say that males and females are cast in the same mould, and that, education and habit excepted, the difference is not great. Plato indifferently invites both the one and the other to the society of all studies, exercises, and vocations, military and civil, in his Commonwealth; and the philosopher Antisthenes rejected any distinction between their virtue and ours. It is much easier to accuse one sex than to excuse the other; as the saying goes,
"Le fourgon se moque de la paele." ["The Pot and the Kettle."]

chapters.title: Of coaches
paragraphs: It is easy enough to see that the great authors, when they write of causes, do not stick to the ones they actually think are true — they reach for any that strike them as elegant or inventive. They speak truthfully and usefully so long as they speak ingeniously. We cannot make ourselves certain of the supreme cause, so we crowd a great many together, on the chance that the right one may be in the heap somewhere:
"Namque unam dicere causam Non satis est, verum plures, unde una tamen sit."
[Lucretius, vi. 704. — The sense is given in the preceding passage.]

Do you ask me where the custom of blessing those who sneeze comes from? We break wind three different ways. The one that escapes from below is too foul; the one that comes out of the mouth carries a hint of gluttony; the third is sneezing, and because it issues from the head and is no offence to anyone, we give it a polite welcome. Don't laugh at the distinction — they say it is Aristotle's.

I think I have seen in Plutarch (who of all the authors I know has best mixed art with nature and judgment with learning) that he gives as the reason for the heaving of the stomach in people at sea that it is caused by fear, having first worked out some chain of reasoning by which he proves fear can have such an effect. I, who am very prone to seasickness, know perfectly well this cause does not apply to me — and I know it not by argument but by necessary experience. Without even bringing in what I have been told, that the same thing often happens to animals, especially pigs, who have no notion of danger; or what an acquaintance of mine told me about himself, that though he was very subject to it, the urge to vomit left him three or four times when he was badly frightened in a violent storm, just as it did that ancient writer:
"Pejus vexabar, quam ut periculum mihi succurreret;"
["I was too ill to think of danger." (Or in reverse:) "I was too frightened to be ill." — Seneca, Ep., 53. 2]

I was never afraid on the water — nor, for that matter, in any other peril (and I have seen enough that would have qualified, if death is one of them) — so afraid as to be stunned out of my judgment. Fear sometimes springs as much from lack of judgment as from lack of courage. All the dangers I have stood in I have looked at without flinching, with open, sound, full sight; and in truth, a man needs courage to be afraid. It served me better, once, than any other help, in arranging and managing my retreat, so that it was, if not without fear, at least without panic and stupor; agitated, yes, but not bewildered or paralysed. Great souls go much further than this and offer us flights that are not only steady and temperate but actually noble. Let me recount what Alcibiades reports of Socrates, his comrade in arms: "I came across him," he says, "after the rout of our army, him and Lachez, last among those who fled, and I took a long look at him at my leisure and in safety, since I was mounted on a good horse and he was on foot, just as he had fought. The first thing I noticed was how much more judgment and resolve he showed than Lachez, and then the courage of his march, nothing different from his ordinary gait; his eye firm and steady, taking in and judging what was happening around him, glancing now at this man, now at that, friend and enemy, in such a way as to encourage the one and signal to the other that he meant to sell his life dear to anyone who came to take it from him — and so they got away, for people are not eager to attack such men, and prefer to chase those they see are frightened." That is the testimony of this great captain, and it teaches us, what we see every day, that nothing throws us into danger so surely as the headlong eagerness to escape it:
"Quo timoris minus est, eo minus ferme periculi est."
["When there is least fear, there is usually least danger." — Livy, xxii. 5.]

Our people are wrong when they say of a man that he is afraid of death just because he thinks about it and sees it coming. Foresight is just as appropriate in things that touch us, whether good or bad. To weigh and judge a danger is, in some sense, the opposite of being stunned by it. As for myself, I do not feel strong enough to bear up under the force and rush of this passion of fear, or any other intense passion: if I were once conquered and laid out by it, I should never get up sound again. Whoever once made my soul lose its footing would never set her upright again — she tastes and probes herself too deeply, too close to the quick, and so she would never let the wound she had received heal and scar over. It has been my good fortune that no illness has yet thrown her off balance: at every attack made on me I keep up my full opposition and defence, which means the first blow that managed to rout me would prevent me ever rallying. I have no second move to play; whichever side the flood breaks my banks, I lie open and am drowned beyond saving. Epicurus says a wise man can never turn into a fool. I hold the reverse: that whoever has once been a thoroughgoing fool will never afterwards be very wise. God gives me cold weather according to my cloak, and passions in proportion to the means I have to resist them: nature, having left me exposed on one side, has covered me on the other; having stripped me of strength, she has armed me with insensibility and a steady — call it dull, if you like — apprehension.

I cannot now stand for long (and when I was young could stand still less) either coach, litter, or boat. I hate every kind of transport except on horseback, both in town and country. But I can bear a litter worse than a coach; and, by the same logic, a rough rocking on the water, where it provokes fear, better than the motion of a calm. The little jerks of oars stealing the boat from under us — I cannot say how, but I find both my head and my stomach upset by them. Nor can I bear to sit on a wobbly chair. When the sail or the current carries us evenly, or we are being towed, the even motion does not bother me at all. It is interrupted motion that upsets me, and most of all when it is slowest; I cannot put it any better than that. The physicians have told me to squeeze and tighten myself round the lower belly with a napkin to remedy this trouble; but I haven't tried it, being used to wrestling with my own defects and overcoming them myself.

If my memory were better, I would not think it time wasted to set down here the endless variety that history offers us of the use of chariots in war — varying with the nations and the age, in my view of great usefulness and effect, so that it is a wonder we have lost all knowledge of them. I will say only this, that very recently, in our fathers' time, the Hungarians made excellent use of them against the Turks: in each one a shield-bearer and a musketeer, and a number of harquebuses stacked ready and loaded, and the whole covered with a pavise like a galliot. They formed the front of their line with three thousand such coaches, and after the cannon had fired they made them all pour their shot into the enemy, who had to swallow that volley before getting to the rest, which was no small advantage; that done, these chariots charged into the enemy squadrons to break them and open a way for the rest. Beyond that, there is the use that might be made of them to flank the soldiers in dangerous country when marching, or to cover a position and fortify it in a hurry. In my own time a gentleman on one of our frontiers, too unwieldy of body to find any horse able to carry his weight, was in a quarrel and rode through the country in a chariot of this kind, and found it very convenient. But let us leave these war chariots.

As if their softness had not been clear enough from better evidence, the last kings of our first race used to travel in a chariot drawn by four oxen. Mark Antony was the first man in Rome to have himself drawn in a coach by lions, with a singing girl beside him.
[Cytheris, the Roman courtesan. — Plutarch's Life of Antony, c. 3. This was the same woman who is introduced by Gallus under the name of Lycoris. Gallus must have known her personally.]

Heliogabalus did the same later on, calling himself Cybele, the mother of the gods, and was also drawn by tigers, taking on the role of the god Bacchus; he sometimes harnessed two stags to his coach, another time four dogs, and another four naked girls, having himself drawn by them in procession, stark naked too. The Emperor Firmus had his chariot drawn by ostriches of a prodigious size, so that it seemed to fly rather than roll.

The strangeness of these inventions puts another thought in my head: that it is a kind of weakness in monarchs, and evidence that they don't sufficiently understand what they are, when they go in for being honoured and looking great through extravagant expense. It might be forgivable in a foreign country, but among their own subjects, where they hold sovereign power and can do whatever they like, it takes away from their dignity at the very pinnacle of honour they can reach: just as, it seems to me, it is unnecessary for a private gentleman to dress lavishly at home — his house, his servants, his kitchen answer for him well enough. The advice Isocrates gives his king seems to me grounded in reason: that he should be splendid in plate and furniture, because it is an expense of long duration that passes on to his successors, and that he should avoid all kinds of grandeur that will soon be forgotten. I loved to dress finely when I was a younger brother, for want of any other ornament, and it suited me well; there are some on whom rich clothes practically weep. We have strange stories of the personal frugality of our kings — kings who were great in reputation, courage, and fortune. Demosthenes was passionately against the law of his city that set aside public money for the splendour of their public games and festivals: he wanted their greatness to be displayed in numbers of well-equipped ships and well-provisioned armies; and there is good reason to condemn Theophrastus, who in his Book on Riches takes the contrary view, holding that sort of expense to be the true fruit of abundance. These are pleasures, says Aristotle, that please only the lower sort of people and vanish from memory as soon as the crowd has had its fill, and no serious or judicious man can have any respect for them. This money would, in my opinion, be much more royally — and also more usefully, justly, and lastingly — spent on ports, harbours, walls, and fortifications, on grand buildings, churches, hospitals, colleges, and on the improvement of streets and highways — and Pope Gregory XIII will leave a fine memory to future ages for just this; and our Queen Catherine would have left to posterity proof of her natural generosity and munificence, had her means matched her inclinations. Fortune has done me a great injury by interrupting the noble work on the Pont-Neuf of our great city, and depriving me of the hope of seeing it finished before I die.

On top of that, it seems to the subjects, who are spectators of these triumphs, that their own riches are being spread out before them, and that they are being entertained at their own cost. For people are inclined to assume of kings, as we do of our servants, that they must see to it that all things needful are provided in abundance, but not touch them themselves. So the Emperor Galba, pleased with a musician who played to him at supper, called for his money-box and gave him a handful of crowns out of it, with these words: "This is not the public's money, but my own." Yet it usually turns out that the people have the right of it, and that their princes feed their eyes with what they need to fill their bellies.

Liberality is not even at its true splendour in a sovereign hand: private men have the most genuine claim to it. For, strictly speaking, a king has nothing properly his own; he owes himself to others. Authority is given not for the benefit of the magistrate but of the people; a superior is never made so for his own gain, but for the gain of his inferiors — a physician for the sake of the sick man, not for his own. Every magistracy, like every art, has its end outside itself. Therefore the tutors of young princes who make a point of impressing on them this virtue of liberality, and preach to them to refuse nothing and to consider nothing better spent than what they give away (a doctrine I have seen highly credited in my time), either care more for their own profit than for their master's, or have a poor sense of who they are talking to. It is too easy a thing to drum liberality into someone who has as much as he wants to practise it with at others' expense; and since the value of the gift is set not by its own measure but by the measure of the giver's means, in such mighty hands it comes to nothing — they find themselves wasteful before they can be called liberal. And it is not much of a recommendation, compared with the other royal virtues; it is the only one, as the tyrant Dionysius said, that goes well even with tyranny itself. I would rather teach the prince this line from the ancient farm-worker:
["That whoever wants a good harvest must sow with his hand, not pour out of the sack." — Plutarch, Apothegms, Whether the Ancients were more excellent in Arms than in Learning.]

he must scatter it about, not heap it all in one place. And since he has to give, or rather to pay and to repay so many people in proportion to their deserts, he should be a loyal and discriminating distributor. If a prince's liberality is without measure or discretion, I would rather he were stingy.

Royal virtue seems to consist mostly in justice; and of all the parts of justice, the one that most marks out a king is the liberality that accompanies it, for this is what kings have especially reserved to be done by themselves, whereas all the other forms of justice they leave to be administered by others. An immoderate generosity is a very weak way of acquiring goodwill — it puts off more people than it attracts:
"Quo in plures usus sis, minus in multos uti possis... Quid autem est stultius, quam, quod libenter facias, curare ut id diutius facere non possis;"

["The more people you use it on, the fewer will be left to use it on. And what greater folly can there be than to arrange things so that what you would willingly do, you cannot keep on doing." — Cicero, De Offic., ii. 15.]

And if it is handed out without due respect for merit, it embarrasses the man who receives it, and is received ungraciously. Tyrants have been sacrificed to the people's hatred at the hands of the very men they had wrongfully advanced: the kind of men — buffoons, pimps, fiddlers, and other riff-raff — who, thinking to secure their possession of benefits they did not deserve, take care to display hatred and contempt for the man they hold them from, joining in the common verdict against him.

The subjects of a prince extravagant in giving become extravagant in asking, and set their demands not by reason but by precedent. We have, in all seriousness, very often reason to blush at our own shamelessness: we are overpaid, by any just measure, when the reward matches our service. Don't we already owe our princes something by natural obligation? If he covers our costs, he does too much; it is enough that he contribute to them. The surplus is called a benefit, and a benefit cannot be demanded — for the very word Liberality has Liberty in it.

In our way of doing things, it is never finished; we never count what we have already received; we are only ever looking ahead to the next generosity. So the more a prince empties himself out in giving, the poorer he grows in friends. How could he ever satisfy immoderate desires, which grow with every fulfilment? Someone whose mind is on what he can take never thinks about what he has already taken; covetousness has nothing more properly its own than ingratitude.

The example of Cyrus will not be out of place here, to give the kings of our day a yardstick by which to judge whether their gifts are well or badly bestowed, and to see how much better that emperor handed them out than they do — they who are reduced to borrowing from unknown subjects, and from those they have wronged rather than those on whom they have lavished their benefits, receiving help in which there is nothing free but the name. Croesus reproached Cyrus for his generosity, and worked out how much his treasury would have come to had he been a little tighter-fisted. Cyrus wanted to justify his liberality, and so sent letters out to all the great men of his realm whom he had particularly helped, asking each of them to send him as much money as he could for an urgent need, and to send him the precise amount each could advance. When all these answers came back, every one of his friends — not thinking it enough merely to offer back as much as he had received from his bounty, and adding to it a great deal of his own — it turned out the sum came to a great deal more than Croesus had reckoned. Whereupon Cyrus said: "I am no less in love with riches than other princes, but I am a better steward of them. You see for what a small outlay I have acquired the priceless treasure of so many friends, and how much more faithfully they hold it for me than mercenary men without bond or affection. My money is better stored than in chests — chests that bring with them the hatred, envy, and contempt of other princes."

The emperors excused the extravagance of their games and public spectacles by the fact that their authority depended, in some way (at least in appearance), on the will of the people of Rome, who from time immemorial had been used to being entertained and flattered with such shows and excesses. But it was private citizens who had built up this custom, in order to indulge their fellow citizens and companions, chiefly out of their own pockets, with such lavishness and magnificence — it had quite another flavour when the masters came to imitate it:
"Pecuniarum translatio a justis dominis ad alienos non debet liberalis videri."
["The transferring of money from its rightful owners to outsiders ought not to be called liberality." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 14.]

Philip, seeing that his son was trying to win the affection of the Macedonians by gifts, scolded him in a letter to this effect: "What? Do you want your subjects to look on you as their cashier, not as their king? Are you going to woo them to win their love? Do it, then, by the gifts of your virtue, and not by those of your purse." And yet it was certainly a fine sight to bring in and plant within the amphitheatre a great number of vast trees, with all their branches in full leaf, representing a great shady forest laid out in excellent order; and on the first day, to release into it a thousand ostriches, a thousand stags, a thousand boars, and a thousand fallow-deer, to be killed and disposed of by the people; on the next day, to have a hundred great lions, a hundred leopards, and three hundred bears killed in his presence; and for the third day, to make three hundred pairs of gladiators fight it out to the death, as the Emperor Probus did. It was also very fine to see those vast amphitheatres faced on the outside with marble, intricately worked with figures and statues, and inside glittering with rare ornamentation:
"Baltheus en! gemmis, en illita porticus auro:"
["A belt glittering with jewels, and a portico overlaid with gold." — Calpurnius, Eclog., vii. 47. A baltheus was a shoulder-belt or baldric.]
all the sides of this vast space filled and ringed, from bottom to top, with sixty or eighty rows of seats, also of marble, and covered with cushions:
"Exeat, inquit, Si pudor est, et de pulvino surgat equestri, Cujus res legi non sufficit;"

["Let him go out, he said, if he has any shame, and rise from the equestrian cushion, the man whose estate does not meet the law." — Juvenal, iii. 153. The Equites were required to possess a fortune of 400 sestertia, and they sat on the first fourteen rows behind the orchestra.]

where a hundred thousand men might sit at their ease; and the area below, where the games were played, made to open up first and crack into chasms, representing caves that disgorged the beasts intended for the show; and then, secondly, flooded by a deep sea full of sea-monsters and laden with warships, to stage a naval battle; and, thirdly, made dry and level again for the gladiators' combat; and, for the fourth scene, strewn with vermilion and storax in place of sand, to set out a solemn feast for that whole vast multitude — the last act of one single day:

"Quoties nos descendentis arenae Vidimus in partes, ruptaque voragine terrae Emersisse feras, et eisdem saepe latebris Aurea cum croceo creverunt arbuta libro!.... Nec solum nobis silvestria cernere monstra Contigit; aequoreos ego cum certantibus ursis Spectavi vitulos, et equorum nomine dignum, Sen deforme pecus, quod in illo nascitur amni...."

["How often have we seen the floor of the theatre sink and split apart, and from a chasm in the earth wild beasts emerge, and then in a moment a grove of gilded trees spring up, putting forth blossoms of enamelled flowers. Nor was it only forest marvels we saw: I watched sea-calves fight with bears, and a deformed sort of cattle that one might call sea-horses." — Calpurnius, Eclog., vii. 64.]

Sometimes they made a high mountain rise up, covered with fruit-trees and other leafy trees, sending down little streams of water from the top as if from a fountain's mouth; at other times a great ship was seen rolling in which opened and split apart of itself, and after disgorging from the hold four or five hundred beasts for the fight, closed up again and disappeared without help. At other times, from the floor of this place, they made jets of perfumed water shoot upwards, so high as to sprinkle the whole vast crowd. To shield themselves from the weather, they had this huge space sometimes covered over with purple needlework curtains, and at other times with silk of one colour or another, which they drew off and on at will:
"Quamvis non modico caleant spectacula sole, Vela reducuntur, cum venit Hermogenes."
The netting that was set in front of the people to protect them from the loosed beasts was also woven of gold:
"Auro quoque torts refulgent Retia."
["The woven nets shine with gold." — Calpurnius, ubi supra.]

If there is anything to be said in defence of excesses like these, it is where the novelty and invention strike us more than the cost; even in these vanities we can see how fertile those ages were in another kind of wit than ours. With this sort of fertility it is as with every other product of nature: not that she there spent her utmost force; we don't really go anywhere — we run back and forth, whirl this way and that, turn back the way we came. I am afraid our knowledge is weak in every direction: we see neither far forward nor far back; our understanding takes in little, and lives only a little while; it is short both in extent of time and in extent of matter:
"Vixere fortes ante Agamemnona Mufti, sed omnes illacrymabiles Urgentur, ignotique longs Nocte."
["Many brave men lived before Agamemnon, but all are pressed by the long night, unmourned and unknown." — Horace, Od., iv. 9, 25.]
"Et supra bellum Thebanum et funera Trojae Non alias alii quoque res cecinere poetae?"

["Why, before the Theban war and the destruction of Troy, did no other poets sing of other events?" — Lucretius, v. 327. Montaigne here amuses himself by giving Lucretius' words a sense directly opposite to what they bear in the poem. Lucretius poses the question: why, if the earth had existed from all eternity, were there no poets before the Theban war to sing of men's exploits? — Coste.]

And the account by Solon of what he learned from the Egyptian priests, about the long life of their state and their way of learning and preserving foreign histories, is not, it seems to me, a piece of evidence to be brushed aside on this point:

"Si interminatam in omnes partes magnitudinem regionum videremus et temporum, in quam se injiciens animus et intendens, ita late longeque peregrinatur, ut nullam oram ultimi videat, in qua possit insistere: in haec immensitate . . . infinita vis innumerabilium appareret fomorum."

["If we could see on all sides the unlimited magnitude of regions and of times — into which the mind, pressing in and stretching out, wanders so wide and far that it sees no edge of the limit at which it could come to rest — in that immensity we should perceive an infinite force of innumerable forms." Here too Montaigne gives the words a sense quite different from what they bear in the original; but the application he makes of them is so apt that one would say they had been put together expressly to express his thought. "Et temporum" is an addition by Montaigne. — Coste.]

Even if everything that reached us by report of our knowledge of past ages were true, and were known to some one person, it would still be less than nothing in comparison with what is unknown. And of this same picture of the world, which is slipping past us while we live in it, how feeble and limited is the knowledge of even the most curious — not just of particular events, which fortune often makes exemplary and consequential, but of the state of great governments and nations: a hundred times more escapes us than ever comes to our knowledge. We make a great fuss about the invention of artillery and printing, when other men at the other end of the world, in China, had them a thousand years ago. If we could see as much of the world as we cannot see, we should perceive, we may reasonably believe, a perpetual repetition and variation of forms. Nothing is unique or rare in respect of nature, only in respect of our knowledge, which is a poor foundation on which to base our rules and which presents to us a very false image of things. As today we vainly conclude that the world is in decline and old age from the arguments we draw from our own weakness and decay:
"Jamque adeo est affecta aetas effoet aque tellus;"
["Our age is feeble, and the earth less fertile." — Lucretius, ii. 1151.]
so he vainly concluded as to its birth and youth, from the vigour he observed in the minds of his own time, which were full of novelties and new inventions:
"Verum, ut opinor, habet novitatem summa, recensque Natura est mundi, neque pridem exordia coepit Quare etiam quaedam nunc artes expoliuntur, Nunc etiam augescunt; nunc addita navigiis sunt Multa."

["But in my opinion the whole world is of recent origin, and did not begin in remote times; which is why some arts are still being refined, and some are only just on the rise; and at present many additions are being made to shipping." — Lucretius, v. 331.]

Our world has lately discovered another (and who can assure us it is the last of its siblings, since the daemons, the sibyls, and we ourselves have been ignorant of this one until now?), as large, well-peopled, and fruitful as the one we live on, and yet so raw and young that we are still teaching it its ABC: it is barely fifty years since it knew neither letters, weights, measures, clothes, grain, nor vines; it was still naked in the mother's lap, and lived on what she gave it. If we are right to draw conclusions about our own end, and this poet right about the youthfulness of his own age, that other world will only just be entering into the light when ours makes its exit. The universe will fall into paralysis: one limb will be useless, the other in its vigour. I am very much afraid that we have hugely accelerated its decline and ruin by our contagion, and that we have sold it our opinions and our arts at a very high price. It was an infant world — and yet we did not whip and subject it to our discipline by virtue of our natural worth and strength; nor did we win it over by our justice and goodness, nor master it by our magnanimity. Most of their answers, and of the negotiations we had with them, show that they were in no way behind us in sharpness or clarity of natural understanding. The astonishing magnificence of the cities of Cusco and Mexico, and among many other things the garden of the king, where all the trees, fruits, and plants were perfectly modelled in gold, in the order and stature they would have in a real garden — and in his cabinet were all the animals bred on his territory and in its seas; and the beauty of their craft work in jewels, feathers, cotton, and painting — all give ample proof that in industry they were no less our equals. But as to devotion, observance of laws, goodness, generosity, loyalty, and plain dealing, it served us well that we had less of these than they; for it is by this very advantage of theirs over us that they have lost themselves, sold themselves, betrayed themselves.

As for boldness and courage, steadiness, constancy in the face of pain, hunger, and death, I would not be afraid to set the examples I find among them against the most famous examples of ancient times we find in our own records on this side of the world. As for those who subdued them, take away the tricks and artifices they used to dupe them, and the just astonishment those nations felt at the sudden, unexpected arrival of bearded men, different in language, religion, shape, and face, from a part of the world so remote they had never heard there was any inhabited land there, mounted on great unknown monsters — they who had not only never seen a horse, but had never seen any other beast trained to carry a man or any other load; sheathed in a hard, shining skin, with a cutting and glittering weapon in his hand, against people who, in wonder at the brightness of a mirror or a knife, would exchange great treasures of gold and pearl, and who had neither the knowledge nor the materials with which, given time, they could have penetrated our steel; add to this the lightning and thunder of our cannon and harquebuses, enough to frighten Caesar himself had he been surprised by them with so little experience, set against people naked, except where they used a little quilted cotton, with no other arms at most than bows, stones, sticks, and wooden shields; people taken by surprise under colour of friendship and good faith, by their curiosity to see strange and unknown things — take away, I say, this disparity from the conquerors, and you take away the whole occasion of so many victories. When I look at that unconquerable ardour with which so many thousands of men, women, and children threw themselves over and over again into certain death for the defence of their gods and their freedoms; that noble stubbornness in enduring every extremity and hardship, and death itself, rather than submit to the rule of those by whom they had been so shamefully abused; some of them choosing, when prisoner, to starve themselves to death rather than take food from the hands of enemies who had triumphed so basely — I see that whoever had attacked them on equal terms of arms, experience, and numbers would have had a hard, and possibly a harder, fight on his hands than in any war we have ever known.

Why did such a noble conquest not fall to Alexander, or to the ancient Greeks and Romans? Why did so great a revolution and upheaval of so many empires and peoples not fall into hands that would gently have levelled and smoothed out what was rough and savage among them, and would have cherished and propagated the good seeds nature had already planted there — mixing not only with the cultivation of the soil and the adornment of cities the arts of this part of the world, in what was necessary, but also the Greek and Roman virtues with those native to the country? What a reparation it would have been to them, what a general good to the whole world, if our first examples and behaviour over there had drawn those people into admiration and imitation of virtue, and had brought into being a brotherhood and mutual understanding between them and us? How easy it would have been to take advantage of souls so innocent, and so eager to learn, having for the most part such naturally good inclinations to start with? Whereas, on the contrary, we took advantage of their ignorance and inexperience with all the more ease to bend them towards treachery, luxury, greed, and every kind of inhumanity and cruelty, by the pattern and example of our own manners. Who has ever set so high a price on his merchandise? So many cities razed to the ground, so many nations exterminated, so many millions of people put to the sword, and the richest and most beautiful part of the world turned upside down, for the sake of trading in pearl and pepper. Mechanical victories! Never did ambition, never did public quarrels, drive men against one another into such miserable hostilities, into such miserable calamities.
