But the judgment of an emperor ought to be above his empire, and to see and consider it as something foreign, external; and he ought to know how to enjoy himself apart from it, and to keep company with himself as James and Peter, regardless of what comes.

I cannot engage myself so deeply and so wholly. When my will gives me to a thing, it is not under such a violent obligation that my judgment is infected by it. In the present civil disorders of this kingdom, my own interest has not made me blind to the laudable qualities in our adversaries, or to those that are blameworthy in those on our side. Others worship everything on their own side; I, for my part, do not even excuse most things on mine. A good work loses no grace with me for being made against me. Setting aside the knot of the dispute itself, I have always kept myself in balance and pure indifference.
"Neque extra necessitates belli praecipuum odium gero;"
["Nor do I carry particular hatred beyond the necessities of war."]

For which I am pleased with myself, and all the more because I see others commonly fail in the opposite direction. Those who extend their anger and hatred beyond the dispute in question, as most men do, show that they spring from some other occasion and private cause — like a man cured of an ulcer who still has a fever, by which it appears that the ulcer had a deeper, hidden origin. The reason is that they are not concerned in the common cause because it wounds the state and the general interest, but only stung by their particular concern. That is why they are so especially fired up, and to such a degree beyond justice and public reason.
"Non tam omnia universi, quam ea, quae ad quemque pertinent, singuli carpebant."
["Everyone was not so much angry about things in general, as about those things that particularly concerned himself." --Livy, xxxiv. 36.]

I would have the advantage on our side; but if I do not get it, I will not go mad. I am heartily for the right party; but I do not want to be picked out as an especial enemy to others, beyond the general quarrel. I deeply resist this vicious form of opinion: "He is for the League because he admires the grace of Monsieur de Guise; he is impressed by the energy of the King of Navarre, therefore he is a Huguenot; he criticises this or that in the king, therefore he is seditious in his heart." And I did not grant even to the magistrate that he was right in condemning a book because it had placed a heretic among the best poets of the age. Are we not to dare say of a thief that he has a handsome leg? If a woman is a prostitute, must she necessarily smell foul? In the wisest ages, did they revoke the proud title of Capitolinus that they had conferred on Marcus Manlius as preserver of religion and public liberty, and stifle the memory of his liberality, his feats of arms, and the military honours granted to his valour, because he afterwards aspired to sovereignty against the laws of his country? If we conceive a hatred of a lawyer, will he not be allowed the next day to be eloquent? I have spoken elsewhere of the zeal that has pushed worthy men into similar errors. For my part, I can say, "Such a man does this thing badly, and another thing virtuously and well." In the same way, when affairs go badly, they would have everyone in their party be blind or a blockhead, and our judgment and conviction subservient not to the truth but to the project of our desires. I would rather lean toward the other extreme, so much do I fear being bribed by my own wishes; to which may be added that I am slightly distrustful of things I want to be true.

I have seen in my time wonders in the careless and astonishing readiness of people to let their hopes and beliefs be led and governed in whichever direction best pleased and served their leaders, despite a hundred mistakes piled one on another, despite mere dreams and fantasies. I no longer wonder at those who have been blinded and seduced by the absurdities of Apollonius and Mohammed. Their sense and understanding are entirely taken away by their passion; their discretion has no other choice than what smiles upon them and supports their cause. I had especially observed this at the beginning of our domestic troubles; the troubles since then, in imitating, have outdone it, and from that I am satisfied that it is a quality inseparable from popular errors. After the first opinion that rolls, others drive each other on like waves on the wind; a man is not a member of the body if he has it in his power to part with it, and if he does not roll along the common way. But for all that, men do an injury to the just side when they try to assist it with fraud. I have always been against that practice; it only works on weak heads. For sound ones, there are surer and more honest ways to keep their courage up and to excuse adverse events.

Heaven never saw a greater animosity than that between Caesar and Pompey, nor ever shall, and yet I notice in those great souls a great moderation toward one another; it was a jealousy of honour and command which did not carry them away into a furious and indiscreet hatred, and was without malice or slander. In their hottest exploits against one another I detect some remnants of respect and good will, and I think therefore that, if it had been possible, each of them would rather have done his business without the destruction of the other than with it. Notice how differently things went between Marius and Sylla.

We must not throw ourselves so headlong after our affections and interests. As, when I was young, I opposed the progress of love, which I felt was moving too fast on me, and took care not to let it become so pleasing as to force, captivate, and entirely surrender me to its mercy — so I do the same in every other case where my will runs on with too warm an appetite. I lean opposite to the side it is going; as I find it about to plunge and get drunk on its own wine, I avoid feeding its pleasure to the point where I could not recover it without infinite loss. Souls that through their own dullness only half-grasp things have this advantage, that they smart less under hurtful things: it is a spiritual leprosy that has the appearance of health, and a health which philosophy does not altogether despise; but we have no right to call it wisdom, as we often do. And in this manner someone once mocked Diogenes who, in the depths of winter and stark naked, was embracing a statue of snow as a test of endurance. The other, seeing him in this posture, asked, "Are you very cold?" "Not at all," replied Diogenes. "Why then," said the other, "what difficult and exemplary thing do you suppose you are doing in embracing that snow?" To take a true measure of constancy, one must necessarily know what the suffering is.

But for souls that are to meet adverse events and the injuries of fortune in their depth and sharpness, that are to weigh and taste them according to their natural weight and bitterness — let such souls show their skill in avoiding the causes and deflecting the blow. What did King Cotys do? He paid handsomely for the rich and beautiful vessel that had been presented to him, but seeing it was extremely fragile, he immediately smashed it himself, ahead of time, to prevent so easy a cause of annoyance with his servants. In the same way, I have willingly avoided all entanglements in my affairs, and never wanted my estate to border on those of my relatives or of people with whom I wanted a close friendship; for from that comes plenty of cause for ill-feeling and falling out. I used to love hazardous games of cards and dice, but gave them up long ago, only because, whatever cheerful face I put on my losses, I could not help feeling vexed inside. A man of honour, who must take an insult or a lie deeply to heart and who must not be content with some shabby apology, should avoid occasions of dispute. I shun melancholy, sour-tempered men as I would the plague, and I never meddle in matters I cannot discuss without emotion and concern, unless duty compels me.
"Melius non incipient, quam desinent."
["It is better never to begin than to have to leave off." --Seneca, Ep., 72.]
The safest course, then, is to prepare oneself beforehand for the situation.

I know very well that some wise men have taken the other route, and have not feared to grapple with and engage many subjects to the utmost. These men are confident in their own strength, under which they shield themselves in any setback, making their patience wrestle and contend with disaster.
"Velut rupes, vastum quae prodit in aequor, Obvia ventorum furiis, expostaque ponto, Vim cunctam atque minas perfert coelique marisque; Ipsa immota manens."
["As a rock, which juts into the vast ocean, exposed to the fury of the winds and the raging sea, endures the whole force and threats of sky and sea, itself unmoved."--Virgil, Aeneid, x. 693.]

Let us not attempt these examples; we shall never come up to them. They set themselves resolutely, and without agitation, to watch the ruin of their country, which possessed and commanded all their will: that is too much, and too hard a task for our more ordinary souls. Cato gave up the noblest life that ever was on this account; we lesser spirits must run from the storm as far as we can; we must provide for feeling, not for endurance, and dodge blows we cannot meet. Zeno, seeing Chremonides, a young man he was fond of, come up to sit beside him, suddenly jumped up, and when Cleanthes asked why he did so, said: "I hear that physicians especially prescribe rest, and forbid disturbance, in all swellings." Socrates does not say: "Do not surrender to the charms of beauty; stand your ground, and do everything you can to resist it." "Flee from it," he says; "avoid the sight and encounter of it, as you would of a powerful poison that shoots its arrows and wounds at a distance." And his fine pupil, inventing or recounting — in my opinion rather recounting than inventing — the rare perfections of the great Cyrus, makes him distrustful of his own strength to resist the charms of the divine beauty of that illustrious Panthea, his captive, and so he commits the visiting and keeping of her to another, who could not have so much liberty as himself. And the Holy Spirit, likewise:
"Ne nos inducas in tentationem."
["Lead us not into temptation."--St. Matthew, vi. 13.]

We do not pray that our reason should not be combated and overcome by lust, but that it should not even be tried by it — that we should not be brought into a state where we even have to face the approaches, solicitations, and temptations of sin; and we beg Almighty God to keep our consciences quiet, fully and perfectly delivered from all dealings with evil.

Those who say that they have reason for their vengeful passion, or for some other troublesome agitation of mind, often speak truly as things now stand, but not as they were. They speak to us when the causes of their error are by themselves being fed and pushed forward; but go backwards — trace those causes back to their beginning — and there you will stop them in their tracks. Will their faults be less for being longer-lived? Will an unjust beginning make a just sequel? Whoever desires the good of his country, as I do, without fretting or wasting himself, will be troubled, but not faint, to see it threatening either its own ruin or a no less ruinous survival; a poor vessel, tossed and steered by waves, winds, and pilot toward conflicting destinations!
"In tam diversa magister Ventus et unda trahunt."

He who does not gape after the favour of princes as after something he cannot live without is not much disturbed by the coolness of their reception and demeanour, or by the inconstancy of their wills. He who does not brood over his children or his honours with a slavish attachment does not stop living comfortably enough after their loss. He who does good principally for his own satisfaction will not be much troubled to see men judge his actions contrary to their merit. A quarter ounce of patience will provide sufficiently against such inconveniences. I find ease in this prescription, redeeming myself at the start as cheaply as I can; and by this means I have escaped much trouble and many difficulties. With very little fuss I stop the first outburst of my emotions, and I leave the subject that is beginning to be bothersome before it carries me away. He who does not stop the start will never be able to stop the course; he who cannot keep them out will never get them out once they are in; and he who cannot reach the beginning will never reach the end of it all. Nor will he bear the fall who cannot stand the shock.
"Etenim ipsae se impellunt, ubi semel a ratione discessum est; ipsaque sibi imbecillitas indulget, in altumque provehitur imprudens, nec reperit locum consistendi."

["For they throw themselves headlong once they have departed from reason; and weakness indulges itself, and from lack of prudence is carried out into deep water, and finds no place to take shelter."--Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 18.]
I am alert in good time to the little breezes that begin to sing and whistle inside me, the forerunners of the storm.
"Ceu flamina prima Cum deprensa fremunt sylvis et caeca volutant Murmura, venturos nautis prodentia ventos."
["As the first breezes, caught in the woods, rumble and roll their hidden murmurs, announcing to sailors the winds to come."--Aeneid, x. 97.]

How often have I done myself a clear injustice in order to avoid the risk of having a worse one done me by the judges, after years of harassment, dirty and vile practices, more hateful to my nature than fire or the rack?
"Convenit a litibus, quantum licet, et nescio an paulo plus etiam quam licet, abhorrentem esse: est enim non modo liberale, paululum nonnunquam de suo jure decedere, sed interdum etiam fructuosum."

["A man should shrink from lawsuits as much as he can, and perhaps a little more than he should; for it is not only generous, but sometimes even profitable, to give up a little of one's own right."--Cicero, De Offic., ii. 18.]

If we were wise, we should rejoice and boast, as I one day heard a young gentleman of good family very innocently do, that his mother had lost her case — as if it had been a cough or a fever, or something tiresome to keep. Even the favours that fortune might have given me through kinship or acquaintance with those who have sovereign authority in such matters, I have very conscientiously and carefully avoided employing to the prejudice of others, or to push my own claims beyond their true right. In the end, I have so far succeeded in my efforts — and I may happily say it — that I am to this day a virgin in matters of lawsuits, though I have been offered fair ones, and with a fully just title, had I been willing to listen; and a virgin in quarrels too. I have nearly passed through a long life without any offence of any consequence, either active or passive, or even hearing a worse word spoken than my own name: a rare favour of heaven.

Our greatest agitations have ridiculous springs and causes. What ruin did our last Duke of Burgundy bring on himself over a cartload of sheepskins! And was not the engraving of a seal the first and chief cause of the greatest convulsion that this machine of the world has ever undergone? For Pompey and Caesar were only the later phases and continuation of two earlier men; and I have seen in my own time the wisest heads in this kingdom assembled with great ceremony, and at the public expense, to negotiate treaties and settlements whose actual decision meanwhile depended entirely on the ladies' cabinet council and the inclination of some scrap of a woman.

The poets understood this well when they set all Greece and Asia to fire and sword over an apple. Look — there is a man risking his life and honour on the chance of his rapier and dagger; ask him to tell you the cause of the quarrel; he cannot do it without blushing, the occasion is so silly and frivolous.

A small thing will get you into it, but once you are embarked, every cord pulls; large supplies are then required, more demanding and more important. How much easier it is not to go in than to get out! Now we should go about it the opposite way from the reed, which at its first springing puts forth a long and straight shoot, and afterwards, as if winded, runs into thick and frequent joints and knots, as so many pauses showing that it has lost its first vigour and firmness. We had better begin gently and coolly, and save our breath and our vigorous efforts for the height and stress of the business. We govern affairs at their beginnings, and have them in our power; but afterwards, once they are under way, it is they that govern us, and we have to follow them.

Yet I do not mean to say that this principle has freed me from all difficulty, or that I have not often had enough to do to curb and restrain my passions; they are not always to be governed according to the measure of the occasion, and often have very sharp and violent entries. Still, good fruit and benefit can be gathered from them — except by those who in doing well are not satisfied with any benefit if reputation is missing; for in truth such an effect is valued only by oneself; you are more content, but not more esteemed, because you reformed yourself before you got into the whirl of the dance, or before the provoking matter was even in sight. Yet not only here, but in all other duties of life, the path of those who aim at honour is very different from the path taken by those whose aim is order and reason. I see some who rashly and furiously rush into the lists and cool off in the course. As Plutarch says of those who, through false shame, are soft and ready to grant whatever is asked of them, and are afterwards just as ready to break their word and to retract — so a man who enters a quarrel lightly is likely to leave it just as lightly. The same difficulty that keeps me from entering it would, once I was hot and engaged in the quarrel, drive me to maintain it with great obstinacy and resolve. It is the tyranny of habit: once a man has engaged himself, he must go through with it or die. "Take on coolly," said Bias, "but pursue with ardour." For lack of prudence, men fall into a lack of courage, which is even more intolerable.

Most settlements of the quarrels of our day are shameful and false; we only seek to save appearances, and meanwhile betray and disavow our true intentions; we paper over the fact. We know very well how we said the thing, and in what sense we said it, and the company knows it, and our friends, to whom we wished to make our advantage clear, understand it well enough too. It is at the cost of our frankness and of the honour of our courage that we disown our thoughts and take refuge in falsehoods to patch things up. We give ourselves the lie in order to excuse the lie we have given another. You are not to consider whether your word or action might admit some other interpretation; it is your own true and sincere interpretation, your real meaning in what you said or did, that you are from then on to maintain, whatever it costs. Men speak to your virtue and your conscience, which are not things to be put under a mask; let us leave these pitiful expedients and dodges to the jugglers of the law. The excuses and reparations that I see every day made and given for indiscretions seem to me more shameful than the indiscretion itself. It would be better to insult your opponent a second time than to insult yourself by giving him so unmanly a satisfaction. You stood up to him in your heat and anger, and now you would flatter and pacify him in your cooler and better sense; and by that you lay yourself lower and at the feet of the man you previously pretended to tower over. I find nothing a gentleman can say so wicked in him as that unsaying what he has said is dishonourable, when the unsaying is extracted from him by pressure — since stubbornness is more excusable in a man of honour than cowardice. Passions are as easy for me to evade as they are hard for me to moderate.
"Exscinduntur facilius animo, quam temperantur."
["They are more easily uprooted from the mind than governed in it."]

Whoever cannot reach the noble Stoic impassivity, let him take cover in the lap of this common dullness of mine; what they achieved by virtue, I train myself to do by temperament. The middle region harbours storms and tempests; the two extremes — of philosophers and peasants — meet in tranquillity and happiness.

"Felix, qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas, Atque metus omnes et inexorabile fatum Subjecit pedibus, strepitumque Acherontis avari! Fortunatus et ille, Deos qui novit agrestes, Panaque, Sylvanumque senem, Nymphasque sorores!"

["Happy is he who has been able to learn the causes of things, and has placed under his feet all fears and unyielding fate, and the noise of greedy Acheron: blessed too is he who knows the country gods, and Pan, and old Sylvanus, and the sister nymphs."--Virgil, Georg., ii. 490.]

The births of all things are weak and tender, and so we should have our eyes fixed on beginnings; for just as in its infancy the danger is not perceived, so when it has grown up the remedy is just as hard to find. I should have met a million crosses every day, harder to swallow in the pursuit of ambition, than it has been hard for me to curb the natural inclination that drew me toward it.
"Jure perhorrui Late conspicuum tollere verticem."
["I justly feared to raise my head conspicuously high." --Horace, Od., iii. 16, 18.]

All public actions are open to uncertain and varied interpretations, because too many heads judge of them. Some say of this civic employment of mine — and I am willing to say a word or two about it, not because it is worth so much, but to give an account of my manners in such matters — that I conducted myself in it as a man too sluggish and of a languid temperament; and they have some colour for what they say. I tried to keep my mind and my thoughts at rest.
"Cum semper natura, tum etiam aetate jam quietus;"
["As being always quiet by nature, so also now by age." --Cicero, De Petit. Consul., c. 2.]

And if they sometimes lash out under some rough and sensitive impression, it is truthfully without my consent. Yet from this natural heaviness of mine, men should not conclude a total incapacity in me (for lack of care and lack of sense are two very different things), and still less any unkindness or ingratitude toward that corporation which used every means in their power to oblige me, both before they knew me and afterwards; and they did much more for me in choosing me a second time than in conferring the honour on me at first. I wish them every imaginable good; and assuredly, if there had been occasion, there is nothing I would have spared for their service; I did for them as I would have done for myself. They are a good, warlike, generous people, but capable of obedience and discipline, and of whom the best use can be made if they are well led. They also say that my administration passed without leaving any mark or trace. Good! They further accuse my abstention at a time when almost everyone was convicted of doing too much. I am eager to act where my will spurs me on; but this very eagerness is an enemy to perseverance. Let anyone who wants to use me in my own way employ me in affairs where vigour and freedom are required, where a direct, short, and even hazardous conduct is necessary; I may do something. But if it must be long, subtle, laborious, artificial, and intricate, he had better call in somebody else. Not all important offices are necessarily difficult; I came prepared to do rougher work, had there been great occasion; for it is in my power to do something more than I do, or than I like to do. I did not, to my knowledge, leave out anything that my duty really required. I easily forgot those duties that ambition mixes with duty and disguises with its label; those are the ones that, for the most part, fill the eyes and ears and give men the most satisfaction; not the thing but the appearance contents them; if they hear no noise, they think men are asleep. My temperament is no friend to commotion; I could settle a disturbance without commotion, and chastise a disorder without being disorderly myself; if I need anger and excitement, I borrow it and put it on. My manners are languid, more faint than sharp. I do not condemn a magistrate who sleeps, provided the people in his charge sleep as well as he does; in that case the laws sleep too. For my part, I commend a gliding, settled, and silent life.
"Neque submissam et abjectam, neque se efferentem;"
["Neither submissive and abject, nor obtrusive." --Cicero, De Offic., i. 34]
My fortune wants it so. I am descended from a family that has lived without splendour or noise and, time out of mind, particularly proud of a reputation for honesty.

Our people nowadays are so trained up to bustle and show that good nature, moderation, equability, constancy, and other such quiet and obscure qualities are no longer thought of or noticed. Rough bodies make themselves felt; smooth ones are handled imperceptibly; sickness is felt, health little or not at all, any more than the oils that soothe us, compared with the pains for which we are soothed. It is acting for one's own reputation and profit, not for the public good, to refer to the public square what could be done in the council chamber, or to noonday what could have been done the night before; or to be jealous to do oneself what one's colleague can do as well as you; some surgeons of Greece used to perform their operations on platforms in plain sight of the people, to attract more practice and more profit. They think that good rules cannot be understood except by the sound of a trumpet. Ambition is not a vice of small people or of such modest means as ours. Someone said to Alexander: "Your father will leave you a great dominion, easy and at peace"; this young man was envious of his father's victories and the justice of his rule; he would not have enjoyed the empire of the world in ease and peace. Alcibiades, in Plato, would rather die young, beautiful, rich, noble, and learned, with all this at the very peak, than fall short of such a condition; this disease is, perhaps, excusable in so strong and so full a soul. But when wretched, dwarfish little souls flatter and deceive themselves, and think to spread their fame for having given a correct judgment in some matter, or maintained discipline at the guard of a city gate, the more they think to raise their heads, the more they show their tails. This petty doing-good has neither body nor life; it vanishes in the first mouth, and goes no further than from one street to another. Brag of it by all means to your son or your servant, like the old fellow who, having no other audience for his praises or witness to his valour, boasted to his chambermaid, crying: "O Perrette, what a fine, clever man you have for a master!" At worst, talk of it to yourself, like a councillor of my acquaintance who, having disgorged a whole cartful of legal jargon with great heat and equal folly, on coming out of the council chamber to relieve himself, was heard quite contentedly muttering between his teeth:
"Non nobis, domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam."
["Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Thy name be the glory." --Psalm cxiii. 1.]
He who gets it from nobody else, let him pay himself out of his own purse.

Fame is not prostituted that cheaply. The rare and exemplary actions to which it is due would not put up with the company of this enormous crowd of petty daily performances. Marble may exalt your titles all you please, for having repaired a yard of wall or cleaned out a public sewer — but men of sense will not. Renown does not follow every good deed unless novelty and difficulty are joined to it; in fact even mere esteem, according to the Stoics, is not due to every action that springs from virtue; nor will they grant bare thanks to a man who, out of temperance, abstains from a bleary old crone. Those who have known the admirable qualities of Scipio Africanus deny him the glory Panaetius attributes to him, of being incorruptible by gifts — a glory not so much his as that of his age. We have pleasures suitable to our station; let us not lay claim to those of grandeur; our own are more natural, and so much more solid and sure as they are lower. If not for conscience's sake, then at least for ambition's sake, let us reject ambition; let us scorn that thirst for honour and renown that is so low and beggarly that it makes us beg it of all sorts of people:
"Quae est ista laus quae possit e macello peti?"
["What praise is that which can be picked up in the market-place (meat market)?"--Cicero, De Fin., ii. 15.]

— by base means, and at however cheap a rate; it is dishonour to be honoured in this way. Let us learn to be no greedier of glory than we are capable of glory. To be puffed up with every action that is innocent or useful is only for those for whom such things are extraordinary and rare; they will value such things at what they cost them. The more noise a good effect makes, the more I subtract from its goodness, suspecting that it was performed more for the noise than on account of the goodness; once on display in the market, it is half sold. Those actions have much more grace and lustre that slip from the hand of the doer carelessly and without noise, and that some honest man afterwards finds out and lifts from the shade to bring it into the light on its own account:
"Mihi quidem laudabiliora videntur omnia, quae sine venditatione, et sine populo teste fiunt,"
["To me, indeed, all things seem more laudable which are done without ostentation, and without the people as witness." --Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 26.]
— says the most ostentatious man who ever lived.

I had only to conserve and to continue, which are silent and unnoticed effects; innovation is full of glitter, but it is forbidden in this age, when we are under pressure and have nothing to defend ourselves against but novelties. Refraining from doing is often as generous as doing, but it is less in the spotlight, and the little good I have in me is of this kind. In short, the occasions during this employment of mine were in league with my temperament, and I am heartily grateful to them for it. Is there anyone who wishes to be sick in order to see his physician at work? And would not a physician deserve a whipping who wished the plague among us so he could put his art into practice? I have never had that wicked humour, common as it is, to wish that troubles and disorders in this city should magnify and honour my government; I have always wholeheartedly contributed everything I could to its tranquillity and ease.

He who will not thank me for the order, the gentle and silent calm that has accompanied my administration, cannot, however, deprive me of the share that belongs to me under the heading of my good fortune. And I am of such a make that I would as willingly be lucky as wise, and would rather owe my successes purely to the favour of Almighty God than to anything I did myself. I had sufficiently announced to the world my unfitness for such public offices, but I have something in me even worse than this incapacity itself, which is that I am not greatly displeased about it, and that I do not work hard to cure it, given the course of life I have set for myself.

Nor have I satisfied myself in this employment; but I have come very near to what I expected from my own performance, and have far exceeded what I promised those I had to deal with: for I tend to promise something less than what I am able to do, and than what I hope to make good. I assure myself that I have left no offence or hatred behind me; as to leaving regret or longing for me among them, I at least know very well that I never much aimed at it.
"Mene huic confidere monstro! Mene salis placidi vultum, fluctusque quietos Ignorare?"
["Should I place confidence in this monster? Should I be ignorant of the look of that seeming-calm sea and those now-quiet waves?" --Virgil, Aeneid, V. 849.]

chapters.title: Of cripples
paragraphs: It is now two or three years ago that they shortened the year by ten days in France. How many changes were supposed to follow from this reform! It was, after all, moving heaven and earth at once. Yet nothing for all that stirred from its place: my neighbours still find their seasons of sowing and reaping, the right times for their business, the unlucky and propitious days, exactly where they had assigned them time out of mind. There was no more error perceived in the old way than there is improvement felt in the change; so great an uncertainty there is in everything; so coarse, dim, and dull is our perception. It is said this regulation could have been carried through with less inconvenience by subtracting, for a few years, the bissextile day (which is in any case something of a nuisance), as Augustus did, until we had exactly paid off this debt — which even this correction does not pay off, and we are still some days in arrears. By the same means, an arrangement might also have been made for the future, so that after the revolution of such-and-such a number of years the surplus day would always be thrown out, and we could never err more than twenty-four hours in our reckoning. We have no other measure of time but years; the world has used only that for many ages, and yet it is a measure we have still not agreed upon, and one whose shape we still doubt as we see other nations have given it variously, and as to what its true use was. What is the meaning of those who say that the heavens, as they grow old, are bowing themselves down nearer to us, and putting us in uncertainty even about hours and days? Or what Plutarch says of the months — that astronomy in his time had still not settled the motion of the moon? What a fine condition we are in to keep records of things past!

I was just now ruminating, as I often do, on what a free and roving thing human reason is. I commonly see that when something is put to them, men are more eager to find reasons than to ascertain the truth: they skip over the premises and look closely into the consequences; they leave the things and run to the causes. Pleasant talkers! Knowledge of causes only concerns the man who has the running of things; not us, who are simply to undergo them, and who have a perfectly full and complete use of them, according to our need, without prying into their origin and essence. Wine is no more pleasant to the man who knows its primary properties. On the contrary, both the body and the soul interrupt and weaken the right they have to the use of the world and of themselves by mixing in the conceit of learning. Effects concern us, but the means not at all. To decide and to distribute belongs to a superior, to one in command; to a subordinate, to accept. Let me criticise our usage. They commonly begin by asking, "How is such a thing done?" Whereas they should be asking, "Is such a thing done?" Our reason is capable of inventing a hundred other worlds and finding out their beginnings and their structure; it needs neither matter nor foundation; let it just run on, and it builds as well in the air as on the earth, and on emptiness as well as on substance:
"Dare pondus idonea fumo."
["Capable of giving weight to smoke."--Persius, v. 20.]

I find that almost throughout we should be saying, "there is no such thing," and I myself would often use this answer; but I do not dare, for they cry that it is a dodge produced by ignorance and a weakness of understanding; and I am obliged, for the most part, to go along with the crowd, and to talk about frivolous subjects and stories I do not believe a word of. Besides which, it is in truth a little rude and quarrelsome to flatly deny a stated fact; and few people will hesitate to assert, especially of things hard to believe, that they have seen them, or at least to name witnesses whose authority will close our mouths. In this way, we learn the foundations and means of things that never were; and the world scuffles about a thousand questions of which both the Pro and the Con are false.
"Ita finitima sunt falsa veris, ut in praecipitem locum non debeat se sapiens committere."
["False things are so close to true that a wise man should not trust himself in a place where the ground falls away."--Cicero, Acad., ii. 21.]

Truth and lies look alike; their bearing, taste, and conduct are the same, and we look at them with the same eye. I find that we are not only slack in defending ourselves against deception, but we go out of our way to be taken in; we love to get tangled up in vanity, as a thing in tune with our being.

I have seen the birth of many miracles in my time; and although they died young, we have not failed to foresee what they would have grown into, had they lived their full age. It is just a matter of finding the end of the thread, and a man may wind off as much of it as he pleases; and there is a greater distance between nothing and the smallest thing in the world than there is between that and the greatest. Now the first who are infected with the beginnings of this novelty, when they set out with their tale, discover from the resistance they meet where the difficulty of persuasion lies, and there they caulk up the gap with some piece of falsehood;

[Voltaire says of this passage, "He who would learn to doubt should read this whole chapter of Montaigne, the least methodical of all philosophers, but the wisest and most amiable." --Melanges Historiques, xvii. 694, ed. of Lefevre.]
besides which:
"Insita hominibus libido alendi de industria rumores,"
["Men having an inbred desire to nourish reports." --Livy, xxviii. 24.]

we are naturally conscientious about returning what has been lent us — but never without some interest and addition of our own. The particular error first creates the public error, and afterwards, in turn, the public error creates the particular one; and thus this whole vast structure goes on forming and piling itself up from hand to hand, so that the most distant witness knows more about it than those who were nearest, and the last informed is more convinced than the first.

It is a natural progression; for whoever believes a thing thinks it a work of charity to persuade another into the same opinion, and, the better to do so, will not hesitate to add as much of his own invention to his tale as he thinks necessary to overcome the resistance or slowness of understanding he meets in others. I myself, who make a great point of conscience about lying, and am not very anxious to give credit and authority to what I say, find that in the arguments I have on hand, when I am heated by another's opposition or by the natural warmth of my own narration, I swell and inflate my subject by voice, gesture, vigour, and force of words, and also by extension and exaggeration, not without some prejudice to the bare truth. But I do it on this condition: that to the first who brings me back to myself, and asks me for the plain and bare truth, I at once give up my passion and hand over the matter to him without exaggeration, without emphasis, or any colouring of my own. A quick and earnest manner of speaking, like mine, is apt to run into hyperbole. There is nothing men are more inclined to than to make way for their own opinions; where ordinary means fail us, we add command, force, fire, and sword. It is a misfortune to be at such a pass that the best test of truth is the multitude of those who believe it, in a crowd where the number of fools so far outweighs the wise:
"Quasi vero quidquam sit tam valde, quam nil sapere, vulgare."
["As if anything were so common as ignorance." --Cicero, De Divin., ii.]
"Sanitatis patrocinium est, insanientium turba."
["The multitude of the mad is a defence for sound thinking." --St. Augustine, De Civit. Dei, vi. 10.]

It is hard to set one's judgment against common opinions. The first impression, taken from the subject itself, possesses the simple, and from them spreads to the wise, under the authority of the number and antiquity of witnesses. For my part, what I would not believe from one, I would not believe from a hundred and one; and I do not judge opinions by their years.

It is not long ago that one of our princes — in whom gout had spoiled an excellent nature and a lively disposition — let himself be so far persuaded by the report he was given of the marvellous cures of a certain priest who, by words and gestures, cured all sorts of diseases, that he undertook a long journey to find him out, and by the sheer force of his own imagination so persuaded and put his legs to sleep for some hours that he got service from them they had long forgotten how to give. If fortune had piled up five or six such incidents, that would have been enough to bring this miracle into nature. But so much simplicity and so little artifice were afterwards uncovered in the man behind these performances that he was thought too contemptible to be punished — as would probably be thought of most such things if they were properly examined:
"Miramur ex intervallo fallentia."
["We admire, across an interval, the things that deceive."--Seneca, Ep., 118, 2.]
Our eyes often show us strange images at a distance, which vanish as we approach:
"Nunquam ad liquidum fama perducitur."
["Report is never fully cleared up." --Quintus Curtius, ix. 2.]

It is amazing from how many idle beginnings and frivolous causes such famous reports commonly arise. This is what blocks information; for while we hunt for solid and weighty causes and ends worthy of so great a name, we lose the real ones; they escape our sight by their smallness. And indeed, a very careful, prudent, and subtle inquiry is required in such searches, one that is impartial and unprejudiced. To this very hour, all these miracles and strange events have hidden themselves from me; I have never seen a greater monster or miracle in the world than myself. One grows familiar with all strange things by time and habit; but the more I keep company with myself, and the better I know myself, the more my own deformity astonishes me, and the less I understand myself.

The principal right of producing such incidents is reserved for fortune. Passing the day before yesterday through a village two leagues from my house, I found the place still warm with a miracle that had recently failed there, with which the neighbourhood had first been amused for several months; then the surrounding provinces began to take it up and to flock there in great parties of all kinds of people. A young fellow of the place had one night, for sport, mimicked the voice of a spirit in his own house, without any other design at the time than fun; but it succeeded better than he expected. To extend his farce with more actors, he took on a stupid country girl, and at last there were three of them of the same age and understanding, who proceeded from domestic to public preaching, hiding under the altar of the church, never speaking except by night, and forbidding any light to be brought in. From words about the conversion of the world and threats of the Day of Judgment (these are subjects under whose authority and reverence imposture most safely shelters), they went on to visions and gestures so naive and ridiculous that hardly anything could be cruder in the games of little children. Yet if fortune had favoured the design even slightly, who knows how high this trickery might in the end have climbed? These poor devils are now in prison, and are likely soon to pay for the common folly; and I don't know whether some judge may not also make them pay for his. We can see clearly into this one because it has been uncovered; but in many similar things that exceed our knowledge, I think we ought to suspend our judgment, whether toward rejection or acceptance.

Great abuses in the world are bred — or, to speak more boldly, all the abuses of the world are bred — by our being taught to be afraid of professing our ignorance and by our being obliged to accept anything we cannot refute; we speak of everything by precepts and decisions. The style at Rome was that even what a witness deposed to having seen with his own eyes, and what a judge determined on his most certain knowledge, was framed in this form of speech: "it seems to me." They make me hate things that are probable, when they try to impose them on me as infallible. I love these words that soften and moderate the rashness of our claims: "perhaps; in some sense; some; it is said, I think," and the like. And if I had been put in charge of bringing up children, I would have put this way of answering into their mouths — inquiring, not pronouncing: "What does this mean? I don't understand it; perhaps; is it true?" — so that they would have kept the manner of pupils at sixty rather than coming out as doctors at ten, as they do. Whoever wants to be cured of ignorance must confess it.
Iris is the daughter of Thaumas;

["That is, of Admiration. She (Iris, the rainbow) is beautiful, and for that reason, because she has a face to be admired, she is said to be the daughter of Thaumas." --Cicero, De Nat. Deor., iii. 20.]

wonder is the foundation of all philosophy; inquiry is its progress; ignorance is its end. But there is a sort of ignorance, strong and generous, that yields nothing in honour and courage to knowledge — an ignorance which to conceive requires no less knowledge than to conceive knowledge itself. I read in my younger years a trial that Corras,
[A celebrated Calvinist lawyer, born at Toulouse, 1513, and assassinated there, 4th October 1572.]

a councillor of Toulouse, had printed, of a strange incident, of two men presenting themselves as one and the same. I remember (and I hardly remember anything else) that he had made the imposture of the man he judged guilty so extraordinary and so far beyond both our understanding and his own, who was the judge, that I thought the sentence condemning him to be hanged a very bold one. Let us have some form of verdict that says, "The court understands nothing of the matter," more freely and openly than the Areopagites did when, finding themselves baffled by a case they could not unravel, ordered the parties to appear again a hundred years later.

The witches of my neighbourhood are in danger of their lives at the report of every new author who tries to give body to their dreams. To take the examples Holy Scripture gives us of such things — most certain and indisputable examples — and tie them to our modern events, when we see neither the causes nor the means, requires a different sort of intellect than ours. It belongs perhaps only to that one all-powerful testimony to tell us, "This is, and that is, and not the other." God should be believed; and certainly with very good reason; but not one of us is for that reason to be astonished at his own narration — and he must necessarily be astonished if he is not out of his wits — whether he is using it about other men's affairs or against himself.
I am plain and heavy, and I stick to the solid and the probable, avoiding those ancient reproaches:
"Majorem fidem homines adhibent iis, quae non intelligunt; --Cupidine humani ingenii libentius obscura creduntur."
["Men give most credence to things they do not understand; and from the appetite of the human mind, obscure things are more readily believed." The second sentence is from Tacitus, Hist. 1. 22.]

I see very well that people get angry, and that I am forbidden to doubt on pain of monstrous insults; a novel way of persuading! Thank God, I am not to be slapped into belief. Let them be angry with those who accuse their opinion of being false; I only accuse it of difficulty and rashness, and I condemn the opposite affirmation just as much, though not so imperiously, as they do. He who tries to establish a proposition by authority and bluster shows that his reasoning is very weak. In a verbal and scholastic argument, let them have as much appearance of being right as their opponents;
"Videantur sane, non affirmentur modo;"
["Let them indeed appear to be so; let them not merely be asserted (Let them state the probabilities, but not affirm.)" --Cicero, Acad., ii. 27.]

but in the real consequences they draw from it, these have a great advantage. To kill men, a clear and strong light is required, and our life is too real and essential to vouch for these supernatural and fantastic accidents.

As for drugs and poisons, I leave them out of my reckoning, since they are the worst kind of homicides; yet even there it is said men cannot always rely on the personal confessions of these people, since they have sometimes been known to confess to the murder of persons later found alive and well. In these other outlandish accusations, I would say that it is enough that a man, with whatever credentials he may have, should be believed about human matters; but in what is beyond his understanding, and of supernatural effect, he ought to be believed only when authorised by a supernatural sanction. The privilege which it has pleased Almighty God to give to some of His witnesses ought not to be cheaply and lightly extended. My ears are battered with a thousand tales like these: "Three persons saw him on such a day in the east, three the next day in the west, at such an hour, in such a place, and in such clothes"; I would not believe it myself. How much more natural and likely I find it that two men should lie than that one man in twelve hours' time should fly with the wind from east to west? How much more natural that our understanding should be carried out of its place by the volatility of our disordered minds, than that one of us, flesh and bones as we are, should be carried by a strange spirit on a broomstick up a chimney? Let us not seek illusions from outside and from the unknown — we who are perpetually unsettled by illusions of our own. It seems to me a man may be excused for disbelieving a miracle, at least wherever one can sidestep its claim to be a miracle by non-miraculous means; and I am of St. Augustine's opinion, that "it is better to lean toward doubt than toward certainty in things hard to prove and dangerous to believe."

It is now some years ago that I travelled through the territories of a sovereign prince who, as a favour to me and to reduce my unbelief, did me the honour to let me see, in his own presence and in a private place, ten or twelve prisoners of this sort — and among them, an old woman, a real witch in foulness and deformity, who had long been famous in that profession. I saw the proofs and free confessions, and I do not know what insensible mark on the wretched creature; I examined and talked with her and the rest as much and as long as I wanted, and gave the best and soundest attention I could, and I am not a man to let my judgment be made captive by preconception. In the end, in all conscience, I would sooner have prescribed them hellebore than hemlock;
"Captisque res magis mentibus, quam consceleratis similis visa;"
["The thing was more to be ascribed to madness than to malice." ("The thing seemed to resemble minds possessed rather than guilty.") --Livy, viii. 18.]

justice has its proper corrections for such illnesses. As for the objections and arguments worthy men have made to me, both there and often in other places, I have met none that have convinced me, and none that have not admitted a more likely solution than their conclusions. It is true that the proofs and reasons founded on experience and fact I do not try to untie, since they have no end; I often cut them, as Alexander did the Gordian knot. After all, it is paying a very high price for one's conjectures to have a man roasted alive on the strength of them.

We are told by several examples — Praestantius's father, for one — that, being more deeply asleep than men usually are, he fancied himself to be a mare and that he served the soldiers as a packhorse; and what he fancied himself to be, he actually became. If sorcerers really dream so materially, if dreams can sometimes so embody themselves in effects, still I cannot believe that our will should on that account answer to justice. I say this as one who is neither judge nor privy councillor, and who thinks himself, by many degrees, unworthy to be either — but as one of the common sort, born and pledged to obey public reason in both its words and its acts. Anyone who recorded my idle talk as something prejudicial to the smallest law, opinion, or custom of his parish would do himself a great deal of harm, and me much more; for in what I say, I guarantee no other certainty than that this is what I had in my mind at the time — a tumultuous and wavering thought. All I say is by way of discussion, and nothing by way of advice:
"Nec me pudet, ut istos fateri nescire, quod nesciam;"
["Nor am I ashamed, as they are, to confess that I do not know what I do not know."--Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 25.]

I would not speak so boldly if it were my right to be believed; and so I told a great man who complained of the sharpness and contentiousness of my exhortations. Seeing you ready and prepared on one side, I propose the other to you, with all the diligence and care I can, to clarify your judgment, not to compel it. God has your hearts in His hand and will furnish you with the means of choice. I am not so presumptuous as even to wish that my opinions should sway you in a thing of such importance; my fortune has not trained them up to such powerful and lofty conclusions. Truly, I have not only a great many quirks but also a great many opinions that I would try to make my son dislike, if I had one. What if the truest are not always the most convenient for man, given how wild a composition we are?

Whether it fits or not, it doesn't much matter — there is a common proverb in Italy that he does not know Venus in her perfect sweetness who has never lain with a lame mistress. Fortune, or some particular incident, long ago put this saying into people's mouths; and the same is said of men as well as of women — for the Queen of the Amazons answered the Scythian who courted her: "Lame men perform best." In this feminine republic, to evade the dominion of the males, they crippled them in infancy — arms, legs, and the other limbs that gave them the advantage — and only made use of them for the one thing that we in these parts of the world also use them for. I would have been inclined to think that the shuffling gait of a lame mistress added some new pleasure to the work and some extra titillation for those at the sport; but I have lately learned that ancient philosophy itself has decided the question, saying that, because the legs and thighs of lame women do not receive their proper nourishment (owing to their defect), it follows that the genital parts above are fuller and better supplied and much more vigorous; or else that this defect, hindering exercise, leaves those who suffer it less worn down by activity, so that they come more intact to the sports of Venus — which is also why the Greeks decried women weavers as being hotter than other women, because of their sedentary trade, carried on without much exercise of the body. What is there we cannot reason about at this rate? I might also say of these weavers that the rocking back and forth at their work rouses and provokes their desire, as the swaying and jolting of carriages does that of our ladies.

Don't these examples bear out what I said at the start: that our reasoning often runs ahead of the effect, and has so endless a range of jurisdiction that it judges and exercises itself even on emptiness and non-existence? Besides our talent for fabricating reasons for all sorts of dreams, our imagination is equally ready to take impressions of falsity from the most trivial appearances; for, on the sole authority of this ancient and common proverb, I formerly made myself believe that I had taken more pleasure in a woman because she was not straight, and put that deformity down as one of her graces.

Torquato Tasso, in his comparison between France and Italy, says he has observed that our legs are generally smaller than those of Italian gentlemen, and attributes the cause to our being continually on horseback; which is the very same cause from which Suetonius draws the opposite conclusion, for he says on the contrary that Germanicus enlarged his legs by the continuation of the same exercise.

Nothing is so pliable and erratic as our understanding; it is the shoe of Theramenes, which fits any foot. It is double and various, and the matters it deals with are double and various too. "Give me a drachma of silver," said a Cynic philosopher to Antigonus. "That is not a present befitting a king," he replied. "Give me then a talent," said the other. "That is not a present befitting a Cynic."

"Seu plures calor ille vias et caeca relaxat Spiramenta, novas veniat qua succus in herbas; Seu durat magis, et venas astringit hiantes; Ne tenues pluviae, rapidive potentia solis Acrior, aut Boreae penetrabile frigus adurat."

["Whether the heat opens up more passages and hidden pores through which the sap can pass into the new-growing herbs; or whether instead it hardens and binds the gaping veins, so that the thin rains and the keener force of the violent sun, or the penetrating cold of Boreas, may not damage them."--Virg., Georg., i. 89.]
"Ogni medaglia ha il suo rovescio."
["Every medal has its reverse."--Italian Proverb.]

This is why Clitomachus said long ago that Carneades had outdone the labours of Hercules in having eradicated consent from men — that is to say, opinion and the courage to judge. This so vigorous fancy of Carneades sprang, in my opinion, originally from the impudence of those who claimed to know everything and their boundless self-conceit. Aesop was put up for sale with two other slaves; the buyer asked the first what he could do, and he, to raise his price, promised mountains and marvels — saying he could do this and that and I don't know what; the second said as much of himself or more; when it came to Aesop's turn and he too was asked what he could do, he said, "Nothing, for these two have taken up everything before me; they know it all." The same has happened in the schools of philosophy: the arrogance of those who claimed the capacity of all things for the human mind created in others, out of spite and rivalry, the opposite opinion that it is capable of nothing; the one party holding the same extreme in ignorance that the others hold in knowledge — to make it manifestly undeniable that man is immoderate throughout, and can never stop except of necessity and from being unable to go any further.

chapters.title: Of physiognomy
paragraphs: Almost all the opinions we hold are taken on authority and trust — and that's not entirely a bad thing; in so weak an age, we could hardly choose worse than by relying on ourselves. The image of Socrates' conversations that his friends have handed down to us, we approve of only out of reverence for public sanction; we don't approve it from our own knowledge. His discourses are not in our style; if anything of the kind sprang up today, few people would value it. We can't recognise any grace that isn't sharpened, puffed out, and inflated by art; whatever glides past in its own purity and simplicity easily escapes a sight as coarse as ours. Such grace has a delicate, hidden beauty that requires a clear and purified vision to discover its secret light. Isn't simplicity, the way we use the word, close kin to foolishness, a quality fit for reproach? Socrates makes his soul move in a natural, ordinary motion. A peasant said this; a woman said that; he has nobody in his mouth but carters, joiners, cobblers, and masons. His arguments and analogies are drawn from the most common, familiar human activities; everyone understands him. We would never have recognised the nobility and splendour of his admirable thoughts under so plain a form — we, who think everything low and flat that isn't lifted up by learned doctrine, and who see no riches except in pomp and display. This world of ours is built only for show: men are puffed up with wind and batted back and forth like tennis balls. He set himself no vain, idle fancies; his aim was to give us precepts and things that genuinely and fitly serve the use of life;
"Servare modum, finemque tenere, Naturamque sequi."
["To keep a just mean, to observe a just limit, and to follow Nature." — Lucan, ii. 381.]

He was also always one and the same, and raised himself, not in bursts but by temperament, to the highest pitch of vigour — or better put, he didn't climb up at all but rather brought down, reduced, and subjected all hardships and difficulties to his original, natural state. In Cato, by contrast, it's perfectly obvious that the procedure goes far beyond the ordinary way of men: in the brave exploits of his life, and in his death, we always find him mounted on the great horse. Socrates, meanwhile, walks always on the ground, and with a gentle, ordinary pace handles the most useful matters; both at his death and in the harshest difficulties that could arise, he carries himself in the common manner of human life.

It has worked out well that the man most worthy to be known and held up as an example for the world should be the one we know most certainly about. He has been examined by the most clear-sighted men who ever lived; the testimonies we have of him are admirable both in their accuracy and their fullness. It's a great thing that he was able to order the pure imaginations of a child so that, without altering or twisting them, he produced from them the most beautiful effects of our soul. He shows the soul as neither elevated nor rich; he simply represents it as sound — but certainly with a brisk, robust health. By these common, natural springs, by these ordinary, popular thoughts, without being shaken or thrown off, he set up not only the most disciplined but the most lofty and vigorous beliefs, actions, and manners that ever existed. He's the one who brought human wisdom back down from heaven, where she was wasting her time, to restore her to man — with whom her most fitting and important business lies. Watch him plead before his judges; observe by what reasoning he rouses his courage to face the hazards of war; with what arguments he fortifies his patience against slander, tyranny, death, and his wife's bad temper. You'll find nothing in all this borrowed from arts and sciences; the simplest person can find his own means and strength in it. It's not possible to be more unassuming or to walk more low. He did human nature a great kindness by showing it how much it can do of itself.

We're all richer than we think we are, but we're taught to borrow and to beg, and brought up to make more use of what belongs to others than of what's our own. In nothing can man fix himself to his actual need: of pleasure, wealth, and power he grabs at more than he can hold; his greed is incapable of moderation. And I find that he's the same in his appetite for knowledge: he cuts out more work for himself than he can do, and more than he needs to do, stretching the usefulness of knowledge to the limits of its subject matter:
"Ut omnium rerum, sic litterarum quoque, intemperantia laboramus."
["We carry intemperance into the study of literature, as we do into everything else." — Seneca, Ep., 106.]
And Tacitus was right to praise Agricola's mother for having restrained her son in his too-violent appetite for learning.

It's a good, if you think about it properly, that has in it — like our other goods — a great deal of vanity and weakness proper and natural to itself, and that costs a lot. Acquiring it is far more hazardous than acquiring any other food or drink. With other things, what we've bought we carry home in some container, and there we have full leisure to examine our purchase — how much we'll eat or drink of it, and when. But sciences we can stow only in the soul from the very first; we swallow them in buying, and come back from the market already either infected or improved. Some only burden and overload the stomach instead of nourishing it; and some, under the pretext of curing, actually poison us. I've been pleased, in places I've travelled, to see men in their devotion take a vow of ignorance alongside vows of chastity, poverty, and penitence. It's also a kind of gelding of our unruly appetites to blunt this craving that drives us to study books, and to deprive the soul of that voluptuous self-satisfaction that tickles us with the opinion of knowledge; and it fully completes the vow of poverty to add to it that of the mind. We need little doctrine to live at ease. Socrates teaches us that this is already in us — and the way to find it, and the manner of using it. All our capacity that goes beyond the natural is pretty much superfluous and vain; it's a lot if it doesn't burden and clutter us rather than help us:
"Paucis opus est literis ad mentem bonam:"
["Little learning is needed to form a sound mind." — Seneca, Ep., 106.]

It's a feverish excess of the mind, a stormy and restless instrument. Just collect yourself, and you'll find within yourself natural arguments against death — true ones, the fittest to serve you when you need them. They're the arguments that make a peasant, and whole nations, die with as much firmness as a philosopher. Would I have died less cheerfully before I'd read Cicero's Tusculan Disputations? I don't believe so; and even when I find myself at my best, I notice that my tongue is enriched but my courage hardly elevated by them. My courage is just what nature framed at the outset, and it defends itself against the struggle only in a natural, ordinary way. Books have served me less for instruction than for exercise. What if knowledge, in trying to arm us with new defences against natural troubles, has only impressed their weight and greatness more deeply on our imagination, rather than securing us with her reasons and subtleties? They're subtleties, indeed, with which she often alarms us to little purpose. Just notice how many slight, frivolous, and — when examined closely — incorporeal arguments the closest, wisest authors scatter around one good one. They're verbal tricks and fallacies to amuse and fool us; but since they may have some profit, I won't sift them further. Many of that sort are scattered up and down this book, either borrowed or by imitation. So one ought to be a little careful not to call something forceful when it's only a clever turn of writing, not to call something solid when it's only sharp, not to call something good when it's only fine:
"Quae magis gustata quam potata, delectant,"
["Which more delight in the tasting than in being drunk." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 5.]
everything that pleases doesn't nourish:
"Ubi non ingenii, sed animi negotium agitur."
["Where the question is not about the wit, but about the soul." — Seneca, Ep., 75.]

To see the trouble Seneca takes to brace himself against death — to see him sweat and pant so to harden and encourage himself, and bustle so long on this perch — would have lessened his reputation in my eyes, if he hadn't held himself very bravely at the end. His so ardent and frequent agitations show that he was, in himself, impetuous and passionate.
"Magnus animus remissius loquitur, et securius . . . non est alius ingenio, alius animo color;"
["A great courage speaks more calmly and more securely. There is not one complexion for the wit and another for the mind." — Seneca, Ep. 114, 115.]

He has to convince himself at his own expense, and he reveals in a way that he was hard pressed by his enemy. Plutarch's manner, in being more disdainful and more sustained, is in my opinion that much more manly and persuasive; and I'm inclined to believe his soul had more assured and more regular motions. The one — Seneca — is sharper, pricks us and makes us flinch, and touches the soul more; the other is more steadily solid, forms, establishes, and supports us, and touches the understanding more. Seneca carries away the judgment, Plutarch wins it. I've likewise seen other writings, more revered still than these, that in describing the struggle they maintain against the temptations of the flesh paint those temptations so sharp, so powerful, so invincible, that we who are of the common herd are as much astonished at the strangeness and unknown force of their temptation as at their resisting it.

To what end do we so arm ourselves with this harness of science? Let's look down at the poor people we see scattered across the face of the earth, head down and intent on their work, who know neither Aristotle nor Cato, neither example nor precept. From these, nature every day extracts effects of constancy and patience purer and more manly than the ones we so inquisitively study in the schools. How many do I see, regularly, who shrug off poverty? How many who long to die, or who die without alarm or regret? The man who is now digging in my garden has this morning buried his father or his son. The very names by which they call their diseases sweeten and soften the harshness of them: tuberculosis is just a cough to them, dysentery just a looseness, pleurisy just a stitch. And as gently as they name them, so patiently do they endure them; the diseases are really great and grievous only when they interrupt their ordinary work. They never take to their beds except to die:
"Simplex illa et aperta virtus in obscuram et solertem scientiam versa est."
["That overt and simple virtue is converted into an obscure and subtle science." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]

I was writing this around the time when a great burden of our domestic troubles lay with all its weight on me for several months. I had the enemy at my door on one side, and the freebooters — worse enemies — on the other,
"Non armis, sed vitiis, certatur;"
["The fight is not with arms, but with vices." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]
and I was suffering every kind of military injury at once:
"Hostis adest dextra laevaque a parte timendus. Vicinoque malo terret utrumque latus."
["Right and left a formidable enemy is to be feared, and threatens me on both sides with impending danger." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 3, 57.]

A monstrous war! Other wars are aimed at strangers; this one is aimed at itself, destroying itself with its own poison. It's of such a malignant and ruinous nature that it ruins itself along with everything else, and in its own rage mangles and tears itself to pieces. We more often see it dissolve of itself than collapse from scarcity of supplies or the force of the enemy. All discipline evades it. It comes to put down sedition and is itself full of sedition; it would chastise disobedience and is itself the example; employed to defend the laws, it rebels against its own. What a condition we're in! Our medicine makes us sick!
"Nostre mal s'empoisonne Du secours qu'on luy donne."
"Exuperat magis, aegrescitque medendo."
["Our disease is poisoned with its very remedies." — Aeneid, xii. 46.]
"Omnia fanda, nefanda, malo permista furore, Justificam nobis mentem avertere deorum."
["Right and wrong, all shuffled together in this wicked fury, have deprived us of the gods' protection." — Catullus, De Nuptiis Pelei et Thetidos, V. 405.]

At the beginning of these popular sicknesses, you can still distinguish the healthy from the sick; but when they go on, as ours have done, the whole body is infected from head to foot. No part is free from corruption — for there's no air men so greedily breathe in, none that diffuses itself so quickly and penetrates so deep, as the air of licence. Our armies subsist and hold together only by the cement of foreigners; we can no longer raise a steady, regular army out of Frenchmen. What a shame! There's no discipline left except what we see in the mercenary soldiers. As for us, our conduct is left to anyone's discretion — and not to that of the chief, but to each man's own. The general has a harder game to play within his own army than against the enemy outside. He's the one who has to follow, to court his soldiers, to give way to them; he alone has to obey: all the rest is dissolution and unbridled licence. It pleases me to notice how much cowardice and timidity there is in ambition, by what abject, servile paths it has to reach its end; but it displeases me to see good and generous natures, capable of justice, being daily corrupted in the management and command of this chaos. Long toleration breeds habit; habit, consent and imitation. We had enough ill-formed souls already, without spoiling those that were generous and good — so that if we go on like this, there'll be scarcely anyone left we could entrust with the health of this State of ours, in case fortune should happen to restore it:
"Hunc saltem everso juvenem succurrere seclo, Ne prohibete."
["Forbid not, at least, that this young man repair this ruined age." — Virgil, Georg., i. 500. Montaigne probably refers to Henry, king of Navarre, afterwards Henry IV.]

What has become of the old precept, "That soldiers should fear their chief more than the enemy"? And of that wonderful example where an orchard enclosed within the perimeter of a Roman camp was seen the day after they broke camp in the same condition — not an apple, however ripe and delicious, pulled off, but every one left to its owner? I could wish our young men, instead of spending their time on less fruitful travels and less honourable pursuits, would devote half of it to being eyewitnesses of naval exploits under some good captain of Rhodes, and the other half to observing the discipline of the Turkish armies; for theirs has many differences from, and advantages over, ours. One difference is that our soldiers grow more dissolute on expeditions, theirs more temperate and circumspect. Thefts and insolences against the common people — which are only punished with a cudgel in peacetime — are capital offences in war. For an egg taken by a Turkish soldier without payment, the fixed rate is fifty blows with a stick; for anything else, of whatever kind, no matter how trivial, that isn't necessary for nourishment, they're immediately impaled or beheaded without mercy. I'm astonished, in the history of Selim — the most cruel conqueror who ever lived — to see that when he subdued Egypt, the beautiful gardens around Damascus, all open and in a conquered land, with his army encamped on the very spot, were left untouched by the soldiers' hands, because they hadn't received the signal to pillage.

But is there any disease in a government worth treating with such a deadly drug? No, said Favonius — not even the tyrannical usurpation of a commonwealth. Plato, likewise, will not allow that a man should violate the peace of his country in order to cure it, and by no means approves of a reformation that disturbs and endangers everything, and is to be purchased at the price of the citizens' blood and ruin. He holds that in such a case it's the duty of a good patriot to leave things alone and only pray to God for his extraordinary help; and he seems to be angry with his great friend Dion for having proceeded somewhat otherwise. I was a Platonist on this point before I knew there had ever been such a man as Plato. And if this person should be absolutely rejected from our society — he who by the sincerity of his conscience deserved divine favour so far that he penetrated deep into Christian light, through the universal darkness in which the world was enveloped in his time — then I don't think it becomes us to be instructed by a heathen on how great an impiety it is not to expect from God any relief that is simply his own, without our co-operation. I often wonder whether, among so many men who meddle in such affairs, there isn't some one of so weak an understanding that he's actually been persuaded he was moving toward reformation by the worst of deformations, and toward salvation by the very causes that most certainly damn us — namely, by overthrowing the government, the magistracy, and the laws, in whose protection God has placed him; by dismembering his good mother and giving her limbs to be mangled by her old enemies; by filling fraternal hearts with parricidal hatreds, calling up devils and furies to his aid; and by all this hoping to support the most holy sweetness and justice of the divine law. Ambition, avarice, cruelty, and revenge don't have natural impetuosity enough of their own; let's bait them with the glorious titles of justice and devotion. No worse state of things can be imagined than where wickedness comes to be legitimate and takes on, with the magistrates' permission, the cloak of virtue:
"Nihil in speciem fallacius, quam prava religio, ubi deorum numen praetenditur sceleribus."
["Nothing has a more deceiving face than false religion, where the divinity of the gods is obscured by crimes." — Livy, xxxix. 16.]
The extremest form of injustice, according to Plato, is when what is unjust is reputed to be just.
The common people then suffered very much — and not only present damage:
"Undique totis Usque adeo turbatur agris,"
["Such great disorders overtake our fields on every side." — Virgil, Eclog., i. 11.]

but future damage too. The living were to suffer, and so were those not yet born; they stripped them — and consequently myself — even of hope, taking from them everything they'd laid up to live on for many years:
"Quae nequeunt secum ferre aut abducere, perdunt; Et cremat insontes turba scelesta casas . . . Muris nulla fides, squalent populatibus agri."

["What they cannot bear away, they spoil; and the wicked mob burn harmless houses; walls cannot secure their masters, and the fields are squalid with devastation." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 10, 35; Claudianus, In Eutyop., i. 244.]

Besides this shock, I suffered others — the inconveniences that come with moderation in such a disease. I was robbed on every side: to the Ghibelline I was a Guelph, and to the Guelph a Ghibelline. One of my poets expresses this very well, but I forget where:
["So Tories called me Whig, and Whigs a Tory." — Pope, after Horace.]

The position of my house, and my friendliness with my neighbours, showed one face; my life and my actions showed another. They didn't bring formal accusations against me — they had no grounds. I never hide from the laws, and anyone who'd questioned me would have done himself more damage than me. It was only mute suspicions, whispered about, which never lack for appearance in so confused a mixture, any more than envious or idle minds do. I commonly lend a hand myself to the injurious presumptions that fortune scatters against me, through a habit I've always had of avoiding to justify, excuse, or explain myself — feeling it would compromise my conscience to plead in its own behalf:
"Perspicuitas enim argumentatione elevatur;"
["For perspicuity is lessened by argument." ("The clearness of a cause is clouded by argumentation.") — Cicero, De Nat. Deor., iii. 4.]

and, as if everyone saw into me as clearly as I do myself, instead of retreating from an accusation I step up to meet it, and rather give it some colour by an ironic and mocking confession — if I don't sit completely silent, as though the thing weren't worth answering. But those who take this manner of mine for too haughty a confidence have just as little affection for me as those who interpret it as the weakness of an indefensible case — namely, the great folks, toward whom lack of submission is the great fault, harsh toward any justice that knows and feels itself, and isn't submissive, humble, and suppliant.
